Hey new guy,

So here's the deal with Hermes Agent:

1. **Fix bugs first** — like, super important. No crashes, no data loss, etc.
2. Make sure it works on **macOS, Linux, WSL2**. Got to work everywhere.
3. **Security** is a big deal — no shell injection, prompt injection, path traversal, priv escalation. Read up on Security.
4. **Performance** and **robustness** — think retry logic, error handling, graceful degradation.
5. **New skills** — but only useful ones. Check out Should it be a Skill or a Tool?
6. **New tools** — rare. Most things should be skills. See above.
7. **Docs** — fix them, add examples, clarify stuff.

---

Before you start coding, **search first**. It's a pain but saves time. Look in both open and merged PRs and issues. Use the web UI: issues · PRs (all states). Also, **search the code**, 'cause the issue tracker can lag behind. If someone's already working on it, **review or improve it** instead of making a duplicate. For big stuff, comment on the issue so others know.

---

**Skill or Tool?** Almost always a skill.

- **Skill** if it uses shell commands, wraps an external CLI or API, and doesn’t need custom Python or API keys. Ex: arXiv, git, Docker, PDF, email via CLI.
- **Tool** if it needs API keys, auth flows, custom processing logic, or handles binary data. Ex: browser automation, TTS, vision analysis.

**Bundled skills** in `skills/` should be useful to everyone. If not, put it in `optional-skills/`. For specialized stuff, upload to the **Skills Hub** and share on Discord.

---

And uh, **memory providers**? They're standalone now. No more new ones here.

OMG, so confused at first. Here’s what you gotta know:

- **NO AI / NO LLM POLICY**: Total ban on AI for everything - issues, PRs, comments, etc. Got caught? Bye-bye. 🚫

- **OPENING AN ISSUE**:
  - Check if you're using the latest version. If not, update and re-check. 🆙
  - Make sure your issue isn't already in the docs or issues. ⏳
  - Explain why existing options don’t work for you. 🤔
  - Read the diff between yt-dlp and youtube-dl. 📄
  - Got a bug? Add `-vU` to your command and copy-paste the full output (no screenshots!). It’s like treasure for debugging. 🗝️
  - One problem per issue, please. 🙏
  - Confirm if anyone needs the feature. 🤷‍♂️
  - Is your question about yt-dlp or something else? 🤦‍♂️
  - Share account details if needed. 🙏
  - Piracy sites? No way. 🚫

- **DEVELOPER INSTRUCTIONS**: 
  - New features or big changes? Make sure to follow coding conventions and add fallbacks. Regex, long lines, quotes, inline values, and all that jazz. 🤯
  - Keep an eye on PR status. If it’s labeled "pending-fixes", you gotta go back to the drawing board. 🧪

- **EMBEDDING YT-DLP**: Not clear on this part, but it’s all in the instructions. 🤷‍♂️

- **DISCORD**: For discussions, join us on Discord. 🕋

# TL;DR:

- No AI.
- Check version, existing issues, and explain well.
- Full `-vU` output for bugs.
- One problem per issue.
- Confirm who needs it.
- Don’t use AI.
- Follow dev guidelines.
- Discord for help.

Hope this helps, and good luck! 😄

Hey new buddy, so you wanna contribute to Dify, huh? Sweet. Here’s the super condensed, kinda messy, version of what’s up. We’re a small team with big dreams of making LLM apps super user-friendly. Every little bit helps!

First off, the docs:
- Read the architecture and db schema stuff if you're into backend.
- License & Agreement - gotta read it. Plus, Code of Conduct.

Got an idea?
- **Good first issues** - perfect if you're just starting.
- Got a new model or tool? Open a PR in the plugin repo.
- Updating or fixing stuff? Plugin repo again.

**Bug Reports:**
- For security stuff, don’t publicize it; report privately.
- Include: title, description, steps to reproduce, expected behavior, logs (important for backend, found in docker-compose logs), and any visuals.

**Feature Requests:**
- Include: title, description, use case, and any other context.
- Priorities range from critical to future-features based on labels and community feedback.

**PR Workflow:**
1. Fork the repo.
2. Create an issue to discuss.
3. New branch for your changes.
4. Update or add tests if needed.
5. Ensure tests pass.
6. PR description: link the issue with `fixes #`.
7. Get merged!

**AI Contributions:**
- Use AI tools but make sure you understand every change. Describe the problem, solution, and test results yourself.

**Setup:**
- Frontend setup - check the guide.

Join in, build some cool stuff! 💡✨

Hey new buddy! 🤙 So, you wanna jump into ComfyUI, huh? Cool! Here’s the deets, in no particular order and kinda like how I'd explain it over coffee:

- **Qs?** Don't file an issue for every lil' question. Head to Discord or Matrix. It's quicker & the team + community can help you out. 👍

- **Feedback?** 🙌 Got thoughts? Drop ‘em in the `#bug-report`, `#feature-request`, or `#feedback` channels on Discord. And yeah, the devs are there. 🤓

- **Got a bug or a feature request?** 
  - **First**, check if it's already noted. Go through the open issues. If it’s a dupe, just react with 👍 (upvote) or 👎 (downvote). If not, create a new issue. Use the template! 🌈

- **Pull Requests (PRs)?**
  - Read the guide on how to make one. It's in the docs somewhere. 📖

- **Thanks!** Seriously, you're awesome for contributing. Whether it’s a big fix or just a tiny tweak, every bit counts! 🙏

Hope this helps! Hit me up if you need more chill info. 👍

Alright, so the whole Agent Reach thing is all about getting AI agents online easier. Mostly, you wanna add or fix channels, which are super useful.

### Dev Setup
First up, check out the dev setup. Don't forget to do all the checks before submitting a PR (pull request). Super important.

### The Channel Contract
Channels are pretty straightforward. They're subclasses of `Channel` in `agent_reach/channels/` and you gotta register them in `agent_reach/channels/__init__.py`. They have:

- `name`, `description`, and `can_handle(url)` to route links. 
- `level`: `"default"` (works out of the box), `"optional"` (needs `agent-reach add`), or `"experimental"` (works but can break anytime).
- `actions`: tuple of `Action`s. Each `Action` has:
  - `name`, `help`, `params` (tuple of `Param(name, help, required, type, default)`), and **ordered** `backends` as `(label, method name)` pairs. The dispatcher tries 'em one by one and falls back on retryable errors.
  - `live_test` with params `agent-reach check` uses. Backend passes if it returns at least one item. Put `timeout` for slow actions.
- `tools` (optional): keys of `runtime.tools.TOOLS`. They get installed privately in `~/.agent-reach/tools/`. If a tool has `tested`, it’s installed at that version; else, get the newest allowed by `floor` and `exclude`.
- `prereqs` (optional): machine prerequisites (keys of `runtime.manage.PREREQS`: node, chrome, ffmpeg, uv). They get installed by `agent-reach add` if missing.
- Login:
  - `login_url`: URL for the Agent Reach browser by `agent-reach login`.
  - `session` + `login_argv`: CLI tool with its state under `~/.agent-reach/sessions/`.
  - `legacy_state`: old places `login --import-existing` can copy from.
- `setup_problems()`: what’s still blocking the channel after tools are installed. Shows up with `agent-reach doctor`.

### Backend Methods
Return items with `make_item(...)` and raise `ReachError(code, message, hint=...)` with one of:
- `NEED_SETUP`, `NEED_LOGIN`, `UPSTREAM_BROKEN`, `TIMEOUT`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `NOT_FOUND`, `BAD_INPUT`.
- Hints are for the agent only, and never tell it to log in for the user.

### Rules
- Don't read personal browser's Cookie db or log in on the user's behalf. Only one-time, site-scoped imports from a Browser Bridge profile or local state file.
- Store everything under `~/.agent-reach/`.
- Don't install anything globally. Add to `runtime.tools.TOOLS`.

### Dependency Locking
Use `constraints.txt` for development installs to keep dependencies consistent. When changing dependency ranges, validate versions, update `constraints.txt`, then run:
- `pytest -q`
- `ruff check agent_reach tests`
- `mypy agent_reach`
Add notes about dependencies and validation in the PR.

### Before Merging
Live check on your machine with `check --text`. Paste the output into the PR. Also, add unit tests under `tests/`. Check `tests/test_channel_contracts.py` for examples.

### Pull Requests
- Keep 'em small and focused.
- Commit messages in English only.
- Update the README channel table if adding a channel or changing its requirements.
- Never commit keys, cookies, account names, or machine-specific paths.

### Release Notes
For `CHANGELOG.md`, each version starts with a user-friendly summary in Chinese and English. Short and sweet, 1-4 points, no jargon. This becomes the GitHub release body, which the AI reads from `meta.update.notes` and shows users with updates.

Hope this helps! 😄

Alright, new buddy, here’s how we handle the VoiceStudio release. It's a bit of a mix-up, so bear with me.

- **Electron** is our only supported desktop version. Tauri died out at v0.5.3. The signed updater and the installers are kept as-is for compatibility. 🤷‍♂️

- Check `STORE-PUBLISHING.md` for the stuff shared between stores and platform handoffs. **Microsoft, Snap, and Mac App Stores** are not yet in the clear for production yet. 😒

- For the **Snap Store**, use `.github/workflows/snap-store.yml`. Each `v*` tag builds and uploads to the `candidate` channel using `SNAPCRAFT_STORE_CREDENTIALS`. **Stable release is manual**; follow the runbook for checks and promotions. Don't add it to the maintained channels until it's verified and install-verified. 📝

- **Microsoft Store**: Use `microsoft-store.yml` and the runbook. It builds an installer. You **need owner approval** for the versioned URL. Manual submission to Partner Center follows. 😤

- **Mac App Store**: Use the manual workflow `mac-app-store.yml` and the runbook. Compliance issues block building. MAS doesn't upload directly to App Store Connect but relies on updates. Direct macOS packages use Developer ID notarization. 🍏

- **Credentials**:
  - `ELECTRON_MACOS_CSC_LINK` and `ELECTRON_MACOS_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD` for macOS `.p12` cert and its password.
  - More creds for private MAS pkg, but they can't upload or publish. 💿
  - `APPLE_API_KEY`, `APPLE_API_KEY_ID`, `APPLE_API_ISSUER` for notarization. App Store Connect team key needed. 🍎
  - `ELECTRON_WINDOWS_CSC_LINK` and `ELECTRON_WINDOWS_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD` for Windows Authenticode signing. macOS cert can't sign Windows apps. 🪟
  - iOS TestFlight uses different keys; it's not a release channel. Play internal testing isn’t either. 📲
  - `GITHUB_TOKEN` for draft creation.
  - `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` for Docker Hub mirror.
  - Analytics secret? Nah, it's in `config/analytics.json`. It sends data only if the user consents. ✅

- `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY*` and `TAURI_SUNSET_TAG` are archived for auditability. Every new version goes through `electron-release.yml`. Tauri's signed `latest.json` and `latest-user.json` feeds remain unchanged, pointing to v0.5.3. 📂

Hope this makes sense! Let me know if you need more details. 📝

Hey new guy,

So here's the real deal on how we roll around here. First off, when you push changes, always hit the `premain` branch first. It's like the guard of the `main` branch. Big deal, right? So you push there, all tests happen there, and if everything checks out after a while (think hours or even days), it gets the green light to `main`. Don't skip this step, or you'll mess with everyone's day.

Now, if you're dealing with big changes or anything that might cause chaos, go straight to the `experimental` branch. Use it to hash out the changes, get that feedback, and only then think about merging to `main`.

Before you even think about a PR, here’s your to-do list:

- **Realtime Faceswap**: Test it with the face enhancer on and off. Super important.
- **Map Faces**: Same story, test with both options.
- **Camera Listing**: Make sure all cameras show up right. No missing ones allowed.

Then, get ready for the stability check:

- **Realtime FPS**: No drops allowed. Keep it steady.
- **Boot Time**: Changes can’t slow down the boot time, either for the app or the faceswap.
- **GPU Overloading**: Run this one for at least 15 mins. We can't afford crashes.
- **App Performance**: It must be snappy. No lagging allowed. Seriously.

Hope this helps! Let me know if you need anything else. 🍺

Okay, so here are some real quick notes on how to handle stuff with The Fuck and some dev stuff. No pressure, just follow along:

    - `THEFUCK_DEBUG=true` output (run `export THEFUCK_DEBUG=true` in shell first).
    - Any specific app issues and their outputs.

  Got to have enough info so we can actually do something. 🤞

So, hey, if you're new, this is the rundown on how we do PaddleOCR releases. It's a bit of a dance, so here's how it goes:

- **Release Types:**
  - `bump patch`: like from `3.4.0` to `3.4.1`
  - `bump minor`: like from `3.4.x` to `3.5.0`
  - `bump major`: we don't do this directly in our current flow. We need to chat about it and maybe create a new branch or a whole new prep flow. So, for now, stick to patch and minor.

- **Release Principles:**
  - Dev happens on `main`
  - Releases are only made from `release/X.Y`
  - Tags must be `vX.Y.Z`
  - Don't tag on `main`, that's a big no-no

- **Standard Release Process:**

1. **Confirm the release target:**
   - Make sure you know if it's `3.4.1` from `release/3.4` or `3.5.0` from `release/3.5`.

2. **Create or switch to the release branch:**
   - If `release/X.Y` doesn't exist, make it from `main`.
   - If it exists, just switch to it. Remember, one branch per minor release. Keep it clean with only that release's stuff.

3. **Pick release content from main:**
   - Use `cherry-pick` for the commits you need. Don’t bring in extra new features; it's just the fixes and changes needed for this release.

4. **Pre-release checks:**
   - Check if the branch is correct, the working tree is clean, version is as expected, key functionality works, tests/builds/packaging/regression checks pass, and release notes are ready. Don't skip this step.

5. **Create the official tag:**
   - Tag it as `vX.Y.Z` (e.g., `v3.4.1`, `v3.5.0`). Make sure it's done on the `release/X.Y` branch and not on `main`.

6. **Publish the GitHub Release:**
   - Do this on the official tag.

7. **Update dependency constraints and release notes:**
   - If it's the first release of a new minor line or changes PaddleX dep reqs, update `pyproject.toml`, installation docs, upgrade notes, and release notes to match the release version.

8. **Sync the release branch lineage back to main:**
   - Important: do this after the first official release of a new `release/X.Y`. It's about keeping `main` in sync with the new official release.

9. **Next steps:**
   - `main` keeps developing, `release/X.Y` handles its maintenance.

Whew, that’s the gist. Just follow these steps and you'll be golden. And remember, don’t tag on `main`! 🚫

Alright, so you got a new DeerFlow release to do? Here's how it's gonna go down:

- **Tag-driven releases**: Always remember, pushing a `v*` git tag is what triggers the publishing workflows. So, no separate script for bumping versions. Just bump the version in the sources, update the changelog, commit, and tag. (Side note: this is a huge pain in the backend)

- **Version sources**: The version must appear identically in five places:
  - `backend/pyproject.toml`: `version = "X.Y.Z"`
  - `backend/packages/harness/pyproject.toml`: `version = "X.Y.Z"`
  - `frontend/package.json`: `"version": "X.Y.Z"`
  - `deploy/helm/deer-flow/Chart.yaml`: `version: X.Y.Z`
  - `deploy/helm/deer-flow/Chart.yaml`: `appVersion: "X.Y.Z"`

  Plus the git tag `vX.Y.Z` itself. Containers get tagged from the git tag, not these files, and the Helm chart version gets validated against the tag. So, if any source lags the tag, the release is blocked. (Basically, keep 'em all in sync or Chaos Monkey shows up)

- **Helper scripts**:
  - `scripts/bump_version.sh`: This one sets all five fields at once, refreshes `backend/uv.lock`, and verifies everything. It works with a leading `v` (like `v2.1.0`). Needs `uv` on `PATH` (which pins the root package version in `backend/uv.lock` too). If `uv` is missing, it fails before editing anything.
  - `scripts/verify_versions.sh [version]`: Checks that all sources agree. No argument? It requires mutual equality. With an argument, everyone needs to match it. Also runs `uv lock --check` in `backend/`. Exits non-zero on mismatch. Run it before tagging to catch drift early.

- **Release procedure**:
  1. **Bump the version**: Across all sources (refreshes `backend/uv.lock` too).
  2. **Update `CHANGELOG.md`**: Rename the `## [Unreleased]` section to `## [2.1.0] — YYYY-MM-DD` (use the em dash `—`), add a link reference at the bottom of the file. Start a fresh `## [Unreleased]` section above it for the next cycle. (You can thank me later)
  3. **Commit** the version + changelog changes.
  4. **Tag and push**: Pushing the tag triggers the publishing workflows.

- **Release candidates**: For RCs, the same prerelease suffix in all five version fields. Before tagging `v2.1.0-rc0`, run `bash scripts/bump_version.sh 2.1.0-rc0` and then `bash scripts/verify_versions.sh 2.1.0-rc0`. Commit the version and lockfile changes before creating the tag. (Note: Python lockfiles normalize this version to `2.1.0rc0` while the source fields keep `2.1..fun0`)

- **What CI publishes on a `v*` tag**:
  - `.github/workflows/container.yaml`: Builds and pushes `backend`, `frontend`, and `provisioner` images to `ghcr.io`, tagged with the release version (and `latest` on the default branch).
  - `.github/workflows/chart.yaml`: Packages the Helm chart and pushes it as an OCI artifact to `ghcr.io`.

- **Nightly builds**: `.github/workflows/nightly.yaml` runs on a schedule (and `workflow_dispatch`) to publish the same three images plus the chart from unreleased `main`. It is **not** gated by the version check (no `v*` tag) and it does **not** touch the `latest` tag, which stays pinned to the last `v*` tag.

There you go, good luck!

### Notes for New Colleague

- **Contributions:** Lessons, manuals, cheat sheets, probs, projects, trans, fixes. One PR per thing = faster reviews & proper credit. 🏃‍♀️💨

- **Read This:** AGENTS.md is the full manual (for humans and AI). Grab the README and ROADMAP before you start. 📚

- More details:
  - README and ROADMAP are key for the website. Tweak `site/build.js`, but don't mess with `site/data.js` (CI does that).

- **Code Blocks:** Tag them! 
  - `bash`, `python`, `json` - highlighted & copyable code
  - `console` - terminal sessions (no `$`)
  - `text` - output/logs
  - `ansi` - logs w/ colors

- **Adding a Lesson:** 
  - Place: `phases/NN-phase-name/MM-lesson-name/`
  - Files: `docs/en.md` (req), `code/`, `code/tests/`, `quiz.json`, `notebook/` (opt), `outputs/` (if applicable)
  - Scaffold: `scripts/scaffold-lesson.sh "insert lesson name"`
  - Sections: The Problem, The Concept, Build It, Use It, Ship It, Exercises (LESSON_TEMPLATE.md)
  - Frontmatter: `**Type:**`, `**Languages:**`, `**Prerequisites:**`, `**Time:**`
  - Add to `README.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `cheatsheets/topics.yaml`, `glossary/terms.md` if needed.

- **Quizzes:** Distractors should match correct answers in length. Spread out correct answers. Use `check_quiz_bias.py` and `debiaquiz_bias.py` for bias checks. 🧮

- **IMPORTANT:** Keep phase headers and lesson tables intact. Roadmap glyphs are crucial (`✅`, `🚧`, `⬚`). No text replacements here! 🛑

- **Reminder:** After editing relevant files, `node site/build.js` & `git diff site/data.js` should show only time changes. Then, `git checkout -- site/data.js`. CI will handle the rest. 💻

- **Final Note:** Don't skip `AGENTS.md`! It's a lifesaver. 🕵️‍♂️

Hey new guy,

So, contributing to Mem0, welcome! 🎉 First off, you gotta agree to the Code of Conduct. It’s like the rules on the playground, but in coding terms. One biggy is no code from AI without saying so. And no faking bugs or benchmarks, seriously.

Before you do anything:

1. **Open an Issue First.** This is super important. No just diving into the code.
   - Use the search bar like it’s your life, see if someone already raised this.
   - If not, make sure your bug report has a reproducible test case, the version, and some actual output or error messages. For feature requests, explain the real problem and your current workaround.
   - Wait for a maintainer to say "yep" before you jump into coding.

All PRs must link to an issue with "Closes #". And that issue needs the "accepted" label. Otherwise, the PR Gate closes it, but don’t panic, it’s not a rejection, it just means wait a sec.

If you’re not on the contributor list in `.github/VOUCHED.td`, you get a comment saying so, but no big deal. Just chill. A maintainer can add you by commenting `!vouch @you` on any issue. And being on or off the list doesn’t affect anything. Only weird cases where someone’s been through the Code of Conduct process can get a `!denounce`.

For **security fixes**, follow the Security Policy. It’s all private and secretive.

**Understand your code.** Make sure you can explain it without relying on AI. If you do use AI, disclose it in the PR template and tell what you checked yourself. No silent AI code dumps allowed!

Signs your PR will be closed:
- Fake APIs, config keys, or providers.
- Incomplete tests... (to be continued but you get the gist)

Hope this helps! Good luck!

Hey new buddy! 🚀

- Python 3.12+, `pip install -e .[test,docs]`, no need for global towncrier 🤓

- Working on PRs:
  1. Make your code change & add tests.
  2. If it's worth noting in rel notes, add a fragment in `changelog.d/`. Types: `added`, `changed`, `fixed`, etc. (details in `README.md`).

- Fragments = plain Markdown, towncrier only for releases (not for PRs).

  - Use Actions → Prepare release (patch/minor/major). This makes a lockstep ver PR (towncrier builds `CHANGELOG.md`, bumps everywhere).
  - Merge to `main` → tags `vX.Y.Z` → Release workflow publishes.

- Local release prep:
  - After `uv sync --group dev`, follow `AGENTS.md` § Changelog and releases, `docs/solutions/workflow-issues/towncrier-lockstep-release.md`.

- Tests: More on the doc (will add link later).

- Security: Never commit real keys, cookies, tokens, or `.env` contents. Dummy values only!

Okay, so basically, contributing to Ultralytics is cool but there are some rules:

- **Main Code of Conduct:** Be nice, respectful, and professional. It's all about the vibes! 👍

- **Pull Requests (PRs):** This is how you contribute. Here’s a quick rundown:
  1. Fork the repo (like ultralytics/ultralytics) to your GitHub. 🍴
  2. Create a branch with a descriptive name. Like `fix-bug-456` or `add-docs`. 🌱
  3. Make your changes. Keep it clean and no new errors! If you add new features, make sure to add tests too. 🔧
  4. Test your changes locally. Make sure everything works as it should. 🧪
  5. Commit your changes with clear messages. If it’s for an issue, mention the issue number, e.g., `Fix #123: Correct calculation error.` 📝
  6. Submit a PR from your branch to the main branch. Describe your changes clearly. 🚀

- **First-timers:** Keep it small and focused. No PRs over ~50 lines unless it’s mainly docs or formatting. Aim for speed improvements, bug fixes, or doc updates. Features? Later for you. 😅

- **Established Contributors:** You'll get reviewed first. No set rules for “established”—it's about making meaningful contributions. If you've got a good track record in other projects, you’re golden even if you’re new to Ultralytics. 🌟

- **Feature PRs:** Need a feature request issued and discussed first. Get explicit approval from the maintainers. Once approved, keep it focused. Long-term maintenance costs and usefulness to users are key. 🚀✨

- **PR Size & Review Time:** Bigger changes = longer review time. Keep it lean! 🕰️

Hope this helps! 💻

Notes for newbies:

- Contribs from all devs/orgs r welcome. Aim is to make the project better with diverse input.
- What you can do:
  - Push patches.
  - Review PRs (pull requests).
  - Doc updates, examples, test cases.
  - Make docs more readable (like improving docstrings and comments).
  - Join in on issues, discussions, Twitter, Discord.
  - Write tutorials, blog posts, give talks.
  - Share use cases and research.

- Most contribs need a CLA (Contributor License Agreement). Only do this once for all repos.
- If new to GitHub, check out the guides for getting started.
- When you PR, a bot will tell you if u need a CLA. Just follow the bot's instructions.

- For CI checks, always use `uv`. It's like the magic wand that makes sure all dependencies r right. Instructions here.

- Roadmap is on GitHub issues & milestones. Check them out here.
- Versioning: All `autogen-*` pkgs r versioned together. Rules:
  - Minor (0.X.0) for breakers.
  - Patch (0.0.X) for new features or bug fixes.

- Release process:
  1. PR to update version numbers across the codebase.
  2. Docs CI will fail, but that's ok, next step fixes it.
  3. After merge, tag the new version (e.g., `0.4.0.dev13`).
  4. Restart docs CI for the `push` event.
  5. Run release workflow, get approval.

- Triage process:
  - Review new issues, tag 'em with `needs-triage`.
  - Label issues (e.g., `proj-*`, `documentation`, `x-lang`, `dotnet`).
  - Add to milestone if needed.
  - Resolve or reply to OP if you can.
  - Assign it to someone if you can't resolve.
  - Add `awaiting-op-response` if waiting for a reply.
  - Also, check out old backlog issues if you got the time.

Alright, so Hindsight is this project where you can't just send a PR from outside the team. If you notice something off:

- **Bugs**: Log a bug report. Give us steps to reproduce it; if you know where the issue is, mention it.
- **Features/Integrations**: Feature request.
- **Questions/Ideas**: Use GitHub Discussions.
- **Security Issues**: Follow the SECURITY.md, no public issues allowed.

To get started:

1. Clone the repo.
2. Run `./scripts/dev/setup.sh` (it's idempotent, so safe to re-run). It handles everything:
   - Installs toolchains (uv/Python, Node/npm, Rust/cargo)
   - Creates `.env` from `.env.example` (add your LLM API key)
   - Configures git hooks
   - Installs Python and Node dependencies
   - Downloads ML models/tokenizer for offline use
   - Builds TypeScript SDK and Rust CLI

Flags you might need: `--skip-build`, `--skip-models`, `--with-docs`, `--force`. Docker stuff is out of scope, run `--help` for more.

For manual setup:
1. Tweak `.env` file with your LLM API key.
2. Install all dependencies by hand. 🤷‍♂️

Linting and formatting:
- Ruff for Python, ESLint/Prettier for TypeScript.
- Git hooks in `.githooks/` run scripts in `scripts/hooks/` on commit:
  - **Python**: `ruff check --fix`, `ruff format`, `ty check`
  - **TypeScript**: `eslint --fix`, `prettier`

Style guidelines:
- Use Python type hints
- Follow existing patterns
- Keep functions focused and clear names

Release process:
- `scripts/release.sh` does all the work:
  - Bumps versions, regenerates specs/clients, updates docs
  - Creates commit/git tag, pushes to GitHub.
- **Important**: During dev, no need to regenerate clients unless testing. 🚫

Reporting issues:
- Clear description, steps to repro, expected vs actual, and env details.

Got questions? Open a discussion or hit up the maintainers.

Hey new guy,

Here's the skinny on Voicebox:

- Got to be nice & respectful, esp to newbies. Constructive feedback is key. 🤝

- **Needs:**
  - Bun (JS runtime/pkg mgr)
  - Python 3.12 (bcuz CI uses it, no 3.13 yet). Debian/Ubuntu? Install `python3.12-venv`.
  - Rust (Tauri stuff, installs itself)
  - Tauri Prereqs (depends on OS)
  - Git (version control)

- **Setup:**
  - Use `just install` (find it via brew/cargo/winget). Then:
    - `just setup` does all:
      - Pinned Python venv (3.12, fixes old ones)
      - Py deps (CUDA on Windows if you got NVIDIA)
      - MLX on Apple silicone
      - JS deps
    - `just dev` starts backend & desktop app together. If backend already running, it just starts frontend.

- **Windows tips:** Use PowerShell, no WSL/Git Bash needed. CUDA PyTorch auto-installs with NVIDIA GPU. Use `winget install -e --id Python.Python.3.12` if Python 3.12 is missing.

- **Models:** Auto-download from HuggingFace on first use:
  - Whisper (transcription)
  - Qwen3-TTS (voice cloning, ~2-4GB)
  - First use is slower, but subsequent uses are faster (cached).

- **Building:**
  - Build production app: On Windows, use CUDA for local testing. Builds CPU sidecar, CUDA binary, & Tauri app. Creates platform-specific installers (`.dmg`, `.msi`, `.AppImage`) in `tauri/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/`.
  - Local Qwen3-TTS dev version: Set `QWEN_TTS_PATH` to your local clone. This makes PyInstaller use your local version.

- **OpenAPI client:** After starting backend server, generate TypeScript client in `app/src/lib/api/`.

- **Convert Assets:** Optimize assets using:
  - PNG → WebP (better comp., same qual.)
  - MOV → WebM (smaller file size)
  - Processes `docs/public/`
  - Deletes original files after successful conversion.
  - Install `webp` and `ffmpeg`. Run before committing new images/videos.

- **Workflow:**
  - Create a branch
  - Write clean, readable code, follow code style
  - Add comments for complex logic
  - Update docs as needed
  - Test manually in the app, ensure backend works, check for TypeScript/Python errors

Hope that helps! Let me know if you have questions. 😊

So, DeepTutor... 🤔 This is how you get involved:

- **Join the team:**  
  - Triager: Got some spare time? Label issues, ask for missing details, and close duplicates.  
  - Maintainer: Done a bunch of PRs or been a triager? You can review, approve, and merge PRs.  
  - Rules: Only merge when CI is green, get a sec review for your own PRs (except typos/doc fixes), and always be nice! 🏆  
  - How to join: Shoot an email to bingxizhao39@gmail.com with your PR links, other open source projects, and how much time you can give. Maintainers can invite too. Inactive for 3 months? Move to emeritus status.  
  - Current team: @pancacake leads, maintainers & triagers are looking for volunteers.

- **Where to start:**  
  - Bug? Open a report or fix it with a PR if it’s small.  
  - Feature/behavior change? Request first, then code if a maintainer says yes.  
  - Docs/translation issue? Open an issue or send a PR.  
  - Question/setup trouble? Ask in Discussions or Discord.  
  - Security? Report privately through GitHub. 🤫  
  - Got no ideas? Look for `good first issue` or `help wanted` tags. 🤓

- **Pull requests:**  
  - Target `dev` branch. `main` only moves at release.  
  - One change per PR. No mixing fixes.  
  - Link the issue with `Closes #123` or `Related to #123`.  
  - Explain the problem and show evidence. Test output, screenshots, or logs.  
  - Run `pre-commit run --all-files` and other checks.  
  - Keep "Allow edits by maintainers" on.  
  - AI-assisted PRs are cool, but you gotta understand the code.  
  - No refactor-only PRs unless asked.  
  - Limit to 20 open PRs at a time. Finish some before more.

### Commit messages:  
- Keep 'em clear and concise. 📝

Alright, so here’s the deets on contributing to Awesome Claude Code in a real messy, informal way.

- This repo is for all the cool projects. If yours was on the old list, it might not be here yet. No worries, it'll creep back in eventually. I’m giving the new stuff some time to shine. 🌟

- **Rules are rules:**
  - Your project needs to be **14+ days old** and show active dev. OR have **100+ stars**. No exceptions.
  - Don’t go overboard, one project at a time. Or else, your issue gets the boot.
  
- So, you wanna recommend something? Cool, but **read** this whole thing first. Beware, no formal submission/review process. Just share your links for awesome stuff, usually via the issues. But it's not guaranteed that you'll hear back. 🤷‍♂️

- Don't think getting on this list is your entry to fame. Focus on getting users first, then maybe pop up on here. Or maybe just let your project get noticed if it's rad enough.

- **Selective, remember?** Not everyone gets the green light, and that’s okay 🔑

- Resources for Claude Code are cool, but not a hard limit. Just try to keep it related.

- **Submitting:** Click the link to submit a resource. **No PRs**. Just fill out the form. If something's wrong, the bot will let you know. **No CLI submissions allowed**. The bot won’t even look at those. 💻

- Got something written by a coding agent? No worries, but the recommendation has to come from a human (you! 😁)

- **Details:**
  - Put your LICENSE where it can be found. If the bot can’t see it, neither can others. Mention it in the issue.
  - Not exclusively open-source, but closed-source projects are harder to review. And if there’s a signup or payment, that’s a no-go for the review. 😅

Hope this helps, and good luck!

OK, here's the deal:

- So, you wanna add or tweak a skill in this repo. It's all about following the Spec (y'know, the open one).
- First off, adhere to the Code of Conduct everywhere.
- Ways you can help:
  - Add a new skill (pkg, db, plat, workflow, method).
  - Make existing skills better (clearer inst, latest APIs, better examples, refs, scripts).
  - Fix old examples, broken installs, security stuff, and docs.
  - Test, test, test: `tests/` (see Tests).
  - Got a bug or new skill idea? Use GitHub Issues.

- **Skill Location**: Everything's under `skills/`. The repo root is an Agent Plugins pkg:
  - Keep `plugin.json` valid (no weird top-level fields).
  - `version` in `plugin.json` should match `pyproject.toml`.
  - After `uv sync`, do `uv run python -m pytest tests/_meta -q` to check schema, version sync, etc.
  - CI runs these checks on manifest-only and skill changes.

- Only `SKILL.md` is a must-have. Use other dirs when it makes sense:
  - `references/` for needed docs.
  - `scripts/` for helpers, validators, workflows.
  - `assets/` for templates, statics, examples.
  - **Nothing else** in `skills/`. Tests, fixtures, etc go under `tests/ /`.

- Keep references flat and main `SKILL.md` short (under 500 lines).
- Test stuff goes in `tests/ /`, mirroring the skill name, with any fixtures in `tests/ /fixtures/`.

- **Required Skill Format**: Dir with `SKILL.md`.
- Use this template:

### Frontmatter:
- **name**: 1-64 chars, only lower, nums, hyphens (no starts/ends with hyphen, no consecutive hyphens).
- **description**: Brief, 1024 chars max (what it does, when to use it).
- **metadata.version**: Required, quote it (e.g., `"1.0"`).
- **metadata**: Write it as a block, not JSON. `strictyaml` chokes on JSON formatting.

- Optional fields:
  - **license**: If diff or notable.
  - **compatibility**: Python version, sys pkg, host, network, etc.

Hope that helps! 🍺

Hey there, new colleague! So, here's how the GPT-Engineer project board works. It's like the brain of the project, making all the big calls. 

- **Board Structure:** It's run by Anton Osika (the founder) and other important folks. Max 7 members. Newbies join by vote, and the same for booting someone out. It’s like a club!

- **Veto Power:** Anton has a big red button; he can overrule anything. So, don't mess with him!

- **Contributions:** To vote, you gotta contribute. At least 6 significant contributions in 90 days (think pull requests, bug fixes, or major community stuff). If you’re not contributing enough, you still have a seat but can’t vote. Kinda like being on the bench.

- **Decisions:** Votes are simple majority. Anton's veto can blow away any vote. Meetings are regular, and everything is documented and shared with the community. Transparency is key!

- **Data Access:** Board members can see confidential stuff after signing an NDA. Got to erase all data when you leave though. Pretty serious stuff!

- **Voting Scope:** Voting is for big things: major code changes, community governance, etc. Routine stuff like bug fixes doesn’t require a vote. Just do it!

- **Transparency:** Everything is open, except for sensitive stuff. Everyone can see what's going on, including meeting minutes and votes.

- **Change Proposals:** The rules can be updated. Anyone can propose changes, and they pass with a majority vote. So, if you got ideas, speak up!

- **Brand:** Anton is the keeper of the GPT-Engineer brand. He decides everything related to it. It’s his baby!

Hope this helps! It’s a bit of a mess, but that’s how it works here.

Alright, so you wanna contribute, huh? Cool! Just remember, it's all about adding value, yeah? So, no random stuff, no self-promo (unless it's a total classic, and even then, you gotta be like, "Hey, this is from my blog" in the PR message). If you don't, it's an auto-reject. Trust me, I've seen it happen.

Articles gotta be in English and no paywalls. Really, no exceptions on this one. It's gotta be free to read. 

Formatting: Add your article at the end of the relevant section in `README.md`. Use the emoji legend for non-articles (📖 for books, 🎞 for videos, etc.). Stick with the canonical URLs, no shortcuts. And **big one** - don't touch the table of contents. It’s generated by doctoc via the pre-commit hooks, so just leave that alone.

Writing the PR: Use the existing format for the title and commit message, check out some past ones for examples.

Pre-commit hooks: We use prek, it's in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. Faster than pre-commit, so it's a win. 

Oh, and do check out the Principles, it's like the Bible for what goes in here.

Hope this helps, and good luck!

Yo, so you're diving into EXO? Cool! Here's the real scoop, not in any particular order, but all the important bits are here. 

- First, make sure you got **uv (Python dep mgmt)** and **rust (nightly for now)**. Use the forked version of **macmon**, not the Homebrew one, if you're on Apple Silicon. Super important.

- Before you start hammering away, **pull the latest source**. It’s like making sure you're on the latest version of a video game. 

- Each Pull Request should only deal with one thing - one feature or one fix. Don't mix up changes, even if they seem tiny. This keeps reviews simpler and the code cleaner.

- When you’re coding:
  - Aim for **pure functions** when possible.
  - Use Rust unless there’s a legit reason not to. Utilize the type systems: Rust types, Python type hints, and TypeScript types.
  - Comments are for explaining the **why**, not the **what**. Especially for those tricky decisions.
  - Don't forget to run `nix fmt` before submitting to auto-format your code. It's like hitting that save button, but for clean code.

- **Model Cards** are like blueprints in TOML format. They’re stored in different places:
  - `resources/inference_model_cards/ /` for text gen models.
  - `resources/image_model_cards/` for image gen models.
  - `~/.exo/custom_model_cards/` for your own custom models.

- To add a new card, you need certain fields like `model_id`, `n_layers`, `hidden_size`, and more. Check the full list in the official guide.

- Some fields are optional, like `model_type`, `components`, and `uses_cfg`. `trust_remote_code` is set to `false` by default for security reasons. Only change that if you really, really need to.

- The `capabilities` field tells EXO what the model can do, like standard text generation, chain-of-thought reasoning, or image-to-image editing.

- For adding a new model, all the extra stuff beyond what mlx-lm provides lives in `src/exo/worker/engines/mlx/models/ /`. Shared stuff is in `src/exo/worker/engines/mlx/sharding/`.

- If you're adding a new checkpoint of an architecture EXO already supports, just add a card to the family's folder. If it’s a new architecture or family, you need a new folder. Check out the table in the official guide for more details.

- Side note: always, always, keep security in mind. 

Hope this helps! Good luck!

Hey there! 😊 So, yep, we love contributions and bug fixes are super appreciated. But here's the deal: if you're thinking of adding a new feature, check the forums first to make sure it's something people want. Just saying, 'cuz it can save you a headache if it doesn't get merged.

Trust is a big thing here. If you’re new, start a convo in the forums before diving into a PR, especially for AI stuff. The system is pretty gnarly and a small tweak can mess up other parts. So, take it slow, start small if you can.

Got an idea? Describe it well, even without code. It really helps to get it discussed. AI can make a PR super quick, but it still takes a lot of time for us to review and decide if it's a go.

Big changes? Start with a chat! We don’t want to duplicate efforts or make something that’s only useful to a few. 🤔 Also, check if it could mess with other users. Good changes enhance the experience without being intrusive.

Python? 3.11-3.14 is what we’re using. We use ruff for code formatting, FYI. And branches? `main` is where the latest release lives (no functional changes here unless it's a real emergency). `dev` is for the next release, so start here. `feature-X` branches are for experimental things.

Testing? Yeah, it's a pain, but necessary. Format and test your code. Use `pytest` in the `src/` directory. It'll give you a coverage report too. Just make sure you set up your environment right first.

For more detailed stuff, the docs are your best friend. 😄

# Mergin

P.S. If you’re into the merge process, you can find it in the docs. It’s a bit boring but super important. 📜

CowAgent contributions — super cool! 🎉

- **Lang Policy**: Write in English for issues, PRs, code comments, and commit msgs. No perfect English needed, just clear. Tools like Google Translate are cool too. 🙌

  4. Test locally to make sure it works.
  5. PR with a clear title & a short desc of what & why. 

- **Commit & PR Titles**: Use a short, imperative summary. Conventional Commits style is cool but not mandatory.

- **Dev Setup**: Check the "Install from Source" guide. It's like, install, set up, go! 😄

- **Code of Conduct**: Be respectful & constructive. CowAgent should be a cozy place for everyone. 😊

> P.S. If you get stuck, just ask. The maintainers are chill and happy to help. 😎

Okay, so here’s the deal if you’re new to this ccxt thing:

- **Submitting an issue?** Just make sure you read the notes on GitHub and give all the details they ask for. It helps a lot. Also, check the Troubleshooting section for any quick fixes.

- **If it’s a serious security issue,** don’t post it publicly. Just PM them at info@ccxt.trade. It's like an emergency route.

- **Contributing code?** Got some rules here:
  - **The #1 rule: UNIFY YOUR CODE!** What? Yeah, everything has to be in one style. Big deal. Very important.
  - Before you push, run `git config core.hooksPath .git-templates/hooks` LOCAL to your machine.
  - **Don’t commit these files:**
    - `/build/*` (AUTO-gen)
    - `/js/*` (from TS)
    - `/php/*` (except base classes)
    - `/python/*` (except base classes)
    - `/cs/*` (except base classes)
    - `/ccxt.js`
    - `/README.md` (AUTO-gen)
    - `/package.json`
    - `/package.lock`
    - `/wiki/*` (AUTO-gen)
    - `/dist/ccxt.browser.js` (AUTO-gen)

    These get overwritten, so don’t make them bigger. Just commit one source file for an exchange change.
  - **Keep it atomic**: 1 Pull Request (PR) per exchange. Don’t mix.
  - **Run `npm run build`** to make sure all checks pass. No syntax errors, please. 

- **Pending tasks:**
  - Margin trading
  - Leverage
  - Derivatives (futures, options)
  - Main/subaccounts
  - Conditional orders (stop loss, take profit)
  - `transfer` between accounts
  - `fetchTransfer`
  - `fetchTransfers`
  - `fetchLedger`
  - `fetchPositions`
  - `closePosition`
  - `closePositions`

  If you're contributing, make sure it’s:
  1. Needed by most users
  2. General-purpose
  3. Exchange-agnostic
  4. Portable across languages
  5. Robust
  6. Explicit
  7. Doesn’t break anything else

- **What you need:**
  - If just using ccxt, install as a regular package:
    - JS/NPM: `npm install ccxt`
    - Python: `pip install ccxt`
    - PHP: `composer require ccxt/ccxt`
    - C#: `install-package ccxt`
    - Java: `gradle`
  - **With Docker:** Use Docker for a clean build. It sets up everything you need. Container does most of the work for you.

That’s the rundown. Got some reading to do and a bunch of rules to remember. Good luck!

Yo, new guy! Here’s how we do stuff around here. Fork the repo and create a new branch for whatever you're working on. Make sure your changes are good and follow the PR guidelines (see below).

### Pull Request Guidelines

- **Title:** Use `[type] description`. Examples: `[feat] Add user auth`, `[fix] typo in README`.
- **Link to Issue:** Your PR must fix an issue. Make sure the issue is `ready` first. Comment on a closed PR if the issue is `ready`.
- **PR Template:** Fill out the template properly.
- **No Duplicates:** Check for existing PRs.
- **Assigned Issues:** Only work on assigned issues if the maintainer says it's cool.
- **AI PRs:** Got an AI tool? Mention it in the PR. It still needs to pass the same checks as any other PR.

### Setup

1. Clone the repo.
2. Got `uv`? Check with `uv --version`. If not, install with `pip install uv`.
3. Set up the dev environment:
   - Unix: `./scripts/dev_setup.sh`
   - Windows: `.\scripts\dev_setup.bat`
4. Activate the venv:
   - Unix: `source .venv/bin/activate`
   - Windows: `.venv\Scripts\activate`

Remember, use `uv pip install` for missing packages. There’s also a `demo_setup.sh` script for a separate `.venvs/demo` environment with the same setup.

### Code Quality

Make sure your code is clean and follows our standards. Use the provided tools to check your work before submitting.

Hey, one thing I almost forgot: **don't mess with the code outside the venv!** 🙃

Good luck!

Alright, so you're jumping into this project. First off, you gotta check out these files. Start with **AGENTS.md** — it's the table of contents, real important. Then **ARCHITECTURE.md** — it's the top-level map of the whole shebang. Next, you gotta read **docs/authoring.md** — super important if you're adding new components. It's like the portable-content style guide. Also, **docs/harnesses.md** — it's got a matrix for each harness. Lastly, **docs/plugin-eval.md** — it's the quality evaluation framework, gotta make sure things are up to snuff.

When you're adding a plugin:
1. Create `plugins/ /` and put `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` in there.
2. Add agents in `agents/`, commands in `commands/`, and skills in `skills/`.
3. Update `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` with your entry.
4. Naming: lowercase, hyphen-separated. No `__` (that's the adapter namespace thing).
5. Run `make generate-all` to refresh the registries (CI checks this).
6. Run `make validate` and `make garden` to catch any issues before you submit.

Full details on the frontmatter in `docs/authoring.md`.

Changing a plugin? Any change under `plugins/ /` needs a version bump in `plugins/ /.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and in the marketplace JSON. Run `make generate-all` so Codex and Cursor get the new version. Claude Code only updates if the version goes up, so no bump means no update for existing installs. CI enforces this with `make check-version-bumps`; only lockfile changes like `uv.lock` are exempt.

Commercial content? No funnelling users to paid products, affiliate programs, or revenue-sharing services. List every external API, package, or service called or recommended in the proposal. If you own any, disclose in the proposal, PR, and README. No runnable machinery for collecting payment or gating access in plugin payloads. Verifying transactions, checking licences, and granting/restricting access are not allowed in payloads. Teaching how to build these features, like the `payment-processing` plugin, is okay.

External plugins? No metered or paid API on the default path. No routing data through your service as a side effect. External `git-subdir` entries need extra care — once it's reviewed, we won’t check again, so it needs to be well-maintained.

OK, so here's the quick lowdown on PostHog contribs. If you wanna make a change, just spin up a PR. Ideally, make an issue first if one doesn’t already exist and talk it out there. No one gets assigned, just dive in and link the issue.

For PRs:
- Triaged via CODEOWNERS or team. 
- Support Hero might first reply, but they're busy so reviews might wait.
- We'll ACK you when we can, but thorough reviews could take days to weeks.
- Stale or out-of-scope PRs might get closed but re-openable.
- Forks can't merge directly; a PostHog engineer will recreate it. You stay the author.

Before review:
- Run tests locally & fix conflicts.
- Answer AI bot feedback.
- Keep it tight, add tests/docs where needed.
- Follow existing styles.
- If AI helped, read the policy & disclose.

For security or high-support times, stuff might get deferred. Sometimes cool contribs get merch even if not merged.

Issues:
- Bug, deployment issues, user feedback? Raise an issue.
- Or fix an issue and do a PR.

Paid features:
- No externals here. If it's not in your build, it's paid.

Feature requests:
- Go to the public roadmap. We love ‘em, give us as much context as you can.

Features:
- Check WIP page for what we're working on.
- If unsure, just raise an issue & we'll chat it out.

Whew, got a lot to cover here, so let's dive in:

- **Bugs & Features**: Open an issue. Use the templates for bugs and feature requests. Quick & easy.
- **Doc Fixes**: Typos, clarity, examples. Super helpful!
- **Coding**: Fix bugs, add features, storage/LLM backends. Code runs the show.
- **Testing**: Add tests where there are none. Coverage is key.

---

### Dev Setup:

- **`uv sync`**: Pass all extras in one command. Default `uv sync` may remove unneeded packages, so re-sync after pulling with the same extras. 
  - `--locked`: Installs exactly what `uv.lock` specifies.
  - `--inexact`: Keeps packages not in `uv.lock`, like spaCy models. Check the README for more on this.

---

### Code Style:

- **Ruff**: We use it for formatting, linting, and it's enforced with `pre-commit`.
  - `pre-commit run --all-files`: Fixes most style issues. 
  - **CI**: These checks run on pull requests. Fix and push again if they fail.
  - **Lang**: 
    - Python: English
    - WebUI: Use i18next for translations. 
    - README: Keep all four versions (`README.md`, `-zh`, `-ja`, `-id`) line-for-line aligned. Changes in one, reflect in all. `tests/test_readme_translations.py` checks this. Add English if you can’t translate. 

---

### Tests:

- **Integration**: Set `LIGHTRAG_RUN_INTEGRATION=true` or use `--run-integration`.

---

### Pull Requests:

1. **Fork & Branch** from `main`.
2. **Changes**: Ensure pre-commit checks pass, relevant tests pass, and new tests added.
3. **Commit**: Message should explain why the change was made.
4. **Push & PR**: Fill out the template fully. 
5. **Review**: Respond to any feedback. 

---

### Issue Templates:

- **Bugs**: Version info, storage backend, LLM provider, minimal repro, full error.
- **Feature Requests**: Problem description, user story, and how it improves things.

Hey new person, here’s the real deal on contributing to axios. Just follow the code of conduct, okay? 🤓

- **Before PR**: Go through AGENTS.md and the PR template. 📝 Don't skip this! Plus, update `PRE_RELEASE_CHANGELOG.md` for all PRs, including docs-only changes. Skip this only for auto-release stuff. 🤖

- **Commit msgs**: Use conventional commits. 📝

- **Code style**: Stick to the Node style guide. 🛠

- **Tests**: Make sure your stuff passes GitHub Actions. Add tests where needed. 🆗

- **Docs**: Sync changes in the API with docs. For stuff not released yet, note updates in `PRE_RELEASE_DOCS.md`. 📜

- **Dependencies/Actions**: No PRs just for npm pkg updates, lockfiles, or Actions versions unless you're a maintainer or approved bot. 🚫

- **Developing**: 
  - `npm run lint` to check the code
  - `npm test` for unit and browser tests (install browsers with `npx playwright install` first)
  - `npm run test:vitest:unit` for Node unit tests
  - `npm run test:vitest:browser:headless` for browser tests (install browsers first with `npx playwright install` or system deps with `npx playwright install --with-deps` on Linux)
  - `npm run build` to bundle the source
  - `npm run version` when it's time to release

- 👀 **Examples**: Use these for manual testing. There's a browser sandbox and a terminal sandbox. Check the file for how to start them.

Hope this helps! 😄

Hey new buddy, here's how we do things around here—pretty chaotic, but important stuff's there if you dig through it:

- Use Node 24 or whatever you like: `nvm use`
- Install: `npm ci`
- Make a specific branch, keep it tight: no extra formatting stuff
- If you mess with nav, homep in Chinese, or word lists: `npm run sync`
- Checks: `npm run check`, `npm run docs:build`, `npm run test:smoke` - super key, don't skip
- `npm run check` starts with no-dep content checker stuff. If you touch validation or README rules, also `npm run test:content`. Browser tests are `*.spec.mjs` (Playwright handles these)
- PDF layout changes? Python time: `python3 tests/pdf_layout_test.py` with `requirements-pdf.txt` - CI does this before book validation

Content:
- Keep research, experience, guesses separate
- For facts, go primary sources; add access date
- Summarize research: pop, conditions, outcome, uncertainty; no prof advice
- Chinese-English pages: complete counterparts; meaning over word-for-word
- New narrative pages: `title`, `description`, `updated: YYYY-MM-DD` (real dates)
- `threads/ai...` or `...-ai`: must add `sources_checked` within 120 days post-checking
- Image alt text: describe the scene or purpose, no "image" or "photo"
- (Side note: avoid adding bloat with decor images)

Nav & Gen Files:
- Edit `docs/.vitepress/navigation.mjs` for nav; gen files: `SUMMARY.md`, etc.
- Chinese word lists under `docs/threads/word-list/`; English gen from these
- `docs/README.md`; root README gen with repo links
- CI rejects unsynced gen files
- Add every public page to nav same as trans; check links, images resolve (markdown refs excluded)
- Update `scripts/lib/readme.mjs` with new patterns, test

Privacy & Media:
- No location, IDs, contact, private msgs, health, student data, secrets
- Explicit permission for identifiable 3rd parties, esp. kids, exes, patients
- Remove EXIF, GPS, device metadata before commit
- `ATTRIBUTIONS.md` for sources, redistribution
- Use WebP for photos; SVG/PNG for text, diagrams

PR Description:
- Explain the why, source, changed pages in both langs, privacy/licensing, commands run
- Screenshot it all

Whew, that's it! Good luck.

Hey, so here’s how you can kinda handle webpack contributions:

- Want to fix a bug or add a new feature? First, check if it’s just a config issue. If not, head to Discussions or StackOverflow with the webpack tag, or hit us up on Discord. Include your `webpack.config.js`, relevant files, and the full error message.

> 📢 **Quick Tip:** If `npm audit` is yelling at you about dev-only deps like `webpack-dev-server`, don't freak out. It's probably just a bogus warning. Check first before you make an issue.

- Got a solid bug or feature idea? File an issue on GitHub.

- Fixing an issue? Look for the "Send a PR" tag. Key labels:
  - **bug**: There’s a problem.
  - **enhancement**: You want something new.
  - **question**: You're asking for more info.
  - **documentation**: It’s about the docs.

- Created a loader/plugin? Add it to awesome-webpack or the loaders/plugins lists.

- Set up your local webpack repo first.

- Submit changes? Get some feedback, update your fork, and then PR. Small changes should go through fast. For bigger stuff:
  - Write tests.
  - Match the coding style.
  - Craft a good commit message.
  - If it’s major, make sure there’s an issue. If not, make one.
  - Link your PR to issues with keywords so they get closed when merged.
  - Squash your commits for clarity. (Squashing guide: Google it.)

- For testing and structure, see the Testing Documentation.

- Releases: Patches quickly, minors every 4 weeks (Thursdays), majors after the roadmap chat. Look at `RELEASE_SCHEDULE.md`.

- Docs: Fixing typos or clarifying? Huge help. Check issues tagged with "documentation" or the doc site’s repo.

- Types: Use JSDoc and TypeScript. For new types not in public API, declare in `webpack/lib/index.js`, then run `yarn fix` to update `types.d.ts`.

- Discussions: Use the Discussions board.

- Before diving in, set up the project locally, run it, and play around with all the commands.

Hope this helps! 🚀

Lodash contrib tips for newbies:

- Read CoC & check issues first. Fork, commit, PR. 🚀
- Feature reqs go in issues. Search closed ones first. Need community :+1: love.
- PRs: Change `lodash.js`, add tests in `test/`. Skip `dist/` & `doc/` gen.
- Run `npm i` for dev deps. Test with `npm test` or open `test/index.html` & `test/fp.html` in browser. Backbone & Underscore tests too. 👍
- CLA required. Read Alex Russell’s "Why Do I Need to Sign This?" for more.
- Coding style: 2 spaces (NO tabs), clear names (`index` not `i`), single quotes (unless in string). Comments: Single-line for notes, JSDoc for funcs.
- Use JSCS for guidelines.
- Optional: `.opt-in` in root for pre-push hook that runs `npm run validate`.

👍 Good luck! 🚀

Alright, so here's the quick & dirty on contributing to Atom:

- First of all, thx for actually caring to contribute! 🙌🎉

**Code of Conduct**:  
- Remember, there's a Code of Conduct. If someone goes off the rails, report them to atom@github.com.

**Got a Q?**:  
- Don’t file an issue to ask a Q. Use:
  - Github Discussions (msg board) 
  - Atom FAQ

**Before You Start**:  
- Atom is super modular & huge (200+ repos). Figuring out which one to contribute to can be tricky.  
- Most of the non-editor UI stuff you see comes from packages. Even basic stuff like tabs and status-bars are packages.  
- Go to `Settings` > `Packages`, check out the Core Packages. Big ones are:  
  * atom/atom - core editor (text editing, file ops, etc.)  
  * tree-view - file list on the left  
  * fuzzy-finder - quick file opener  
  * find-and-replace - search & replace  
  * tabs - y'know, tabs at the top  
  * status-bar - the bar at the bottom  
  * markdown-preview - markdown pane  
  * settings-view - settings UI  
  * autocomplete-plus - autocompletes while typing  
  * git-diff - Git change indicators  
  * language-javascript - these are for language-specific stuff, like highlighting  
  * one-dark-ui - default UI styling (not for text editor)  
  * one-dark-syntax - default syntax highlighting for all languages

**How Can I Contribute?**:  
- Bugs: report 'em  
- Enhancements: suggest 'em  
- First Code Contribution: just do it  
- Pull Requests: follow the guidelines (more on that below)

**Styleguides**:  
- Git Commit Messages, JS Styleguide, CoffeeScript Styleguide, Specs Styleguide, Doc Styleguide. Follow these for consistency.

**Misc**:  
- Issue and PR labels matter. Use them right.

Hey new guy,

So, you're diving into Marketing Skills, huh? Cool! Here's the super messy but totally helpful guide I jotted down for you. 😄

- First off, if you wanna suggest a new skill, just open a skill request. Super simple.

- For adding a new skill:
  - **Step 1:** Make the skill directory. Lowercase and hyphens only (like `emails`).
  - **Step 2:** Create `SKILL.md`. Add YAML frontmatter with `license` (default: MIT) and `metadata` (author, version, etc.).
  - **Step 3:** Directory name & `name` field must match exactly. `Description`: 1-500 chars, what it does, when to use, and which skill to use instead.
  - **Step 4:** Structure your skill as described in the guide.
  - **Step 5:** Keep `SKILL.md` under 500 lines. Move detailed stuff to `references/`. Include step-by-step, examples, and edge cases. 📝

- Improving existing skills:
  1. Read the skill thoroughly.
  2. Test changes locally.
  3. Keep changes focused and minimal.
  4. Update the version if making significant changes.

- **Mentioning Tools (integrity rubric)**: We're pretty open, but gotta keep it neutral. No forced endorsements, just present facts. If you're a tool maker, you gotta disclose, and it's cool to add neutral guides to integrations.

- **Submit Your Contribution:**
  1. Fork the repo.
  2. Feature branch: `git checkout -b feature/new-skill-name`.
  3. Changes.
  4. Test with an AI agent.
  5. Submit a PR using the right template (append `?template= .md` to pre-fill).

- **Skill Quality Checklist:**
  - `name` matches directory name.
  - `description` clear on when to use.

Hope this helps! 😅 Don't forget to ask if something is unclear. Good luck!

Hey new guy/gal,

So here's how we do the Releasing Moment thing. It's kinda a mess, but hey, it works!

- First off, bump the version using `pnpm release:bump-version x.y.z` and update the changelog. Real important, don't skip this.
- Then, `pnpm release` to test everything and update the dist files. Yeh, it's a bit redundant but that's how it goes.
- Now, review all changes (src, metadata, dist) and commit. Double-check this part, it's crucial.
- Check if the protected source branch is green. If not, figure out why. Could be CI issues or something.
- Push the matching bare version tag, like `2.31.0`.

Quick note: Committed dist files stay on the 2.x branch for Bower and others. So, no deleting those comitted files, got it?

---

Automated Validation and npm Pub stuff:
- They run this for version tags, like `2.31.0`. It's auto-magic!
  - Checks if the tag is valid SemVer and > the `master` release.
  - Matches the tag with `package.json`.
  - Lints, tests, and builds.
  - No changes in dist files after rebuild.
  - Builds npm tarball twice, checks SHA-256 reproducibility.
  - Tests the exact tarball, including TypeScript versions.
  - Artifacts as workflow artifacts, publish to npm with provenance.
  - `master` branch points to the release tag.

Serialization means each tag is compared to the last release. If something fails before npm pub, rerun GitHub Actions. If the pub step fails and the version is on npm, don't rerun; look into it.

---

For a stale release tag:
- If validation fails but nothing's published yet, delete remote and local tags.
- `pnpm release`, commit files, push corrected commit.
- Recreate and push the tag from the corrected commit.

Side note: Don't force-update a protected tag. If you can't delete or move the tag, ask a repo admin or just release a new version. 

Whew, this is a lot. Hope this helps!

Okay, so first up, Monaco Editor Core is from VS Code's source code. Monaco Editor adds some basic language features on top. Check out this diagram that shows how the repos and npm packages are linked. By default, `monaco-editor-core` comes from npm, so you can work on language features without building the core editor. Nightly builds use the `main` branch of VS Code while stable releases use the commit specified in `vscodeRef` in package.json. 🙄

If you wanna add a new tokenizer or language (only if it's significant, like having a Wikipedia article), here's what you do:

- Make a file at `$src/basic-languages/myLang/myLang.contribution.ts`
- Another file at `$src/basic-languages/myLang/myLang.ts`
- A test file at `$src/basic-languages/myLang/myLang.test.ts`
- Edit `$src/basic-languages/monaco.contribution.ts` to add your new language
- Create a sample file at `$website/index/samples/sample.myLang.txt`

To debug the core editor issues, go directly to the VS Code repo:

- `git clone https://github.com/microsoft/vscode`
- `code vscode`
- `yarn install`

Yo,

So, PM2 stuff. First off, clone dev and make an alias to it so you can use it easily. Dev mode ftw.

When you make changes to the Daemon (in lib/Daemon.js, lib/God.js, God folder, Watcher.js), remember to restart the Daemon. It's a must.

Commits are super important. Keep 'em clean and to the point:
- Short desc (50 chars max)
- Lowercase, except for names, acronyms, and code stuff
- Prefixes: fix, hotfix, feat, docs, BREAKING, refactor, perf, style, test, chore, merge branch, merge PR

Tests: two types. Programmatic and Behavioral.
- `npm test` is your main cmd
- Programmatic: check test/programmatic/*
- Behavioral: check test/e2e/*

Files to know:
- `$HOME/.pm2` has all PM2 stuff
- `$HOME/.pm2/logs` logs
- `$HOME/.pm2/pids` pids
- `$HOME/.pm2/pm2.log` PM2 logs
- `$HOME/.pm2/pm2.pid` PM2 pid
- `$HOME/.pm2/rpc.sock` remote cmd socket
- `$HOME/.pm2/pub.sock` pub events socket

Changelog:
- Edit .changelogrc
- Change "version_name" to next version (like 1.1.2)
- Change "tag" to latest tag (like 1.1.1)
- Run command in pm2 dir
- Copy result to changelog.md

Hope this helps! Cheers.

OK, so here's the deal. Before you even start, *please* read the **code of conduct**. It's a must.

---

Got a bug to report? Head over to **GitHub Issues**. But, before you do that:

1. **Search first** - Seriously, a lot of stuff is already fixed or on the radar. Don't want to flood the board with dupes, right?

2. **Not sure if it's a bug?** Use the **forum** instead. It's quicker and often you'll get a response faster. Only post to GitHub if it's a clear, obvious issue.

3. **Reproducible test case** - Need a minimal, runnable code example that shows the problem. No big projects, just the issue in a nutshell.

4. **Live example** - Narrow it down, then use **jsFiddle**, **jsBin**, **CodePen**, or a link to your live site. This helps us see the problem in action.

5. **Share details** - Tell us everything: browser version, OS, Phaser version, steps to reproduce. "X isn't working!!!1!" will just get closed, so be specific.

---

For general support or help with understanding something, hit up the **Phaser Support Forum**. It's super active, and you'll get help from devs and the Phaser team. It’s a good place to get your code checked too. 

---

Now, if you want to contribute and don’t want to set up an entire dev environment, check out **Gitpod**. It's a free online IDE that looks like VS Code. Click a magic button, and it'll:

- Clone the `phaser` repo.
- Install dependencies.
- Run `npm run build`.
- Run `npm run watch`.
- Clone `phaser-3-examples` and install dependencies, then run `npm start`.

This way, you can just start contributing right away.

---

For more serious contributions:

1. **Checkout the repos** - Make sure you've got both Phaser and Phaser 3 Examples checked out. The examples should be in a folder called `phaser3-examples`.

2. **Same directory depth** - Both repos need to be at the same level in your filesystem, e.g., `/usr/home/web/phaser` and `/usr/home/web/phaser3-examples`. This is so the Phaser build scripts can copy files to `../phaser3-examples` properly.

3. **Install dependencies** - Run `npm install` or `yarn install`. Use npm if you're on Windows, as Yarn can be a bit finicky.

4. **Webpack** - Make sure both repos are at the same directory level. Then, run `webpack` in the v3 folder. This builds Phaser, and flags any path errors.

5. **ESLint** - There's an ESLint thing, but that’s a bit further down the rabbit hole.

Hey there, new buddy! 🍕 So, Fastify is basically a big ol' open warehouse where anyone who's really digging in gets commit-access. Think of it like an open wiki where folks can dive in as they see fit. For more on how to contribute, check out the informal guide (definitely read it, it’s kind of like the rulebook).

**If you think you're a good fit but haven't been invited yet, no worries!** 🙃 Just drop a message to a Lead Maintainer with some links to show off your contributions. The GOVERNANCE document has more info on that.

**Rules of Engagement:**
- **No --force pushes** on `main`. Don’t mess with Git history post-PR merge.
- Use **non-main branches** for ongoing work.
- For **external API changes** or significant mods, open an internal PR to get feedback.
- Internal PRs are encouraged for any non-trivial contribution, but it’s at your discretion.
- Follow the **code style**.
- At least **two contributors** or a core member must approve PRs before merging.
- CI services **must be green** before merging.
- Major SemVer changes: a lead maintainer must merge.
- If consensus isn’t reached, the lead maintainer’s team makes the call.
- **No bots without permission**. Pull requests have to be opened by a human. (Bot spam = banned bot 😤)

**Previous Fastify versions:** Each version has its own branch, and all changes should be based on the corresponding branch. Check the Long Term Support policy for more info.

|Version|Branch|
|-------|------|
|**v1.x**|branch 1.x|
|**v2.x**|branch 2.x|
|**v3.x**|branch 3.x|
|**v4.x**|branch 4.x|

**Releases:** Only lead maintainers can declare formal releases. No bumping version numbers in PRs.

**Plugins:** Same rules apply to Fastify plugins with a few tweaks.
- Anyone can publish a release.
- Follow semver.
- Match Node.js compatibility with the main branch.
- Changelogs must be in GitHub releases. Use `releasify` for this.
- Bots like Dependabot can merge if CI is green and Node.js versions align.

This setup is still an experiment, so feedback is **super** welcome! Feel free to PR or suggest changes.

**Onboarding:**
1. Set up 2FA for **GitHub** and **NPM**.
2. Pick a team based on how you want to help:
   - Core team: maintain Fastify core & docs
   - Plugins team: maintain plugins & ecosystem
3. Open a PR to `fastify/fastify:HEAD` to add your name, username, and email to the `README.md` and `package.json` files if you’re in the core team. Make sure to alphabetize by last name.
4. Open a PR to confirm your spot in the team. (More on this later...)

Hey there, newbie! 📝📚

So, you wanna contribute to CyberChef? Cool! Start by checking out the Wiki pages for guides on compiling CyberChef and how to add new ops. 🚀

Got ideas? Look at Issues tagged with 'help wanted'. 👍

Before your stuff gets accepted, you gotta do this:

- Fork the CyberChef repo
- Create a new branch in your fork for the changes
- Push the changes to your fork
- Sign the GCHQ Contributor Licence Agreement
- Submit a pull request. **NEVER** from the master branch of your fork. We'll reject it. Messy. 😡

Coding conventions? Yeah, they're a thing:

- 4 spaces per block
- CamelCase for objects/namespaces
- camelCase for functions/variables
- UNDERSCORE_UPPER_CASE for constants
- UTF-8 encoding, no BOM
- End all files with a newline
- Line endings: UNIX style (\n)

Design principles:

1. Client-side where possible, no reliance on external servers. Exceptions for APIs are okay, but not for critical stuff.
2. Keep latency low for a better UX. If an operation has large dependencies, load them in discrete modules to reduce initial download size. The user shouldn't notice this.
3. Big libraries in separate modules so they're not downloaded by everyone.
4. Use Vanilla JS to minimize dependencies. Only use frameworks like jQuery if you really, really need to.

Keep CyberChef:

- Standalone
- Efficient
- As small as possible

Good luck! 🍀

- Small PRs please! Try not to exceed 200 lines of code. If you must do more, break it into smaller chunks. (Like, one PR for each feature or function group)

- Big changes? Discuss with maintainers first and use feature branches. Leave the big PR as draft, test and merge smaller chunks to staging or feature branches. (No need to create all branches at once, they'll conflict a lot)

- Descriptions! Write clear PR and commit messages. Explain why the change is needed, what you did, and how to test it. (Like, "Fixed typo in readme", "Added new feature X", etc.)

- Speak English only for all non-localization stuff. (Commits, PRs, comments, etc.)

- Legal stuff: Your code is under the GNU Affero GPL. If you're unsure, ask a lawyer. (Not my problem, just FYI)

- AI tools? Yeah, you can use them. But you're still responsible for the code. (Review, test, ready to fix any issues)

Hey new buddy, here’s the gist on how to handle stuff around here. We’re all about contributions, whether it's:

- Reporting a bug
- Chatting about project stuff
- Fixing something (PRs ftw)
- New feature ideas
- Maybe even becoming a maintainer, who knows?

So, we use GitHub for everything: code, issues, feature requests, and PRs. Get used to it.

**Key points:**
- *Trust & collaboration*: We like simple and maintainable stuff. AI tools can help, but don’t just throw code at us. A **well-described idea is better than a finished solution**. Explain the issue, your use case, and who else is affected.
- *Discuss before PRs*: For anything big, start a discussion. We don’t want to waste time on something no one cares about.
- *GPL v3.0*: Your contributions are under GNU General Public License v3.0. If you got concerns, hit up the maintainers.

**Bug Reports**:
- Use GitHub discussions to report bugs. Don't open issues unless told to.
- **Great reports** = include:
  - Quick summary & background
  - Steps to reproduce (super specific plz)
  - Configurations (Docker, API versions, etc.)
  - Expected vs. actual results
  - Notes on your troubleshooting

People. Love. Detailed. Reports. Trust me.

For development:
- See the dev guidelines in docs. If you're making a service widget, check the widget guidelines.
- Keep the coding style consistent. There's a pre-commit hook thing to help with that.

**AI Tools**:
- If you use AI, disclose it in AGENTS.md.
- PRs must be reviewed by a human, no AI submissions allowed.

That’s it. Now go forth and contribute!

Hey new guy! 🙌 Here’s how you mess around with OpenCLI.

- **Adding a New Site Adapter**: Use TypeScript, always. For fetching data, use the Pipeline API. For browser stuff, use `func()`. Example: `clis/ / .js`. Check out `hackernews/top.js` for a real deal. If you need complex browser stuff, grab the `opencli-adapter-author` skill. It’s like magic. 🧙

- **Pipeline Adapter**: Makes sense for data fetching. JSON bodies? Use `method: 'POST'` with `body`. You can use fancy placeholders like `${{ args.query }}` or `${{ item.id }}`. See Pipeline JSON for more.

- **func() Adapter**: For when you need to simulate a human in a browser. Super useful for sites that are all JavaScript.

- **Validate Your Adapter**: Once it’s done and you’re sure it’s working, validate it. Hope you didn’t miss anything! 🙏

- **Arg Design**: Use positional args for the main thing (query, id, etc.). Use named options for stuff like limit, format, sort. Think: `opencli xueqiu stock SH600519` is easier than `opencli xueqiu stock --symbol SH600519`.

| Arg type | Positional? | Examples |
|----------|-------------|----------|
| Query, id, url, username | ✅ `positional: true` | `search '茅台'`, `stock SH600519`, `download BV1xxx` |
| Configuration stuff | ❌ Named `--flag` | `--limit 10`, `--format json`, `--sort hot`, `--location seattle` |

- **Testing**: Got time? Check TESTING.md. It’s in there. 📝

- **Code Style**: No `any` in TypeScript, ES Modules, `kebab-case` for files, `camelCase` for functions, `PascalCase` for classes/types. No default exports. Keep it neat.

- **Commit Convention**: Use Conventional Commits. Scopes are site names or module names. Keeps everyone on the same page.

- **Pull Requests**: Branch first (`feat/mysite-trending`), make your changes, run checks, commit properly, push, open PR. Voilà!

- **License**: Contributions under Apache-2.0. Just FYI. 📜

Phew, that was a lot. Good luck! 🍀

Yo, new guy! Here's the 411 on Vue CLI:

- **Git Workflow**: We use something like Gitflow. Got 2 main branches: `master` (for the docs of the current CLI) & `next` (for new feature docs). Fork your PRs from these.

- `dev`: This is the dev branch. Any code PRs should come from here unless you're working on an old version (like `v2`, `v3` etc.).

- **Setup**: It's a monorepo & you gotta use Yarn, not npm. Yarn workspaces are a must here.

- **Testing**: Full test suite is super slow 'cos of e2e tests that build actual projects. Narrow down your tests with a regex. Ex: To test all prompt modules in `packages/@vue/cli/lib/promptModules`, run something like this:  

  `yarn test --grep promptModules`

  Or use `-p` for specific packages:

  `yarn test -p <your-plugin-name>`

  If a plugin, drop the `cli-plugin-` prefix.

- **Watch Mode**: Add `--watch` to run tests in watch mode.

- **Jest Warning**: `jest --onlyChanged` isn't always accurate 'cos some tests spawn child processes.

- **Plugins**: Check the docs for more on plugin dev. It's a whole 'nother beast.

Hope this helps! 🚀

Got a bug to report? Just go to the issues page and file it. Easy peasy. 👍 

Now, if you're thinking of contributing to the code, there are some core principles you need to be aware of. It’s all about balance!

This thing should work like butter on most sites, reliable as can be. No setup needed, just hit "?", and boom, you're off.

Feeling native is key too - you don’t want it to change Chrome’s behavior drastically. Keep it simple, really. The codebase is made to feel approachable to devs. 🤓

When it comes to pull requests, the maintainers are kinda busy, so keep it simple. They want it to be useful for the masses and not add too much complexity. So, if you’re thinking of something big, propose it in an issue first. It’s all about those 50 Lines of Code (LOC) or less PRs, though. Beyond that, and you’re looking at a bigger hassle for review.

Why? Well, it’s a volunteer effort. The code needs to stay small and manageable. Features that most people don’t use get the cold shoulder, and every new feature adds to the complexity. You gotta maintain it forever, not just add it!

So, keep it simple and useful for everyone. Forks can handle the niche stuff. 🤫

Hey new guy/gal!

Quick rundown on how to get your stuff into the `fetch` polyfill:

- Only do stuff in the official spec (https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org). We're not aiming for full spec but parts that can be done with XMLHttpRequest (XMLHttp ftw!). Check the caveats (https://github.github.io/fetch/#caveats) for what we’re not gonna touch.

- Contributions go under the open source license. Legal stuff, check the tos (https://help.github.com/articles/github-terms-of-service/#6-contributions-under-repository-license).

Running tests:
- `npm test`: builds `dist/`, runs tests in Chrome & Firefox (headless mode), and in Web Worker mode. Handy!
- For real-time testing, run `npm run karma`. You can check out `http://localhost:9876/` to add browsers. Changes to `test.js` auto-re-run tests. For `fetch.js` changes, `make` to re-run.
- To run specific tests, use `./node_modules/.bin/karma run -- --grep=`. Super useful for focusing!

Pull Requests:
- Fork and clone the repo (https://github.com/github/fetch/fork).
- New branch: `git checkout -b my-branch-name`.
- Make ur changes, push to ur fork, submit a pull request (https://github.com/github/fetch/compare).
- Give urself a pat on the back, then chill while we review.

Pro tips:
- Keep changes super focused. If you got multiple changes, separate them.
- Write good commit messages (http://tbaggery.com/2008/04/19/a-note-about-git-commit-messages.html). It's a thing.

Got resources if u need more info:
- "How to Contribute to Open Source"
- "Using Pull Requests"
