Hey new guy, here's the scoop on filing issues and contributing to localForage:

- Check the existing issues first, no need to duplicate stuff. (duh!)
- If it's a bug, file it. Also, create or edit an example if you can.
- Want a feature? File an issue but be aware PRs for tiny stuff (like adding a line in a config) get more love than just filing an issue.
- Some issues will be rejected, like Node.js support (it's a browser thing, not for servers) and legacy browser support (no love for anything worse than localStorage).

Contributing? Sweet! Here's how to do it:

- Thanks buddy! <3
- Just open a PR and someone will review it. If it’s good, it gets merged.
- **All drivers must have the same API:** check the API tests to ensure this.
- Work on a feature branch to keep things tidy.
- Try to rebase master into your branch to keep the commit history clean.
- **Write tests** for new features or when fixing bugs not caught by tests.
- Run `grunt build` before committing to make sure your tests pass and files in `dist/` are built.
- Commit changes at the top-level and `src/` together, not separately. This is for bower to use `localforage.js` and `.min.js`.

Got Qs or need help? Hit up the IRC, `#apps` channel on irc.mozilla.org. The team is usually around.

## Coding Style

- Run `npm test` to check if your code follows the styleguide. Check `.jshint` and `.jscsrc` for the nitty-gritty rules.

That's pretty much it! Happy coding! 😄

Hey new guy, here are some messy notes on contributing to Request. Don't get overwhelmed, just follow these:

- First off, thanks a ton for jumping in! 🎉

- When you submit an Issue:
  - Make sure to include a tiny, self-sufficient code snippet to show the issue. If it's not reproducible, your issue might get closed for “Not enough info”.
  - Use `request-debug` and paste it all in code blocks like this: \`\`\`
  - If it's not related to Request, it'll get marked as "Help (please use Stackoverflow)".

- For a Pull Request (PR):
  - You pretty much always need tests. Don't skip!
  - Run `npm test` locally and fix any issues before pushing to GitHub.
  - Wait for TravisCI to finish and make sure everything passes.

- To become a Contributor:
  - If you make significant contributions, you get commit access. It's like an open wiki, not a locked-down GitHub.

- Ground rules:
  - No `--force` pushes or altering Git history!
  - Use non-master branches for ongoing work.
  - Every change must go via a PR.
  - For API changes & major stuff, do an internal PR for feedback.
  - Any big contribution, wait 24 hours before merging so the global team can chime in.
  - Try to follow the code-style.
  - Always run `npm test` locally before submitting a PR. To test a single file, use:
    - `node_modules/.bin/taper tests/test-file.js`
    - `node tests/test-file.js` to see raw tap output.

- Maintainer's job: Declare releases.
- If you think this doc needs changes, you can always PR. It's an experiment, so feedback is good! 👍

Hope this helps! Hit me up if you have questions. 🤓

Alright, so you're jumping into n8n. Cool. First, check out the `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`. It's in the root, and if anyone's a jerk, email jan@n8n.io.

Directory structure is crazy. Key dirs:

- `/docker/images` - Docker stuff
- `/packages` - All the modules
  - `/packages/cli` - CLI, APIs
  - `/packages/core` - **This one's super important**, contact n8n before touching
  - `/packages/frontend/@n8n/design-system` - Vue components
  - `/packages/frontend/editor-ui` - Workflow editor
  - `/packages/node-dev` - CLI for new nodes
  - `/packages/nodes-base` - Base nodes
  - `/packages/workflow` - Workflow code

Dev setup:

- **Node.js** - v24 or newer
- **pnpm** - Install with `npm` or other method if `npm` isn't there
  - pnpm workspaces - auto-links modules
- Build tools - Debian/Ubuntu, CentOS, Windows: check docs for details
  - MacOS - no extra stuff

And if you're messing with workflow files:

- **actionlint** - only needed for `.github/workflows/*.yml` changes
  - **macOS (Homebrew):** `brew install actionlint`

DB stuff:

- **tbls** - needed for db schema docs if you're modifying migrations
  - **macOS (Homebrew):** `brew install tbls`
  - Or just have Docker Available. Runs automatically via git hooks.

Contributing:
- Make sure your changes follow the PR guidelines.
- Test suite - do unit tests, code coverage, E2E tests.
- Releasing - follow the official process.
- Creating custom nodes - follow the template.
- Extending documentation - keep it clear and concise.
- Contributing workflow templates - follow the template.

Legal:
- **Contributor License Agreement** - don't forget this.

Messy, right? Good luck! 😄

  - 1 issue per report. No listing multiple stuff.
  - Don't comment unless exact same issue.
  - Info overload! Include:
    - VS Code version
    - OS
    - Extensions list
    - Steps to repro
    - What you expected vs actual
    - Pics, vids, code snippets (no .gif for code! Copy-paste must work)
    - Errors from Dev Tools Console (Help > Toggle Dev Tools)
- Pull Requests? Check the guide. 📜
- Final checks:
  - ☐ Issue search
  - ☐ Disable all exts to see if it's the issue
  - ☐ Simplify your code to isolate the problem
- Issue submitted? Track it. Devs might need more info. Don't be down if they can't repro right away. They'll ask. 👍✨

Good luck! 🍀

Hey new guy/gal, here’s how to get started with gstack if you're feeling adventurous:

- First off, dev mode is your friend. It lets Claude Code use skills directly from your work tree. No more copying or deploying. Just run `bin/dev-setup`. This sets up everything you need for developing, including the Claude Agent SDK, TypeScript, and Prettier. Also, it marks your clone as a contributor with `git config gstack.contributor true`. Super handy! 

- Quick note: If you already did `bun install` without `bin/dev-setup`, you’ll need to set `git config gstack.contributor true` or use `GSTACK_CONTRIBUTOR=1`. Just a one-off thing.

- Full clone vs. shallow: If you used `--depth 1` by mistake, switch to a full clone with `git fetch --unshallow`. You'll need the full history for git log, blame, bisect, etc. 

- For type checking, make sure `typecheck` is clean (zero errors). `typecheck:test` is a bit trickier; it compares against the baseline in `scripts/typecheck-test-baseline.json`. New diagnostics fail, so run `bun run typecheck:test --write-baseline` to update it. Don't forget `bun run format:cso` before committing files in `lib/cso/*.ts`.

- Now you can edit `SKILL.md`, use it in Claude Code (e.g., `/review`), and see it live. When you’re done, remember gstack learns from failures. It logs learnings in `~/.gstack/projects/{slug}/learnings.jsonl`. Just type `/learn` to check them.

- Workflow quick rundown:
  1. Use gstack normally — it logs learnings automatically.
  2. Check learnings: `/learn` or list them manually.
  3. Fork and clone gstack.
  4. Symlink your fork into the project. `setup` asks for your skill prefix preference; use `--no-prefix` to skip the prompt.
  5. Fix your issue — changes go live right away.
  6. Test the fix in your project.
  7. Open a PR from your fork.

That's it! The best way to contribute is fixing gstack while you do your actual work. Hope this helps! 🚀

OK, so here's the deal for contributing to OpenDesign:

- **Design template**: If you want OD to render a new artifact (like an invoice or iOS screen), add a `Design template`. Lives in `design-templates/`. You need one folder with `SKILL.md` and its rendering assets. 📂

- **Skill**: For adding a new capability, like a "send email" function. Lives in `skills/`. One folder with `SKILL.md` and some optional resources. 📄

- **Design System**: For a new brand’s visual language. Lives in `design-systems/`. One package: `manifest.json`, `DESIGN.md`, and `tokens.css`. 🎨

- **Agent adapter**: Hook up a new CLI. Lives in `apps/daemon/src/runtimes/defs/`. One definition + registry entry. ⚙️

- **Code**: If you're fixing a bug or adding a new feature, look at `apps/web/src/`, `apps/daemon/`. Just do a normal PR. 🖥️

- **Docs**: Improve them, translate things, fix typos. Files: `README.md`, `QUICKSTART.md`, `docs/i18n/README.fr.md`, etc. One PR. 📝

If you're not sure where your idea fits, open a discussion and we'll point you in the right direction.

---

### Local setup

- Use Node `~24` and pnpm `10.33.x`. Use `nvm` or `fnm` if you want to manage Node that way: `nvm install 24 && nvm use 24` or `fnm install 24 && fnm use 24`.
- macOS, Linux, and WSL2 are the main setups. Windows is supported but read `docs/windows-troubleshooting.md` for gotchas. 💻

### Docker setup

- Install Docker Desktop with Compose v2.
- Start OpenDesign and open in your browser.
- Common commands and override env stuff in `deploy/.env`.
- Docker persists projects and database data using volumes. 🐳

---

### Adding a new Design template

- **Quick start**: clone → copy the closest template → run `pnpm tools-dev run web` → test in picker → open PR.
- **What is it**: not a feature, not an integration. Read `docs/skills-contributing.md`.
- **Anatomy**: minimum folder layout and `SKILL.md` frontmatter. 📝
- **Running locally**: 4 commands matter.
- **Merge bar**: checklist of things reviewers check.
- **PR description template**: fill it in with details.
- **Common rejections**: Reasons we might reject and examples. 💔

- **Protocol spec**: in `docs/skills-protocol.md`, for advanced stuff. 📜

Hope this helps! Good luck! 🍀

Hey there! So, Stirling-PDF is a project where you can contribute in ways other than just coding—like reporting bugs, suggesting features, or helping with translations. 🚀

### License Stuff
When you contribute, your stuff gets licensed under the project's license—mostly MIT and source-available. Make sure to check which license applies to the part you're working on. PRs are cool in all dirs, just be careful of the license. 👍

### Issues
Use issues to report bugs, request features, or ask questions. First, check if someone else has already opened an issue on the same thing. If you're stuck, hit us up on Discord. 📢

### Pull Requests (PRs)
Before diving in, comment on or create an issue and wait for it to be assigned to you. If someone else is assigned but hasn't been active in a while, chat with them to avoid duplication. 🤝 Once assigned, you can start working. When ready, submit a PR. For more on PRs, there's a guide.

### Dev Quick Start
Use `Task` to run commands. After cloning the repo:
1. Install `task` CLI: https://taskfile.dev/installation/
2. Run `task install` for dependencies
3. `task dev` starts backend + frontend or `task desktop:dev` for desktop
4. Always run `task check` before a PR
Side note: `task --list` shows all commands. 📋

### PR Guidelines
- Use the PR template
- Keep titles short and sweet
- One commit per change
- Commit messages clear and easy to follow
- Always refer to the issue number
- Comments in diffs should explain what the code doesn't

### PR Size
PRs are capped at 1000 changed lines. If over, the PR gets a `too-large` label and needs to be split. If still over after 7 days, it gets closed. 🚫

### Stale PRs
PRs that seem abandoned will get closed. If changes are requested, you'll get a `waiting-on-author` label. If no activity within 7 days after getting `waiting-on-author` or `has conflicts` labels, you get a `Stale PR` label and closed after another 7 days. If a draft PR has no activity for 30 days, it's `Stale PR`. Closed PRs can be reopened. 👍

That's it! If you have any questions, just ask! 🤓

Hey buddy, so here’s the lowdown on releases and stuff. Super important to get this right:

- **Versioning is a pain**: you gotta change the version in the package's manifest and do it via a reviewed PR on `v2/main`. The version doesn’t just get stamped at release time. Got it? Typescript stuff uses semver, so watch out.

- **Changesets are your friend**: for packages like `everything`, `filesystem`, etc., use `npm run changeset` to create a tiny file in `.changeset/`. It’s got to have the package name, the bump type (patch, minor, major) and a log line. This is super important.

- **PR magic**: when you push changes to `v2/main`, a workflow called `version-packages.yml` creates a rolling PR. This PR bumps the versions in `package.json`, updates the `CHANGELOG.md`, fixes `package-lock.json`, and gets rid of the changeset files. Merge that PR and you’ve got a new version.

- **Bump types**:
  - **patch**: bug fixes
  - **minor**: new tools, prompts, options
  - **major**: breaking changes (renamed tools, schema changes, etc.)

- **Semver & date-stamped versions**: old versions were date-stamped (`2025.x`, `2026.x`) which sort above any semver number. But `npm install` and `npx` use the `latest` dist-tag, so once you publish `1.x`, that’s what users get. `release.yml` always specifies the dist-tag to avoid moving `latest` back. If you’re republishing an older version after a newer one, use the `backfill` tag.

- **GitHub trickery**: until the first milestone merge, you gotta run the script locally on a branch from `origin/v2/main` and open the PR manually.

- **Workflow notes**: these workflows will push their PR branch with a workflow token, which won’t start new workflows (only `workflow_dispatch` can). So they dispatch TypeScript, Python, DCO, and MCP diff workflows and show up on the PR as `(dispatched)`. Wait for these to pass before merging.

- **Re-running workflows**: use `gh workflow run` and specify the `.yml` file and branch. The Version Packages PR gets its body updated on every `v2/main` push, so it links to the release issue and adds a `Part of #N` comment.

Whew, that’s a lot. Good luck! 🤞

Okay, so here's the deal:

- We're all about contributions! Any type, any skill level. Just want to help? We're down!
- New to open source? No worries! Here’s how you can pitch in:
  - Propose a new feature with an RFC (reqs reqs)
  - Fix our docs (probably needs some TLC)
  - Add more code snippets for different JS frameworks (like Vue or React)
  - Improve framework integration or add a new one (always expanding here)
  - Write an addon to make Storybook even better (think of it as a plugin)
- Not sure where to start? Try this:
  - Report a bug (find 'em, flag 'em)
  - Answer questions on GitHub discussions (be the helper)
  - Grab a "Good First Issue" (these are usually quick and easy fixes)

> **Reminder**: Read the Code of Conduct before jumping in and hit up the `#contributing` Discord channel if you need any help.

---

Quick note on AI contributions:
- Use AI as a personal assistant, but make sure a real human is always behind the scenes
- AI-generated PRs need to disclose the tool (e.g., Claude, Codex)
- Fully AI-generated stuff gets closed after 3 days if no human steps in
- Spammy or incorrect AI comments get hidden, and there’s a ban if it's a recurring issue

---

### Prerequisites (in no particular order):
- Storybook runs on a specific Node.js version (check `.nvmrc` file)
- Use fnm to manage Node.js (install and configure shell with `fnm env` params)
- Windows users, you'll need WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) - follow the link for instructions

### Editor Setup:
- CI uses TypeScript 7 for type checking (`yarn task check`)
- VS Code defaults to TypeScript 6 (some tooling still needs it)
- You can switch to TypeScript 7 in VS Code with the right extension (and some toggling)
- Disable TypeScript 7 when working with Vue or Svelte stuff (they still use TypeScript 6 plugins)

Hey there! Just a quick rundown of how to get started with Hyperframes. It's a bit of a mess but I'll try to keep it straight.

- Fork it! Then clone it locally: `git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/hyperframes.git`
- Install all the stuff: `bun install` (don't forget this, it's super important)
- Make a branch: `git checkout -b my-feature` - super important! Don't mess up the main branch.

For the skills, they're in `skills/`. Install them with `npx hyperframes skills update`. If you're working on a separate video project, use `npx skills add ...` but be careful not to overwrite anything uncommitted in `skills/`. Also, `.claude/skills/` and `.agents/skills/` are already included. 📁

When picking what to work on, start with "newcomer" or "help-wanted" issues. Check the discussion and existing PRs first; you don't want to overlap with anyone else. Mention your approach in the comments and get approval from a maintainer. The labels like `difficulty/easy` and `help wanted` are your friend. Check out `TRIAGE.md` for the full scoop on what to look for. 🧵

For substantial features or API changes, talk to a maintainer first. But if it's a tiny fix, just jump into a PR and explain the issue and how you fixed it.

Linting and formatting? Git hooks (via lefthook) auto-activate after `bun install`. They enforce linting and formatting before each commit. 😅

Type safety:
- **Avoid `any`, use `unknown` and narrow it.**
- **Avoid `as T` type assertions;** use type guards, `instanceof`, or centralized helpers.
- **Acceptable `as` use with comments.**
- **Avoid `!` non-null assertions**; use `??` or guard clauses instead.

Comments:
- Don't repeat the code.
- Rename variables or extract functions instead of explaining them.
- Simplify the code first if you can't write a clear comment.
- Explain code that looks wrong on purpose.
- Link the source of copied code with a stable URL.
- Link external references where they help.
- Explain bug fixes with what the code must do and how to reproduce the bug.
- Mark unfinished work with a `TODO(name)` or `TODO(issue)`.

That's it! Good luck and have fun! 😄

ok, so here's the quick n' dirty on contributin' to code-server:

- reqs: same as VS Code, basically
- `node` v24.x
- `git` v2.x+
- `git-lfs`
- `npm` - for JS packages and scripts
- `nfpm` - .deb, .rpm packages
- `jq` - for builds
- `gnupg` - sign commits, read GitHub stuff or that tutorial
- `quilt` - patch manager
- `rsync`, `unzip` - for releases
- `bats` - script unit tests

Linux-specific:
- same as VS Code wiki

workflow:
1. `git clone https://github.com/coder/code-server.git`
2. `git submodule update --init`
3. `quilt push -a`
4. `npm install`
5. `npm run watch` - code-server localhost:8080, live-reload, manual refresh needed

* pulling changes:
  - if patches, use `quilt`
  - if vscode updates, `submodule update --init` and re-apply patches

* changelog updates if you touch marketplace stuff

* builds take _forever_, and loading in dev mode too

* lang support only in full build, not dev mode

* PRs usually squashed, but you can rebase if you need to keep commits clean

ver updates:
1. `quilt push -a`
2. if conflicts, `quilt push -f`, add back code, `quilt refresh`
3. `./ci/build/update.sh`
4. commit, push, update PR checklist

* verify unreleased changelog before merging

patchin':
1. `quilt push`, `quilt pop`
2. `quilt new {name}.diff` or use existing
3. `quilt add [-P patch] {file}` - add before changes
4. make changes, each patch should keep code-server working
5. `quilt refresh`
6. comment on why the patch exists and how to repro the fix, add e2e test

build:
- long process, so be patient

testin':
- unit tests
- script tests
- integration tests
- end-to-end tests

structure:
- mods to Code
- known issues

phew, that's the gist. Good luck, and remember, patience is key here.

Alright, so you wanna contribute to Cline, eh? Cool, here's the lowdown:

- **Reporting Bugs**: Check for duplicates first, then use the template on the issues page. If it’s a security issue, use the GH security tool. 🐛🔒

- **Before Contributing**: Start with a GitHub Issue unless it’s a tiny fix (typos, etc.). For bigger stuff:
  - Check the Feature Requests board.
  - Create a new request if needed.
  - Wait for maintainers’ 👍 before diving in.
  - PRs without approved issues might get closed. So, don’t skip this step!

- **First Contribution?**: Look for "good first issue" or "help wanted" tags. Also, docs contributions are super-needed! Head to `/docs` and see what needs fixing or expanding.

- **Setup Dev Environment**:
  - Clone the repo (needs git-lfs).
  - Open in VSCode.
  - Install bun.
  - Install dependencies for the extension and webview-gui.
  - Generate Protocol Buffer files (needed before first build).
  - Debug by pressing `F5` or `Run`->`Start Debugging`. Might need the esbuild problem matchers extension for build issues.

- **Create a PR**:
  - Commit your changes.
  - Push your branch & create a PR.
  - CI does tests and checks.
  - Test locally with `cd apps/vscode && bun run test`.
  - Before PR, run `bun run format:fix` to auto-format your code.

- **VS Code Extensions**:
  - VS Code will ask to install recommended extensions when you open the project. Accept all prompts.
  - If you missed it, install manually from the Extensions panel.

- **Linux Setup**: Need these system libraries for the test environment:
  - `dbus`
  - `libasound2`
  - `libatk-bridge2.0-0`
  - `libatk1.0-0`
  - `libdrm2`
  - `libgbm1`
  - `libgtk-3-0`
  - `libnss3`
  - `libx11-xcb1`
  - `libxcomposite1`
  - `libxdamage1`
  - `libxfixes3`
  - `libxkbfile1`
  - `libxrandr2`
  - `xvfb`

Remember, we gotta follow the Code of Conduct for a happy community! 🤝

So, Docusaurus, basically our tool to make open source docs easier. There's a bunch of stuff here, and if you're new, it can be a bit overwhelming. First off, go check out the Open Source Guides website. Seriously, it has guides like "How to Contribute to Open Source" and "Building Welcoming Communities" — super helpful for both contributors and newbies. 🌟

Quick note: There’s a Code of Conduct thing. You gotta read it, it’s not super long, but it’s important for knowing what’s tolerated and what isn’t. Meta – they got this covered.

Alright, so how do you actually get involved? Start using Docusaurus. Check out the Getting Started guide. If anything's off, let us know by opening an issue. 🚨

Issues? Check them out. Help out by suggesting workarounds, asking for clarification, or flagging stuff that might need labels. If you see an issue you can fix, esp. ones tagged as “Good first issue,” open a PR (Pull Request). 🌈

The docs can always use a bit of TLC. If something’s confusing, click "Edit this page" at the bottom and suggest changes. And if you see an awesome feature request, consider chipping in and opening a PR.

Need help? Tag us on X at @docusaurus. We’re here to help. 😊

Also, we have a Discord channel called `#contributors` where you can discuss all things Docusaurus dev. You can also help in `#help-and-questions`.

Triage is a big thing. Help out by asking for more info, suggesting labels, flagging stale issues, and asking for test plans. It’s super useful and you don’t even need to code!

Now, our dev process is all on GitHub. Everything is public from the start. We’ve got a `main` branch, and we use feature branches with deploy previews for new features. 🏗️

Issues: When you open one, fill out the template. It’s super important. No template fill = delayed response. Also, don’t use issues for questions. Use our support channels for that. 📣

For bugs: Check if it’s already reported. If not, submit a bug report. One issue, one bug is the rule. Provide a repro case, and make sure to fill out the template. 💪

That’s pretty much it! Hop in, and don’t be afraid to ask for help. We’re a friendly bunch. 🤗

Hey there! 🙌 So you wanna get into contributing to Plane, eh? Cool! Here's how you can get started. Super important stuff first:

- **Issues**: Before you open a new issue, make sure you check the issues tab and forums. Someone might've already logged it. If not, you gotta give us a minimal repro scenario. Like, if it's a bug, tell us what fails and with what versions of 3rd-party libraries. No repro, no fix. Use the issue form to open it.

- **Naming issues**: Use these prefixes: `[bug]` or `[feature]`. Example:
  - `[bug]: API token expiry time not saving correctly`
  - `[feature]: Allow custom time selection for token expiration`

Next up, the setup:

- **Requirements**: Docker (with `docker-compose-local.yml`), Node.js 22.22.0+, pnpm (use Corepack to enable: `corepack enable pnpm`), Python 3.12, and uv (only if you're running the API outside Docker). Need at least 12GB RAM; 8GB will crash stuff. Use cloud stuff like GitHub Codespaces if you can't upgrade.

- **Setup**: The project is a monorepo, so both backend and frontend are in one repo. The backend is in `apps/api`. Steps:
  1. Clone the repo.
  2. Run `setup.sh`. This script copies `.env.example` files, generates a `SECRET_KEY` for Django and storage credentials, then runs `pnpm install` to set everything up. Check the `.env` files if you need to tweak anything.

- **Env vars**: Make sure these are right, or stuff won’t connect:
  - `DATABASE_URL` in `apps/api/.env` (default: `postgresql://plane:plane@plane-db:5432/plane`)
  - `REDIS_URL` in `apps/api/.env`, `apps/live/.env` (API: `redis://plane-redis:6379/`, Live: `redis://localhost:6379/`)
  - `PORT` in `apps/live/.env` (default: `3100`)

Ports after setup:
- Web: http://localhost:3000
- Admin: http://localhost:3001
- Space: http:/ (still working on this one)

Hope that helps! 🚀

Fork `nuxt/nuxt` repo & clone it, got that?  
Use latest Node.js, 'cuz it's important.  
Corepack needs to be enabled: `corepack enable` - do it.  
Install deps: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` - super important, don't skip.  
Dev env prep: `pnpm dev:prepare` - gotta do.  
Branch time: `git checkout -b my-new-branch` - name accordingly.

Monorepo stuff:
- `packages/kit`: @nuxt/kit - toolkit for Nuxt modules
- `packages/nitro-server`: @nuxt/nitro-server - default server builder
- `packages/nuxt`: nuxt - core
- `packages/schema`: @nuxt/schema - cross-version stuff
- `packages/ui-templates`: built-in HTML templates
- `packages/rsbuild`: @nuxt/rsbuild-builder - Rsbuild bundler
- `packages/rspack`: @nuxt/rspack-builder - deprecated, use rsbuild instead
- `packages/vite`: @nuxt/vite-builder - Vite bundler
- `packages/vite-server`: @nuxt/vite-server - experimental Vite server
- `packages/webpack`: @nuxt/webpack-builder

Check `ARCHITECTURE.md` for how all this stuff connects.  
Before you start:
- Bug fixes: check for existing issues.
- Features: open a feature request, get a thumbs up from a maintainer before PR.
- Typos: batch them.

Commit conventions:  
- `fix:` and `feat:` for code  
- `docs:` and `chore:` for docs and typos  
- Scope commits like: `feat(kit): add utility`

Testing & linting:  
Need Chromium: `pnpm exec playwright-core install chromium` - do it once.  
Add tests at the cheapest layer that covers your change.  
`ARCHITECTURE.md` has layers and fixture matrix.

AI tools are cool, but:
1. Don't let AI speak for you, write in your own words.
2. Don’t let AI think for you, only submit what you understand.

Hey new guy! 🙌 Here’s how we roll at Appwrite. Super important to follow this to avoid a PR disaster! 😂

- **First things first:** Read AGENTS.md (coding contract, y'all!). This is where all the coding rules live. Whether you’re coding solo or with AI, you gotta follow the rules. Got it?

- **Hacktoberfest?** Cool, but you gotta contribute to issues labeled `hacktoberfest` only. Easy peasy.

- **How to Start:**
  1. **Find an issue** (pref: good first issue or help wanted). If confused, hit up the **maintainers channel** on Discord.
  2. **Assign yourself.** Comment on the GitHub issue and open a **Discord thread** in the maintainers channel. The team might miss your GitHub comment.
  3. **No unsolicited PRs.** If not assigned, open an issue first. For large features, discussions and some RFCs are needed.

- **Code of Conduct:** Read it, follow it. 🤓

- **Branch naming:** Use `TYPE-ISSUE_ID-DESCRIPTION`. Like `doc-548-submit-a-pull-request-section-to-contribution-guide`. `TYPE` options: `feat`, `doc`, `cicd`, `fix`, `refactor`.

- **Commit Message:** Super important — describe the change.

- **PR Steps:**
  1. Fork repo, keep `master` up to date (`git pull`).
  2. Create branch from `master` with the right naming.
  3. Commit on that branch. Follow AGENTS.md rules, even if AI helped.
  4. Push and open PR against this repo.
  5. Wait for a core dev to review. Once approved, they merge and GitHub deletes the branch.

- **Other ways to help:**
  - Write/speak about Appwrite, tag @appwrite, add to Awesome Appwrite.
  - Present at meetups/conferences, we can review talk abstracts.
  - Report bugs & give feedback on GitHub/Discord.
  - Open an issue for new ideas.
  - Improve docs (spellcheck, grammar, you got this!).
  - Help others on Discord/GitHub/Stack Overflow. 🙌

Hope this helps, buddy! Don't get overwhelmed, just dive in and ask questions. We're here to support.

Hey new buddy, here's the quick and dirty on contributing to Flowise. 😄

- **Star and share** the Github repo. It's a quick way to show support. 🌟

- Got a **Q&A**? Check if the question is already up there. If not, just create one. It might help someone else too. 👍

- Don't forget to **share your chatflows** in JSON format. Throw in a screenshot too. This is how you show off your cool stuff. 📑

- Got an **idea** for a new feature or integration? Drop it in the Ideas section. We're all ears! 🤔

- If you find a **bug**, report it right away. It helps us keep things running smoothly. 🐛

- For the **code contributors**: 

  - You need PNPM v10. Install it first! 🚀

  - **Fork and clone** the Flowise repo. Create a new branch and name it like `feature/` or `bugfix/`. 🗂️

  - **Install** all the dependencies with `pnpm install`. Then `pnpm build` all the code. 🛠️

  - Start the app at `localhost:3000`. Set up your `.env` files for `VITE_PORT` and `PORT`. 🚀

  - For dev: changes in `packages/ui` or `packages/server` reflect at `localhost:8080`. Changes in `packages/components`? Do another `pnpm build`. 🔄

  - Before committing, run the tests to make sure everything's good. 🧪

  - Commit your changes and submit a **Pull Request** to the main branch. 📥

- **Credentials**: For secret fields, always use `type: 'url'` or `type: 'password'`. Anything else is a big no-no. 😱

- **Testing**: Unit tests are right next to their source files. Just run them from the package directory. 🧪

Alright, that's pretty much all you need to know. Dive in and start contributing! 🚀✨

Hey new buddy! 🙌 Got some quick tips for ya on contributing to the Ionic Framework:

- **Contributing Etiquette**: Read the Code of Conduct. LOTS of rules there. 📜

- **Creating an Issue**:
  - Qs about using the framework? Go to the Ionic Forum or Discord. 🗣️
  - Make sure to have a **clear** description of the steps to reproduce the issue. Don't be vague! 🙅‍♂️
  - Only bug reports and feature requests here. Other issues get closed real quick. 🚦
  - If your issue needs a reply and you don't bump it within 14 days, it's game over. 👾
  - Check for duplicates before filing. Seriously, do it. 🔍
  - Use the issue form! Fill it out properly. 📝

- **Creating a Good Code Reproduction**:
  - It’s a mini-app that shows the issue. Keep it tiny and focused. 🕳️
  - Use the Ionic CLI: `ionic start myApp blank` to kick things off.
  - Add only what's needed to show the issue. Leave out unnecessary plugins. 🚫
  - Put it on GitHub and add the link in your issue. Also, include reproduction steps. 🚀
  - Benefits? Latest Ionic version, less code to wade through, no proprietary code exposure, and you get help fixing your issue. 🎯

- **Using VS Code on Windows**: Just FYI, it’s pretty standard. No special tips here. 🖥️

- **Creating a Pull Request**:
  - **Requirements**: Check them first.
  - **Setup**: Basic stuff.
  - **Core**: You'll be modifying components, previewing, linting, docs, tests, and building. Angular, React, and Vue, same deal.
  - **Submitting**: Follow the guidelines and you’re good. 🚀

- **Commit Message Guidelines**: Super important. Follow the format. Examples are your friend. 📝

- **License**: Keep it in mind. 📄

Hope this helps! LMK if you have more Qs. 👋

Yo, new guy! Here's how you deal with PixiJS stuff:

- **Reporting Issues:** Use GitHub Issues but first, do a search. Seriously, no duplicates. Make a reproducible test case using [jsFiddle][fiddle], [jsBin][jsbin], or just link to your live site. Share all the info, like browser, OS, and steps to reproduce. "X isn’t working!!!1!" will get you nowhere. 🤦‍♂️

- **Contributing Changes:**
  - Install node.js from [nodejs.org][node]. Use v24+ 'cause Pixi needs modern JS.
  - Fork the [pixi.js][pixi] repo. If unsure, check GitHub guides for the [command line][fork-cli] or [GitHub Client][fork-gui].
  - Run `npm install` in your fork to get dependencies.
  
- **Making a Change:** Checkout the right branch:
  - `main`: For urgent hotfixes.
  - `dev`: For non-urgent bugfixes or BC features.
  - `v4.x`, `v5.3.x`, etc: If your fix is for older versions.

- **Testing Your Change:**
  - Run `npm test` to test your changes. Add a test for fixed bugs to prevent regressions.
  - Tip: `npm start` for incremental compiling. `npm run test unit` for unit tests, `npm run test visual` for visual tests. 🚀
  - `npm run test unit debug`: Debug with DevTools. 👍
  - Individual check categories:
    - `npm run test lint`: ESLint.
    - `npm run test types`: Type checking.
    - `npm run test unit`: Unit tests.
    - `npm run test visual`: Visual tests.

- **Visual Regression Testing:** Use custom visual tester in visual scenes dir. Run `npm run test visual` or `npm run test visual debug` for dev. 🎨

> NOTE: For support, check [FAQ][faq], [forums][forums], [wiki][wiki], or [tutorials][tutorials].

That’s the gist. Go get 'em! 🏆

Alright, so you're diving into GitNexus. First off, remember this is under the PolyForm Noncommercial License (check the root README). 

- Need to talk? Go to the GitHub Issues section for bugs or feature requests. Community chats are on Discord, linked in the README.

Dev setup:
- You gotta have Node.js versions right. `gitnexus/` needs `^22.18.0 || >=24.11.0` and `gitnexus-web/` needs `^20.19.0 || >=22.12.0`. Use `nvm install` to set up.
- Clone the repo first.
- For CLI setup: `cd gitnexus && npm install && npm run build`. The `prepare` script builds `gitnexus-shared`. Don't run `npm install` inside `gitnexus-shared/`—that’s just for the web compile.
- If working on the web UI, `cd gitnexus-web && npm install`. If skipped the CLI build, compile shared first: `cd gitnexus-shared && node ../gitnexus-web/node_modules/typescript/lib/tsc.js`.
- Tests? Check TESTING.md.

The CLI build needs `gitnexus-shared/dist` before the typecheck. Uses the TypeScript `lib/tsc.js` from the parent package.

### Hook runtime stuff
- Claude/Codex hooks use `gitnexus-hook`. Edit `claude-hook-runtime.cjs` once.
- `gitnexus setup` installs a launcher. The Claude plugin loads the same hook script. When not available, it gets the npm package.
- Recovery uses the validated package location and has a retry cooldown after failures. Checkouts and filtering are in the runtime.

Bootstrap: `gitnexus-claude-plugin/hooks/gitnexus-hook.js` is the source. Normal CLI build handles this.

### Optional: Containerized dev
- If you want an isolated environment, use VS Code with the Dev Containers extension. Run **Dev Containers: Reopen in Container**. Auth and WSL2 setup details in `.devcontainer/README.md`.

### Branching and PRs
- Use short-lived branches off the default branch.
- PR titles must follow the conventional-commit format (`pr-labeler.yml` enforces this). Descriptions need to cover changes, reasons, verification commands, and any risks or rollback instructions.

### PR Titles Format
- `[(scope)][!]:`
- Allowed types (check `.github/release.yml`):
  - `feat`: `enhancement`, 🚀 Features
  - `fix`: `bug`, 🐛 Bug Fixes
  - `perf`: `performance`, 🏎️ Performance
  - `refactor`: (more labels and details in `.github/release.yml`)

Hope this helps! 🙃

Prisma 8 stuff for newbies! 🚀

- We're on RC mode rn, `8.0.0-rc.N`. Expect changes till final in 4-8 wks.
  - Diffs between RCs are normal. Every RC has a `upgrading/` guide. 📚
  - Only latest RC gets security patches. Prisma 7 gets 18 mos of love after `8.0.0`. 🧪
  - New proj? Use Prisma 8 RC. Existing Prisma 7 apps: move slowly. 🏃‍♂️💨

- Target `main` for Prisma 8, `v7` for Prisma 7 fixes.
  - Tiny fixes: just PR. 🐛
  - Big changes: open an issue first. 🚧 Get feedback before coding. Maintainers reply in 5 biz days.
  - Substantial changes? Coord. on docs, examples, etc. They’ll tell you.

## Setup

- **Node.js:** Use `mise` to match `package.json` (currently `>=24`). `.tool-versions` / `mise.toml` help. CI uses `mise` too.
- **pnpm:** Use Corepack. `corepack enable` and go.
  - Don't install pnpm globally! 🛑
- **git:** Commit signoff must be set (DCO stuff). 👍

Optional:

- **Docker:** Only needed for Cloudflare worker tests (`pnpm test:vite-plugin`). Others use in-built dbs. 🚢

## Running checks

Use Turbo for fast tasks. Choose based on your changes:

- Tiny type errors? `pnpm typecheck`
- Linting? `pnpm lint`
- Unit tests? `pnpm test:packages`
- Examples? `pnpm test:examples`
- Postgres/SQLite e2e tests? `pnpm test:e2e`
- DB integration? `pnpm test:integration`
- Vite plugin/Cloudflare stuff? `pnpm test:vite-plugin`

Hope this helps! 🍻

Hey there! 📝 So, Quill is all about community love. You can get involved in a bunch of ways:

- **Bugs:** Report 'em, detail 'em, repro 'em. Check Github Issues first! 🕵️‍♂️
  - Include: faulty behavior, repro steps, expected vs. actual, OS/browser, Quill version.
  - If you skip details, it'll get autoclosed. 🚫

- **Quick fixes & docs:** Just do it! PRs for typos/docs are super easy to get in. 🚀

- **Feature requests:** Again, check Github Issues. If it's new, be detailed:
  - Feature description, why it's Quill core, your use case, and how it helps your product.
  - Community support goes a long way! 🤝

- **Discuss first:** For big contributions (bugs, features, PRs), talk it out first. Make sure it aligns with Quill's goals. 🗣️

- **PRs:** Fork from main, pass linter, squash commits, add tests, one purpose only, keep the tests green.
  - **Big note:** You're giving up rights to your work by making a PR. 🤷‍♂️

Hey new buddy! Here’s how stuff works in Jest. Don’t get overwhelmed, it’s a bit of a process.

1. **Code of Conduct**: Yeah, there’s one. Check `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` in the repo. Basic respect and all that.

2. **GitHub**: Everything happens on GitHub. No exceptions. Core team and outsiders all do PRs. Same review process for everyone.

3. **`main` is a bit wild**: We try to keep it clean but stuff changes fast. So, `main` might not always work with your app. Watch out for API changes. We’ll try to let you know.

4. **Workflow & PRs**: Before you submit a PR, follow these steps:

   - Fork the repo and branch off `main`. Need a guide? Check: https://help.github.com/articles/fork-a-repo/
   - Open your terminal and:
     - Run `corepack enable` for Yarn.
     - Got Python? Check `python --version` (needed for `yarn install`).
     - Install `node` (use `v20.x`).
     - `yarn install` to get everything set up.
     - `yarn build` to transpile TypeScript and run type checks.
     - Add tests for any new code (use watch mode to streamline).
     - If you touch APIs, update docs.
     - Ensure all tests pass with `yarn jest`. If you’re on macOS, install Mercurial: `brew install hg`.

5. **Changelogs**: For new features and bug fixes, add a changelog entry. Structure it like the existing ones. Use the GitHub interface to edit after you open your PR and know its number and link. Alphabetize entries by package name.

   - For cleanup, refactoring, or dependency updates, use the "Chore & Maintenance" section.

6. **Testing**: Everything needs tests to make sure it works as expected. There are two types: unit and integration.

   - **Unit tests**: If your changes only need a unit test, put it in the `__tests__` directory within the respective package.
   
   - **Integration tests**: If it’s more complex and needs an integration test, find the `e2e/__tests__` directory. Use `runJest.js` for running Jest and test `status`, `stdout`, and `stderr`. Write the files that Jest will run in the other `e2e` subdirectories. Check existing tests for a guide.

Yeah, lot to take in, but you’ll get the hang of it. Good luck! 💪

*Whew, contributing to Project NOMAD can be a bit of a maze, so here's a quick rundown to get you up and running without too much hassle...*

**First things first:**  
- Check out the *Code of Conduct*. Be nice, it's not a party, but you still gotta play nice with others.  
- **Before coding anything big:** open an issue to discuss. No need to dive in and write code only to have it shot down.  
- Quick fixes (typos, small bug fixes) can go straight to a PR though. If in doubt, ask!  

**Setting up your environment:**  
- You need a Debian-based OS (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS is the go-to).  
- You'll need `sudo` or root access.  
- Docker must be running and ready.  
- A stable internet connection is key for dep downloads.  
- Node.js is a must if you're messing with the frontend.  

**Fork & Clone Steps:**
1. Click "Fork" on the top right.
2. Clone the forked repo to your local machine.
3. Add the upstream remote so you can sync later.

**Gotcha:** Don't install a release version of NOMAD on your dev machine. Docker is your friend here, and installing a release can lead to conflicts with ports and volumes. Running a separate Docker env for dev is the cleaner route.

**Workflow High Points:**
1. Sync with upstream before starting new work. Use `git rebase` to keep your history tidy.  
2. Create a feature branch from `dev`. Give it a descriptive name.
3. Make your changes, following the existing style.  
4. If you're touching the AI Assistant or RAG, test thoroughly with metrics. Don't rely on a quick spot check.  

*Remember, the maintainers have the final say on what gets merged, so make it count!*

- Then submit a pull request. 🤞

Hey new person! 😄 So, you wanna contribute to Novu? Cool! Here’s the quick & dirty rundown:

- Before you submit a new issue, **check existing ones first**. No point in opening something that’s already listed. If you find one, you can add info. If not, open a new one. Check the issue form for that.

- If you're fixing a bug, **you gotta give us a repro scenario**. Otherwise, it’s gonna be hard to fix. Use a repo or gist. Mention 3rd-party libs & versions. Detail the failing use case. No repro, no fix!

- **Node.js**: Get Node.js v22.23.0 (LTS) using NVM. Here’s the super-quick steps:
  1. Open terminal
  2. Install NVM if you don’t have it: [NVM GitHub](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm)
  3. Use `nvm install 22.23.0`
  4. Set as default with `nvm alias default 22.23.0`

- **MongoDB & Redis**: Install Redis based on your OS. Windows? Follow this guide. Linux? Follow that guide. macOS? You got it.

- **Optional**: pnpm (for installing new packages) & localstack (only for S3 related stuff).

- **Project Setup**: It’s a monorepo, so once you clone your fork, `npm run setup:project`. For more details, check the guide on running Novu locally.

- **Missing a Feature?**: If you spot a missing feature, request it by choosing "🚀 Feature" when you raise a new issue. Wanna implement it? Propose it first.

- **Coding Guidelines**: Test everything with unit-tests. Use Biome’s default rule guide. An auto-formatter is available.

- **Need Help?**: Got questions or thoughts? Open a GitHub Issue. Or hit us up on Discord.

- **Ways to Contribute**: 
  - Try the API, give feedback
  - Add new providers
  - Tackle or create issues
  - Share thoughts/suggestions
  - Create tutorials/posts
  - Request features
  - Report bugs
  - **Improve docs**: Fix any missing or unclear stuff.

Hey there! So Trilium is this cool note-taking app that helps you build your own knowledge base. It's pretty small, so we love small, focused contributions. 🙌

- First off, check the issues and PRs to make sure no one's already working on what you want to do. Really important!
- For bug fixes or doc changes, just go ahead and open a PR. For features, though, you gotta open a feature request or find one that exists and wait for a maintainer to say 👍. Some PRs get declined 'cause they don't fit Trilium's vibe. Save everyone some time.
- Setting up your build? Go to Env Setup and Proj Struct. 📂

Key constraints:
1. Everything works offline. No loading from CDNs.
2. Keep the bundle size low. New deps gotta be super light.
3. Data should last decades. No proprietary formats w/o import/export options.
4. Talk to maintainers before touching storage, sync, or encryption. They can mess with user data badly.

Bug fixes:
- Test on the latest nightly. If you can't, note which version you checked.
- Give repro steps, logs, or a test. Makes it easier to accept.
- Solve the root issue, not just hide the symptom.

For features:
- Implement something already requested, keep default behavior intact, reuse existing components.
- No new deps or tiny ones that are really useful.
- Be wary of scriptable stuff, duplicates, single-use case settings, or things better handled outside Trilium.

Discuss all features before coding, especially if you're touching default behavior, UI, or new settings. Some areas like mobile apps, encryption, or the storage model are maintainer-led. Get their OK first.

For big features, map out the design and delivery phases. Explain how it won’t mess with users.

PR tips:
- Keep them small and focused.
- Link the issue. Use closing keywords only if it’s fully resolved.
- Add tests for the changes. Check Testing guide.
- Screenshots or short recordings for UI changes are a must.

Hey there! So, you wanna contribute to omp? Cool. Here’s the deal:

- **PRs are open to everyone right now as a trial run.** They might change their minds later, so watch out for that.
  
- **Small changes** (bug fixes, docs updates, and minor tweaks) → just go straight to a PR. Easy peasy.

- **Major changes** (think new subsystems, big UI changes, new dependencies, etc.) → **talk about it in Discord first.** No GitHub issues can replace that chat.
  
  > *Side note:* Issues are for reporting problems or proposing work you’re not already PRing. If there’s already an issue, link to it in your PR.

- **AI contributions:** Use them as tools, not as unattended geniuses. Before you PR:
  - Make sure the AI is within the agreed scope and reject any unrelated changes.
  - Review every file the AI touched, and make sure you understand what it did.
  - Run all the checks yourself and test the changes.
  - Only submit after you reviewed, not letting the AI submit on its own.

- **PR requirements:**
  - You **must** include a sentence in your PR explaining what changed and why. Like: "I reviewed the full diff; this change fixes duplicate PR reviews by reusing the existing delivery guard."
  - **Make sure the changes work.** Just saying `bun check` passes isn’t enough. Actually test the feature/fix/UI.
  
- **Keep each PR focused on one thing.** No unrelated cleanups or drive-by refactors allowed.

- **Licensing:** Contributions are MIT licensed. No CLA or DCO needed. Just make sure you’re allowed to submit your contribution and that you preserve copyright notices and attributions.

- **Review:** Maintainers will review the behavior and your understanding. Respond to feedback yourself and only use suggestions you’ve checked.

- If you skip the prior discussion for major changes, your PR might get closed.

Hey new buddy,

So this AdGuard Home stuff, pretty chill but got some rules. Don't post "+1" comments. Use the :+1: reaction instead. It's better for seeing how much support an issue is getting. Also, don't file issues about localization errors or send updates as PRs. All that is handled through [CrowdIn][1]. And the same goes for filtering-rule lists, they're in a separate repo[2].

Got to follow the template instructions when posting an issue. Make sure you provide the data needed to reproduce the issue. Keep the title in English, rest is good in any language. 

Search first for dupes or questions. If it's a dupe, thumbs it up. If it's a question, check the [Wiki][3] and if you still can't find it, hit up the [Discussions][4] page.

For PRs, discuss first in an issue. Maintainers need to evaluate it before you start coding. Due to a lot of low-effort and AI-generated PRs, they can't review unsolicited stuff. So make sure you chat about it first. If you skip this, your PR might get closed quick.

Follow the [code guidelines][5] for your changes. And, of course, make sure your code passes linters and tests. For backend, it's `make go-check`. For frontend, run `make js-lint`. And yeah, a manual test is often needed too.

Remember, this place is a bit of a noob trap if you don't follow the steps. Good luck!

Alright, so here’s the deal with releasing Recordly:

- We use `electron-builder` + `electron-updater` for macOS, Windows, and Linux auto-updates. This is better than Sparkle.framework for our Electron app.
- When you hit a GitHub release with a tag like `v1.2.3`, `.github/workflows/release.yml` does a bunch of stuff:
  - Checks `package.json` is at `1.2.3` (make sure you bump it first).
  - Builds macOS x64 and arm64 (and gets them notarized).
  - Merges the dual-architecture into one release asset.
  - Builds and signs the Windows installer and Linux AppImage.
  - Publishes everything to GitHub and dispatches the Homebrew tap workflow.

The app checks for updates using:
- `latest-mac.yml` (macOS)
- `latest.yml` (all)
- `latest-linux.yml` (Linux)

Got secret stuff to set (yeah, that's bad, I know):

- **macOS signing**: `APPLE_SIGNING_CERTIFICATE_P12_BASE64`, `APPLE_SIGNING_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_ID`, `APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_TEAM_ID` (needs a `Developer ID Application` cert, not just `Apple Development` - do NOT mess this up).
- **Windows signing**: `WINDOWS_SIGNING_CERTIFICATE_P12_BASE64`, `WINDOWS_SIGNING_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` (Authenticode cert).

**Homebrew tap**: `HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN` (if you want the PR to open auto-magically).

Release flow (keep it simple, silly):

1. Bump `package.json` to the version.
2. Commit and push.
3. Tag it `vX.Y.Z`.
4. Create and publish the GitHub release (use the helper for custom notes + GitHub-generated stuff).
5. CI handles the rest (builds, signs, notarizes, uploads, publishes metadata).

Rebuild an existing release? Just manual dispatch `.github/workflows/release.yml` with the old tag.

P.S. Don’t forget the `zip` target for macOS auto-updates (it’s a pain but necessary). And, `build.yml` is set to `--publish never` to avoid accidental uploads to drafts.

Hey new buddy! Here’s a super quick and messy breakdown of how to get started with Drizzle ORM. 🤓

- First off, Drizzle ORM is maintained by the cool folks like @AndriiSherman, @AlexBlokh, and @dankochetov. 🤝 They need to approve everything that gets merged in. So ya, pretty strict.

- You can contribute in a bunch of ways:
  - 🐛 **Bug Reports**: Got a bug? Head over to the issue form and choose Bug Report.
  - 💡 **Feature Requests**: Wanna see a new feature? Same drill, go to the issue form and choose Feature Request.
  - 😄 **Feedback**: You can give feedback on Discord, add a new ticket in Discussions, or just ping the Twitter account.

- **Setup Before Contributing**:
  - Install Node, pnpm, Docker, and clone the repo. You'll need this for the project.
  - **Repo Structure**:
    - `drizzle-orm/`: Core ORM stuff for all dialects.
    - `drizzle-kit/`: Main stuff and tests for dialects.
    - `drizzle-typebox/`, `drizzle-valibot/`, `drizzle-zod/`: Code for extensions.
    - `eslint-plugin-drizzle/`: For the ESLint plugin.
    - `changelogs/`: All changelogs for the modules.
    - `examples/`: Usage examples.
    - `integration-tests/`: A bunch of tests for all supported databases.
  - To build the project, run a script from the root folder or specific package folder.

- **Commit Messages**: Follow these rules:
  - Clear, concise, and informative. 📝
  - Sign commits before PRs. Check the docs if you're unsure.

- **Contributing to `drizzle-orm`**:
  - **Project Structure**:
    - `pg-core/`, `mysql-core/`, `sqlite-core/`: Core packages for each dialect.
    - `sql/`: Expressions and SQL templates.
  - **Running Tests**: All integration tests create Docker containers with actual databases and run through scenarios. Make sure your tests are clean! 🧪
  - **PR Guidelines**: Coming up next.

- **Contributing to `drizzle-kit`**: Same boat, different river. 🚤
  - Follow the struct and run tests as you would for `drizzle-orm`. PR guidelines apply here too.

Hey new guy,

So you wanna help with Web Check, huh? Cool! But FYI, no AI contributions, they're a no-go. 😄

### Setup:

- Node: 22.23.4+ or 24.16+, yarn, git - gotta have these.
- Chromium and `traceroute` are opt. Just skip stuff if they're not around. (ida about that)

So start the API on 3001 and frontend on 4321. Env vars are in `.env.sample` - optional but check it out.

### Adding a check:

1. Write your API function in `api/ .js`, wrap it in `middleware`. If nothing to show, return `{ skipped: 'reason' }` instead of errors.
2. Make a results card in `src/client/components/Results/`
3. Register it in `src/client/jobs/registry.ts`
4. Docs go in `src/data/checks/ .ts` and list it in `index.ts`

Each check gets its own page at `/ `. Pick a unique id. If it goes to a third-party, add to `publicOnlyChecks` in `api/_common/check-skipper.js`. Need an API key? Handle missing keys with `requireEnv` and list in `.env.sample`.

### Bugs & Security:

Got a bug? Open an issue with repro steps and how you're running Web Check. Security? No public posts, check `SECURITY.md`.

### CoC:

Be nice and constructive. We use the Contributor Covenant. Contributing means you're okay w/ the MIT license.

-End of notes, hope it helps! 🍻

Hey new guy,

So, ya wanna contribute to Remix? Awesome! Here's the skinny:

- Bugs go to GitHub Issues, but only if you can make it happen **every time** (read: minimal, runnable reproduction). No repro, no matter how legit it sounds, gets closed. Got a question? Discord or Q&A Discussions. Got a large doc change idea? Treat it like a feature request. Follow the Proposing Features process.

- Feature requests? Start with a **Proposal Discussion**. Explain the problem, give use cases, and maybe some sample code. Let the community decide if it's worth the API work. **No PRs** unless a maintainer tells you to do it.

- Pull Requests (PRs)? Cool, but they gotta link to the issue they're solving, like: `Closes #1234`. Before you PR:
  - Keep it tight to the issue.
  - Tests? Add or update 'em.
  - Docs? Update when you touch a public API.
  - Add a change file if it affects public behavior.
  - Run the local validation (see below).

- Setup:
  - Grab Remix via pnpm on Node 24.3+.
  - Fork, clone, and do `pnpm install` from the root.

- Validation:
  - Quick feedback: Run the `changed-workspace` command (compares your stuff to `origin/main`).
  - For bigger changes that might affect everything, better to run full tests and typechecks.
  - Formatting check? Just run it, no file changes needed.

- Testing: No build needed, tests run straight from the source.
- Building: TypeScript is your friend.

- Making Changes: Everything's in the `packages` directory. That's the gist, man. Good luck! 🙌

Hey new buddy,

So here's how things go down around here in a bit of a jumbled way. 😄

- First off, if you got questions, head over to the repo's Discussions page. It's like a big chat room where you can ask about stuff, share your thoughts, or just show off how you're using the library. (Totally chill, no judgment here.)

- Now, if you come across a bug or something that's not working right, check the Issues page real quick. Make sure someone else hasn't already flagged it. If it's new, log an issue with full details. Like, what's happening and what you expected. And if you can, throw in a reproduction link (like from CodeSandbox). That's a big help. 🛠️

- Got a great idea for a new feature? Sweet! But first, let's get some community vibes on it. You can start a discussion on the Discussions page or create an issue to outline your idea. Bonus points if you can also throw in some tech details on how it could be implemented or discuss other possible solutions. 🤔

- When you're ready to code (bug fix or new feature), you'll want to get the local setup going. Check out the `examples` folder and make sure to build the SWR assets first. Then, install the dependencies for the specific example you're working on. All examples use Next.js, so you can use its commands for building and running stuff.

- Lastly, if you're updating the documentation, you'll be working in the website repo. Remember to keep the info super clear and user-friendly. 📝

Hope that helps, and yea, we're glad to have ya!

Okay, so here's how it goes down:

- First off, if you're feeling a bit lost, just head over to our Discord `#contrib` channel and ask us. We got your back. No pressure, no crazy rules. Just chill and ask for feedback.

  - **V2**: This is split into 3 parts:  
    1. Server (Haskell)  
    2. CLI (Go)
    3. Console (JavaScript)  
    All of these are versioned by git tags or branch + commit SHA. Also, you need to sign a CLA here. A bot will remind you if you forget.  

  - **V3**: This is just the V3 engine written in Rust. It’s the main event. Check the README.  

- **First timers welcome**: If you're new, we're here to help. Check out issues labeled for first-timers.  

- **Areas for contributing**:  
  - **V2 Docs**: Hey, if you see missing content or errors, just fix them or add to the docs. The guide is at `docs/CONTRIBUTING.md`.
  - **V2 Community content**: If you've got some learn content, add it to the learn tutorials. If you're thinking of a new tutorial, hit us up first to avoid dupes.
    - Also, you can contribute boilerplates, sample apps, or tools.  
  - **V2 CLI**: If you know Go or want to learn it, there are some issues to work on in the CLI.  

- **Ways of contributing**:  
  - **Reporting an Issue**: Before you report, make sure you're on the latest released version. Give us steps, your Postgres version, graphql-engine version, and your provider (Docker, Heroku, etc.). Include server logs if it helps.  
  - **Working on an issue**: We use **t** [note: the text cuts off here, so the rest about working on an issue is missing].

P.S. If you got something cool to add, even if it's not on the list, just submit a PR. We're flexible like that.

Hey new guy/gal,

So, Harbor's a big ol' open-source project, and we're always improving it thanks to users, contributors, and maintainers like YOU! 🙌

**Quick pointers:**
- Join the [bi-weekly community meetings](https://link.to.meetings) (or watch past ones on [YouTube](https://youtube.link)).
- Chat with folks on [CNCF Slack](https://cncf.slack.com) - `#harbor` for users, `#harbor-dev` for devs.
- You can also join the `harbor-users` and `harbor-dev` distro lists (email things).

Follow us on [Twitter](https://twitter.com/project_harbor) too! 😉

**Getting started:**
1. Fork the Harbor repo on GitHub to your personal account. (Remember to change `$USER` to your GitHub username and set `$GOPATH` to your directory of choice).
2. Build the project - follow the build guideline. (The main working dir is `harbor/src`).
3. Set up your dev environment:
   - **Go:** Check the Go version table (ex: Harbor 2.16 needs Go 1.27.2).
   - **Web:** Clarity + Angular. Check the version table (ex: Harbor 2.16 needs Angular 12.0.3 & Clarity 5.3.0).

**Contribute Workflow:**
- **PRs:** Small fixes are cool too. For big changes, document them as issues first.
- Submit PRs in small chunks. A big PR is hard to review. (And make sure each PR doesn't break anything when it goes to `main`).

**Fork and clone:**
- Fork the repo and clone it to your local workspace. (Check out Go's workspace instructions).

Hope that helps! If something's missing or wrong, just shout out. 😊

Hey new guy/gal,

So, contributing to Authelia? Cool! Just hop into our PRs (pull requests) or chat rooms for discussions. Can also drop some coin if you're in that mood. 🤑

Got a bug or a new idea? First, search the repo (repository) to avoid replying the wheel. Then create a bug report or feature request. Simple!

Before diving in, create an issue to discuss your idea. Let the maintainers know too, so no one else tackles the same thing. 🤝

PRs only merge when `authelia-scripts --log-level debug ci` passes and coverage is good. No force pushing to your PR branch after creation, esp. if someone’s reviewing. Commits get squashed on merge.

Exceptions: Adjust commit messages to fit guidelines or rebase. 🧹

If you need a re-review, use the re-request feature, not mentions. 📢

Navigating the codebase can be a maze. If you're stuck, we have chat rooms and emails to help you out. Don't hesitate to ask! 🙏

Hope this helps! Good luck!

Yo, new guy! Quick rundown on how we do stuff around here:

- Read this guide before u do anything. It's important. (And yeah, it's kinda long, but it's worth it.)

- For bugs:
  - Use GitHub issues. Check if the bug is already there or in FAQs.
  - Use the issue template. Describe the problem and how to repro. If u can, attach a minimal repro repo.

- Adding features:
  - 🎟️Proposal: Describe your feature request in detail, add refs or lit. Get community approval.
  - 🎟️Feature Issue: Once approved, describe how it’ll be implemented.
  - 🎟️PR: Implement it, then submit a PR. Link back to the proposal and feature issues.
  - After merge, close all issues.

- Submitting code:
  1. Fork the repo.
  2. Create a branch (e.g., feature-log).
  3. Write your code.
  4. Push to your branch.
  5. Submit a PR. Make sure it follows coding specs & has tests.
  6. Wait for review & merge.

- Commits:
  - Use Conventional Commits. Types: fix, feat, deps, break, docs, refactor, style, test, chore, ci.
  - Scope: transport, examples, middleware, config, cmd, etc.
  - Commit message: "Imperative, present tense, no caps, no dot."
  - Body: Why the change and contrast with prev. behavior.
  - Footer: Note any breaking changes & reference related issues.

- Releasing:
  - Use `kratos changelog dev` to gen a log. Types: Breaking Change, Dependencies, Bug Fixes, Others.

Hope this helps! It's a bit chaotic, but it covers everything. Good luck! 🍀

Hey new colleague! 👋 Here's the quick & dirty on contributing to NSQ:

- Commit in logical chunks. Keep commit msgs clear. 📝
- Tests? If fixing a bug or adding functionality, write a test. 🚀
- Run `fmt.sh` & `test.sh` in the repo root. It's like auto-correct & spell check. 🔍

To submit:
- Push your changes to your forked branch.
- Submit a PR to nsqio's repo. 📝
- When you're done, comment in the PR: "ready for review". 

P.S. It's a bit of a maze, but once you get it, it's smooth sailing! 🚤

Hey new guy/gal, here are some notes on contributing to Delve. It's a bit of a mess but should cover it:

- Contributing to Delve is cool! Any help is appreciated.
- If you're doing a big change, write a design doc or start a convo on the dev mailing list. Other devs & users can weigh in.

Filing issues:
- You gotta answer these 6 qs when filing an issue:
  1. Delve version (`dlv version`)
  2. Go version (`go version`)
  3. OS & arch
  4. What you did
  5. Expected outcome
  6. Actual outcome

Contributing code:

- Install deps as per README.
- Build stuff:
  - Go (check `go.mod` for version)
  - goreleaser v2 needed for `make build`. Install it with: `go install github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser/v2@latest`
- Guidelines:
  * Stick to Go conventions (docs on new stuff, proper punctuation).
  * Test your code, new stuff must have tests.
  * Major changes? Create an issue first.
  * Os/arch specific code goes in os/arch specific files. No Linux stuff in non-Linux files.

Commit messages:
- Follow the commit msg format: subject (what), blank line, body (why).
- Subject < 70 chars, body < 80 chars. Makes it easier to read everywhere.

Code of Conduct:
- Follow the standard Go code of conduct: https://go.dev/conduct

Hey there! So, zap is basically the coolest logging library in Go, and we'd be stoked if you could help make it even better. Here's the lowdown:

- First off, if you wanna add new exported APIs, hit up the [issues page] and open one. It's like a pre-REQ for smoother review convo. And, ya know, be nice! We take the CoC real seriously.

## Setting Up

1. Fork and clone the repo.
2. Make sure tests & linters pass. `make lint` and `make test` are your friends here.

## Making Changes

1. New branch for your changes. `git checkout -b your-new-branch`
2. Make your changes, then re-run `make lint` and `make test` to make sure everything still works.
3. Push to your fork.
4. Use the GitHub UI to open a PR. 🚀

Now, you're in review mode. We try to get back within a few business days, but you know how it is. Might need some tweaks or different ideas. Once approved, a maintainer will merge it.

Tips to get approved quicker:
- Add tests.
- Good commit messages. [Here's a guide](http://tbaggery.com/2008/04/19/a-note-about-git-commit-messages.html).
- Backward compatibility is key. 😶

[issues page]: https://github.com/uber-go/zap/issues/new

Hope this helps, and good luck!

Temporal Server dev setup tips:

- **CLA:** Make sure to fill out the Temporal Contributor License Agreement. No merge without it!

- **Prereqs:**
  * Go (check go.mod for version)
  * mise 2026.10.9+ (manages Go, protoc, protobuf plugins)
    - macOS: `brew install mise`
    - Other OS: check the installing mise guide
  * Temporal CLI
    - macOS: `brew install temporal`
    - Else: download from https://github.com/temporalio/cli
  * docker (optional but super handy)
  * docker-compose (optional: UI, databases, metrics services)

- **Windows:** Install WSL2 + Ubuntu, then follow the Linux steps.

- **Clone & setup:**
  * `git clone <repo url>`
  * `make setup` (installs toolchain, Go, protobuf tools)
  * Use `mise` if you installed Go through mise to get `go` on `PATH`

- **Build:**
  * First build: `make` (installs all build deps)
  * Quick build: `make build` (skip tests)

- **Tests:**
  * Unit: `go test ./...` (no setup needed)
  * Integration: `make test-integration`
  * Functional: `make test-functional`
  * All: `make test-all`

- **Running Server:**
  * Dockerize with `docker-compose up` (optional)
  * SQLite (default): `make run`
  * Cassandra + ES: `make run-cassandra-es`
  * SQLite (file): `make run-sqlite-file`
  * Postgres: `make run-postgres`
  * MySQL: `make run-mysql`

- **CLI stuff:**
  * Create namespace: `temporal namespace register --name default` (use "default" while learning, see samples)

- **Samples:** Go | Java | TypeScript | .NET | Python | Ruby (try the helloworld)

- **Cleanup:** `Ctrl+C` for `docker-compose`, `make clean` for everything else.

Hey there, newbie! 📝 Here are some of the key points you might wanna know about contributing to listmonk:

- **Big news**: Until the next big version (v7.0.0), no PRs for the admin frontend/UI. It's all about moving to a server-side-rendered UI to ditch the Vue setup. So, no Vue/SPA stuff post v7. 🛑✨

- **Docs**: If you spot any errors or want to improve the docs, hit the docs repo. 👍

- **i18n Translations**: Love languages? You can add new ones or correct current translations. There's a handy UI for translations. 🌍🔗

- **PRs**: These are like tricky puzzles. 🧩 Everything has to fit the project's scope, style, and performance. Reviewing them is a huge task. 🏋️‍♂️ So, make your PRs small and focused. 🏃‍♂️ Propose first, then code. 🤝 Multiple features in one PR? Not cool. 😒

- **Squashing**: When a PR is ready, all the commits get squashed into one. 📝✨

- **Respect**: Remember, these are the fruits of the maintainers' labor and love. Be kind and respectful. 💚🌟

Hey there, new buddy! 🤙 So, you wanna know how to do a SOPS release, huh? Here's the mess of what you gotta do. Don't worry if it's all over the place; that's how it works in real life.

- First up, make sure every single change you want in the release is merged into `main`. That means all the PRs tagged for this release milestone need to be in. If some PRs shouldn't be in this release, move them out. 🙄

- You'll need to update the `CHANGELOG.md` file with a pull request. Sum up all the changes since the last release, throw in some PR links. While you're at it, bump the version number in `version/version.go`. 📝

- Get at least one other maintainer to approve that PR and merge it into `main`. Then, check that CI is green on `main`. No reds, please! 🚢

- Now, you gotta make sure your local `main` is up to date. Got that? Great. Time to make a signed tag for the release. This is your command:

  ```
  git tag -s vX.Y.Z -m "vX.Y.Z"
  ```

  Where `vX.Y.Z` is your semantic version, okay? Real smart stuff here.

- Push that tag to GitHub:

  ```
  git push origin vX.Y.Z
  ```

- Then, watch the GitHub Actions magic happen. It'll build everything you need with GoReleaser, craft different packages and SBOMs, and do checksums and signatures with Cosign. It even builds Docker images for Debian and Alpine and pushes them to the GitHub Container Registry and Quay.io. All signed, of course. And it generates SLSA provenance metadata for you. 🎩✨

  - `go test -cpu 1,4 -timeout 7m ./...` for normal testing.

Hey new guy,

So, here's the deal with this project. You're gonna be working on this thing called 'hub', which is basically a wrapper for git to make GitHub integration smoother. Remember, the stuff you do here is gonna be open source, so keep that in mind. Also, there's a CoC (Code of Conduct) - check out `./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` if you're curious or need to refer to it.

You'll need:
- Go 1.11+ (though setting this up can be a pain)
- Ruby 1.9+ with Bundler
- git 1.8+
- tmux & zsh (optional but super helpful for shell completion tests)

If installing Go or Ruby is a hassle, just run `script/docker`. It's a Docker container that has everything set up for you.

For a feature to be a good fit:
- It should be something that helps with GitHub workflows specifically. If it’s just a generic git thing, people will prefer a script.
- If you’re adding a new command like `hub foo`, double-check it doesn’t clash with other Git projects.
- Security fixes? Read the `SECURITY.md`.

How to get it all running:
1. Clone the project.
2. Make sure all tests pass with `make test-all`.
3. Create a new branch: `git checkout -b feature`.
4. Work your magic. Writing tests first really helps!
5. After changes, run the tests again.
6. Fork the project on GitHub: `make && bin/hub fork --remote-name=origin`.
7. Push your changes to the fork: `git push -u origin HEAD`.
8. Open a pull request: `bin/hub pull-request`.

Quick note: Go dependencies are managed with `go mod`. Check `go help mod` for details. Tests for Go are in `*_test.go` files and run with `make test` (super quick). Most of the tests are in Cucumber style in the Features folder. 

Hope this helps! Good luck, buddy.

### Releasing Go-Redis: My Messy Notes

Okay, so you gotta release a new version of go-redis. Here's the quick rundown:

- **Versioning**: Stick to SemVer. Patch for bug fixes (`vX.Y.Z+1`). Minor for new stuff that doesn't break anything (`vX.Y+1.0`). Major for big changes (`vX+1.0.0`). Need to get approval from the team first for majors. Pre-releases go by `vX.Y.Z-beta.N` or `vX.Y.Z-rc.N`. Got that?

- **Checklist Before Releasing**:
  - Master branch is clean and CI is green.
  - All PRs for this release are merged.
  - No open issues in the release milestone (if used).
  - `CHANGELOG` and release notes are up-to-date (ignore dependabot and doc-only changes).
  - Confirm the version number and if it's a patch/minor/major.

- **Drafting Release Notes**:
  - Grab the draft release from release-drafter on GitHub.
  - Add a new section to `RELEASE-NOTES.md` using `.github/RELEASE_NOTES_TEMPLATE.md` as a guide.
  - Pick 3-5 **Highlights** — the top user-facing changes.
  - Remove dependabot and typo fixes.
  - Make sure each PR has contributor attribution and links.
  - If you need a review before bumping versions, open a PR just for the release-notes change. Otherwise, it goes in the release PR.

- **Bumping Versions & Opening PR**:
  - Branch from `master` and name it `release/vX.Y.Z`.
  - Run the release script on that branch. It:
    - Checks that the `TAG` matches semver.
    - Updates all `go.mod` files to point at the new `TAG`.
    - Runs `go mod tidy` in each sub-module.
    - Updates `version.go`.
    - Doesn’t switch branches, commit, tag, or push.
  - Review the changes, commit, and push.
  - Open a PR from `release/vX.Y.Z` into `master`.
  - Wait for CI checks to pass (build, golangci-lint, doctests, etc.).
  - Get at least one maintainer approval.
  - Merge the PR (merge commit so the tag points to the merge SHA).

- **Tagging the Release**:
  - After merging, pull `master`, and do a dry-run of the tagger.
  - Apply the tag with `-t` (`vX.Y.Z` for the top-level and `vX.Y.Z` for each public sub-module, skip examples and internals).

- **Publishing the GitHub Release**:
  - Open the draft release on GitHub (created by release-drafter).
  - Set the tag to `vX.Y.Z` and target `master`.
  - Replace the auto-generated body with the notes from `RELEASE-NOTES.md`.
  - For pre-releases, check the pre-release box.
  - Publish it.

- **Post-Release**:
  - Check pkg.go.dev to see if the release shows up (visit the version URL if needed).
  - Announce on Discord (use the link in `CONTRIBUTING.md`).
  - Close the release milestone if used.
  - Open follow-up issues if anything was deferred.

- **Hotfix/Patch Release**:
  - Branch from the latest release tag: `git checkout -b hotfix/vX.Y.Z+1 vX.Y.Z`.
  - Cherry-pick only the fix commits.
  - Follow the normal release flow but use `TAG=vX.Y.Z+1`.
  - Make sure only the fix is added (ignore other stuff).

Got all that? It’s a bit of a process, but it’ll make sense once you do it a few times. Good luck!

Hey there! So, you wanna dive into excelize, eh? Cool! Just make sure you read the community guidelines before you jump in. Here’s what you gotta do, in kinda no order:

- **Security Issues**: Super important! If you find something, don’t file a public issue. Send it to xuri.me. They really appreciate it and will thank you publicly. No bounties yet, but might happen in the future (cross fingers).

- **Other Issues**: When you hit a snag and want to report it, make sure to check if it’s already in the issue database. If it’s there, hit the "subscribe" button. No need for "+1" comments. If you can re-create the issue or have something to add, comment away. Always include `go env` output and steps to reproduce if possible. Long logs? Post as a gist https://gist.github.com. Remember to remove sensitive data (write "REDACTED" instead).

- **AI Policy**: So, you’re thinking of using AI tools like LLMs? Cool, but you’re on the hook for the code you submit. You have to understand it and explain it. No auto-generated comments or PR descriptions with AI, k? All code is BSD 3-Clause licensed. You must own the copyright or include compatible licenses. AI-generated code might have copyright issues, and you're responsible. They might reject PRs if the copyright is questionable.

- **Pull Requests**: Go for it! Found a typo or a bug? Fix it and send a PR. For major changes, create a GitHub issue first (no big deal). They’re happy to get PRs. If it’s not accepted on the first try, don’t sweat it.

- **Design Proposals**: Want to suggest a design change or a whole new feature? Go ahead! They love when folks get creative and want to improve things. 

Hope that helps! Good luck!

Alright, so here’s the deal:

- **Code reviews**: Everyone needs to get their stuff reviewed. Even the cool kids. No exceptions. 😅

- **Want to regenerate files after changes?**

  - **Docker**: At the repo root, just run the command. You might need to auth with GitHub for `ghcr.io/grpc-ecosystem/grpc-gateway/build-env`. Check the GitHub Package docs for how to do that. It's a bit of a headache, but you'll get it.

- **Making a release**:

  1. Tag it on `main`.
  1. Use command line or GitHub UI to create the release. If using the UI, you can make it a draft and get it reviewed.
  1. Update the release description with highlights, links to PRs, and shoutouts to contributors.
  1. Update `.github/ci.yaml` for the new release version.
  1. Sit back, pat yourself on the back, and give yourself a :clap: for a job well done.

Hope this helps, and good luck! 🍀

Hey there! 👋 So you wanna dive into Keploy? Good call. 🙌 First off, if ya don't know where to start, just hop into our Slack channel and ask. Everyone's super chill there. 

- **Code of Conduct**: Read it and respect it. We take it seriously. 

- **Prereqs**: Git, Go, and Markdown are kinda important. Set up Keploy locally and play around with it to get comfy. 

# How to Contribute?

1. **General Contribution Flow**:
   - **DCO (Developer Certificate of Origin)**: You gotta agree to this for each commit. Use `-s` or `--signoff` when committing. No pseudos here!
       - Example:
           ```
           git commit -s -m "Your commit message"
           ```
       - Add this to your `.gitconfig` if you haven't already.
           ```
           [alias]
           ci = commit -s
           ```

2. **For Changes**:
   - **GitHub Issues**: Create issues for anything more than typos or small fixes.
   - **Fork and PR**: Fork the repo and send your PRs. All branches from your fork.

3. **Setting up Docs Locally**:
   - Fork the repo.
   - Clone it with:
       ```
       git clone https://github.com/yourusername/keploy.git
       ```
   - Go into the directory and start editing.
   - Docs will auto-publish when PR is merged: https://keploy.io

# Keploy Contribution Flow

- **Keploy Server**:
   - **Report a Bug**: Use the Bug Report template. Be detailed!
   - **Feature Requests**: Got an idea? Use the Feature Request template.
   - **Close a Bug**: Go find those "Good First Issues" and solve 'em!

- **Keploy Documentation**:
   - **Docusaurus 2**: Static site generator. Make changes without needing a browser.
   - **Keep Docs Up-to-Date**: Use the Doc Improvement template. We might miss updating docs when shipping features.

Remember to check out the full Keploy Docs Contrib for detailed guidance. Good luck! 🍀
