## Dev Setup

### Prerequisites (messy, but you need 'em):

- **Node.js**: 20.19+ or 22.12+ (use 22.12.0 as per `.node-version`)
- **pnpm**: 10, use `corepack enable` once, then you're set.
- **Rust**: 1.95; rustup takes care of it on first build.
- **Platform-specific Tauri 2 stuff**: 
  - Windows: Microsoft C++ Build Tools, WebView2 (usually preinstalled on Win 10/11)
  - macOS: Xcode Command Line Tools
  - Debian/Ubuntu: Use install command from CI.

No need to install Tauri CLI globally; `pnpm install` does it.

### Quick Start:

- `pnpm dev`: Starts Vite on `http://localhost:3000`, then the Tauri window. If port 3000 is taken, it fails, no auto-switch.

### Useful Commands:

- `pnpm dev`: Dev server (hot reload)
- `pnpm build`: Prod build + packaging
- `pnpm build:renderer`: Frontend build only, goes to `dist/`
- `pnpm typecheck`: Strict TypeScript checks (unused imports/params are errors)
- `pnpm format`: Format `src/` with Prettier
- `pnpm format:check`: Check code formatting in `src/`
- `pnpm test:unit`: Run frontend unit tests
- `pnpm test:unit:watch`: Watch mode for frontend unit tests

Rust backend (inside `src-tauri/`):

- On a fresh clone, first run `mkdir -p dist` (or `pnpm build:renderer`) at the root; otherwise, cargo fails due to missing frontend output.

### Local Build:

- `pnpm build` signs auto-update bundles; you need `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY`. For debugging, `--debug` works (use JSON file on Windows).

## Testing

- **Frontend**: vitest runs `*.test.ts(x)` under `tests/` and `src/`. Tauri calls are mocked with MSW in `tests/msw/`. Component tests use @testing-library/react.
- **Backend**: unit tests next to source (`#[cfg(test)]`), integration tests in `src-tauri/tests/`. CI runs `cargo test` on Linux, macOS, and Windows.
  
> **Real config isolation**: Some tests read/write `~/.cc-switch` and `~/.codex`. Use `CC_SWITCH_TEST_HOME` to point at a temp dir. Don't change `HOME` or you'll trigger a full rebuild.

## Architecture

- **SSOT**: Everything (providers, MCP, prompts, etc.) stored in `~/.cc-switch/cc-switch.db` (SQLite).
- **Device-level settings**: Settings specific to this machine.

> Side note: if you're confused, just ping someone older than you.

Alright, so you want to jump into Rust, huh? Cool! First things first, head over to the #new members Zulip stream. It's like the front desk – everyone can help you out there. 🏡✨

Got a bit more time? Dive into the [rustc-dev-guide] (that's the compiler dev guide) or the [std-dev-guide] (the std lib guide) – they're super helpful. But honestly, start with the Zulip stream. 🙌

Now, if you're messing with submodules or subtrees, don't just barge into `rust-lang/rust`. For submodules, go to their specific repo. Subtrees? Same deal, unless it's a big change like a compiler update. Then you gotta hit `rust-lang/rust`.

The [rustc-dev-guide] is your buddy for understanding how rustc works. It's like a map of the compiler's insides. Read it before you dive in, trust me. 🧪

Oh, and about LLMs (that's Large Language Models, by the way)? There's a policy on Forge and guidance in the dev-guide. 👀🔍

Got stuck? Need help? Zulip is your go-to. But there’s also the internals forum. Both are chill and can hook you up with a mentor. 🤓

If a compiler error message sent you here, and you want to file an ICE (internal compiler error) report, just find the section on bug reports in the dev-guide. Open an issue on the template they provide. 🛠

Alright, so configure Bun's dev env. It'll take you around 15-25 mins, depending. Make sure you got like 10GB of free space, 'cause you're gonna need it for the repo and all the build stuff.

If you're on Windows, you gotta go to this specific guide. [link to guide]

There's an alternative with Nix. It's a flake that gives you all the dependencies without needing to run as root. Just one of those things to save you time and hassle.

For installing dependencies manually, use your system's package manager. [tabs for different OS]

Bun is written in Rust and needs a specific nightly toolchain. You'll find the version pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml`. Use `rustup` instead of your distro's packages. The build scripts use `rustup` to auto-install and update the pinned nightly. [tabs for different OS]

You need a release build of Bun already installed. We use the bundler to transpile minify code and generate scripts.

Optional: Install `ccache`. It caches compilation artifacts, which can significantly speed up builds. [tabs for different OS]

Install LLVM 23.1.1 — this is super important as Bun needs it for memory allocation. Most likely, you can install it through your system's package manager. [tabs for different OS]

If you can't install LLVM through your system, you gotta do it manually. Make sure Clang/LLVM 23 is in your path. [tabs for different OS]

> 🚨 Ubuntu users, note that installing LLVM through your package manager may cause issues. You might need to use the manual method. 🚨

For debugging, you can use `bun run rust:check` to type-check Rust changes without linking. `bun run watch` will auto-check Rust changes every time you save. `rust-analyzer` in VSCode should just work if you install the recommended extensions. Use "CodeLLDB" for debugging. Set `BUN_DEBUG_ = 1` for debug logs. You can dump logs into a file with `BUN_DEBUG= .log`. Debug logs are removed in release builds.

Codegen scripts are essential:
- `./src/codegen/bindgen.ts` generates bindings for Rust, C++, and TypeScript.
- `./src/codegen/cppbind.ts` auto-generates Rust FFI wrappers for C++ exports.
- `./src/codegen/bundle-modules.ts` bundles built-in modules like `node:fs` and `bun:ffi`.
- `./src/codegen/bundle-functions.ts` handles global JS/TS functions.

Hope this helps! 🤞

So, here’s the deal with Zed contributions:

- Keep PRs to 3 max at a time. Start with just one & finish it. 1st PR is a big deal & helps out the rest. P.S. Old PRs tend to get forgotten as `main` changes. 🤷‍♂️
- Talk to us before coding new features. No code without a green light. Start with a GitHub discussion or find a confirmed issue. Zed Feature Process is a must-read before big changes.
- Everything in Zed forums is Code of Conduct territory. 👮‍♀️

Things we won’t merge:
- **Extension stuff**: new langs/themes, Zed Extension API changes, new file icons (no out-of-the-box SVGs), features that are too complex for the number of users, giant refactors, non-trivial changes without tests, style-only changes, and LLM-generated work you don’t get.
- **Docs**: fix or extend the docs, look at the docs issues.
- **Issues**: close issues curated for the community (good first issues & good non-first issues).
- **Bugs**: fix bugs with confirmed repro steps or browse by label.
- **Enhancements**: make existing stuff work for more people, like support for more platforms.
- **Small features**: little things like keybindings or actions.
- **Community Programs**: join Let's Git Together or The Guild.
- **Featured boards**: build stuff we’ve invited contributions for.

**AI Policy**: Use LLMs, but always have a human in the loop. No autonomous agents. No full LLM-generated comms with maintainers. If you’re using LLMs for translations, put the machine translation in quotes & include the original in your native language. If sharing context from an AI chat, use a quote block, disclose it, & add commentary.

**Send changes**: build & test locally before a PR. MacOS, Linux, Windows, or FreeBSD. Self-review, AI-assisted or not. 🧪

That’s about it! 🤓

Hey there, new buddy! Here's how you can dive into contributing to our project without getting too tangled up. 

- Look for issues tagged with `help wanted`. These are like, "Hey, we need some help here!" and you can just jump in. No need to ask first... just lemme know you're on it so someone else doesn't start working on the same thing.

- For issues without `help wanted`, check with us first. Like, "Hey, I wanna work on this," so we can be sure everyone's on the same page with the solution. 

- If you find a `bug`, that's a good one to tackle. But stay away from `needs-decision` or `needs-design` – those are tricky and not ready for pull requests yet. 

- And, no new features without talking to us first. We appreciate new ideas, but every new feature is a long-term upkeep thing, so we need to make sure the team's cool with it.

- Oh, and about that AI thing... we've got a policy. Make sure you follow it; otherwise, your PR might get closed.

**Setup time:**

- Rust and a C compiler are your essentials. On Ubuntu or Debian, you can get a C compiler with `sudo apt-get install build-essential`. Fedora? Use `sudo dnf install gcc`.

- On Windows? Get NASM via WinGet and add it to your `PATH`. If you don't, a prebuilt blob will be used, but setting `AWS_LC_SYS_PREBUILT_NASM=0` ensures NASM is used if it's installed.

**Testing:**

- Use `nextest` for testing. To run a specific test, it's like `nextest run test_name`. Logging in tests? Use `UV_INTERNAL__TEST_RUST_LOG`.

- For all tests and accepting snapshot changes, it's `nextest run --accept`. Updating snapshots for a specific test? `nextest run test_name --update-insta`.

- Python stuff: `pyenv install 3.9.16` and `pyenv install 3.10.9`. The storage dir? Set with `UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR`.

- Snapshot testing? Use `insta` and `cargo-insta` for an easier review. Check the docs for `cargo-insta`.

- And for certain tests, make sure Git and Git LFS are installed.

- To run your dev version of uv, just `cargo run --`. Add `UV_INTERNAL__BUILD_GIT_INFO=1` if you want git info in your builds. 

**Formatting and Linting:**

- Linting? Install `shellcheck` and `hawk` separately.

That's pretty much it! Good luck, and if you get stuck, don't hesitate to ask. 🙏

Hey there! So you're diving into Union? Cool. Here’s the rundown:

- **First off**: Always start with an issue. Talk about the changes with the core team first. Don’t jump into coding without discussing. (This is super important)

- **Reading up**: Check out the `ARCHITECTURE.md` file. It's your guide to the build system. You'll need `nix` for running tests (`nix flake check`). Important: Only use nix v2.25. If you're on macOS, use NixOS 24.11 for nix v2.24. Not earlier versions, they break stuff. (Side note: I've been bitten by this one a few times)

- **Adding new packages**: Use nix for any CI updates. Your changes must work across all supported targets. No x86_64-linux-specific stuff. Reuse existing Nix files if possible. CI will pick up any new checks automatically.

- **PR time**:
  - Write a good description. Mention the related issue with `closes #XXXX`.
  - Conventional commits only. They must be signed. (Trust me, signing commits is a good habit)
  - Before pushing, run `nix fmt` and `nix build .#checks.your-architecture.spellcheck`.
  - Rebase over main if you have conflicts. No merge commits here. (Clean git history = happy maintainers)

- **Reviews**: Be quick with fixes. Fewer PRs = happier team. Stay cool and polite, even if it feels harsh at times.

- **After merge**: You're officially a contributor! 🎉

- **Editors**:
  - Helix: No extra setup needed.
  - VS Code: Get Nix Environment Selector and Dprint Code Formatter.

Good luck!

OK, so here's the lowdown on contributing to Alacritty. Don't get overwhelmed, just take it one step at a time.

- **Feature Requests:** Go to the Alacritty issue tracker. Seriously, first check if anyone's already asked for the same thing. You don’t want to be that guy with duplicates. Enhancement and missing feature issues are your friends here.

- **Bug Reports:** Again, use the Alacritty issue tracker. If you can pinpoint the exact commit that broke things, that'd be awesome. Helps everyone.

- **Patches / Pull Requests:** Everything has to be sent via GitHub as PRs. For newbies, look at the "help wanted" and "easy" issues. Rust version in `alacritty/Cargo.toml` should be checked (`cat alacritty/Cargo.toml | grep "rust-version"`), and keep it consistent. Also, bump `alacritty_terminal`’s version using semver when needed.

  - **Testing:** Before you hit "send" on that PR, make sure everything’s tested. Run `cargo test` to start. If there’s new functionality, add tests, either with the `#[test]` annotation or ref tests. For ref tests, create a release version of the binary and use `--ref-test`. Copy those generated files to `./tests/ref/NEW_TEST_NAME`, and enable it by editing `ref_tests!` in `./tests/ref.rs`. 

  - **Performance:** If your changes touch performance (throughput or latency), benchmark using `vtebench` (check its README) and `typometer` (for latency). Stay on Rust stable, not nightly, for consistency.

  - **Documentation:** Document your code where it makes sense. Follow `rustfmt` rules. Changes in `config.rs` should be reflected in man pages. User-visible changes (not just code refactoring) go in `CHANGELOG.md`. Big changes to `alacritty_terminal` get their own entry in `alacritty_terminal/CHANGELOG.md`. Style guides matter here.

  - **Style:** CI will catch formatting issues. If it fails, `rustup component add rustfmt` and `cargo fmt` are your friends.

So yeah, that’s the gist. Hope this helps! 🤓

Hey new buddy! 🚀 So here’s the *super* condensed version of getting up to speed with Warp (skip the Slack join if you’re already in tho):

- 🐛 Bug fixes: Once it’s clear what's going on, you’re good to go. Just make sure it's reproducible.
- 🚀 Features: Need to be marked `ready-to-spec` then `ready-to-implement`. Spec first, then code.
- ❌ `warp:reserved-internal`: Oz (our bot) will block you if you try to PR these. Just don’t.
- 👀 Got a big idea? Specs are where the magic happens. Both product and tech specs under `specs/`.

**Oz**: Our auto-triage bot. Does a lot of the heavy lifting: triages issues, reviews PRs. Once it gives a 👍, human review follows.

**How it works**:
- Start with an issue. Discuss there before any PRs.
- Feature requests need a spec PR first (product + tech under `specs/`).
- Bugs can go straight to code if it's clear what's wrong.
- Your PRs must have manual testing proof. Don’t forget that.

**Ready labels**:
- `ready-to-spec`: Problem known, design open. Go write that spec PR (product + tech docs).
- `ready-to-implement`: Time to code. No spec needed for bugs if it's obvious.
- `needs-mocks`: Wait for the design mocks from the team. Don't rush this.
- `warp:reserved-internal`: Warp team’s stuff. Leave it.

Got a triage issue? Ping **@oss-maintainers** to get it looked at.

**Filing an Issue**:
- Avoid duplicates. Use the `/feedback` command if you're in Warp already.

Bug reports need:
- Clear title
- One-paragraph summary (keep going...)

So, yeah, you wanna contribute to Rustlings, cool! Just make sure you’re clear on the LLM stuff:

- Update an old exercise? ➡️ PR

Fork repo, commit changes. Git issues? Ask for help! 🤗

Adding an exercise:
- File: `exercises/yourTopic/yourTopicN.rs`

- Solution: `solutions/yourTopic/yourTopicN.rs` with explanations.
- Metadata: `rustlings-macros/info.toml`. If no tests, add `test = false`.

OK, so here's the deal:

- **Changelog**: Update the `CHANGELOG.md` if you're changing stuff like `bat` behavior, syntax mappings, themes, build stuff, etc. (Not needed for doc updates or typos) [!NOTE: CI checks for this, so if you don't need it, just ignore the fail]

- **New Syntaxes/Themes**: Read the Customization section in README. No new default themes atm. For mapping file patterns to syntaxes, read here.

- **Regression Tests**: Add 'em! They ensure stuff works and makes code reviews easier. For functional changes, add a test to `tests/integration_tests.rs` (look at existing tests for guidance). For theme/syntax changes, read the Syntax tests section in `assets.md`.

- **Ensuring `bat` is available for tests**: Syntax test script (`tests/syntax-tests/update.sh`) needs `bat` available. If you only built with `cargo build`, add `target/debug/bat` to PATH. If installed with `cargo install`, `bat` is in `~/.cargo/bin` (usually in PATH).

Hey new colleague,

So here's the quick and dirty on contributing to Meilisearch. First off, props for considering this!

- Remember, you can contribute in ways other than coding. Tutorials, docs, bug reports, etc. (Look into `milli` and `charabia` if you're into languages).

- **Table of Contents:**
  - AI tools: Nope for external contributions. You gotta own your stuff. Seriously, no Copilot or ChatGPT in your PRs.
  - Assumptions: Know GitHub, read Meilisearch docs, join the Discord (it's legit helpful).

- **How to Contribute:**
  1. Check and create issues (this is where you can gauge if your change is even wanted).
  2. Fork Meilisearch on GitHub.
  3. Create a new Git branch.
  4. Dev workflow (check out the section on this).
  5. Make changes (disclose AI usage in PRs).
  6. Submit PR to `main` branch. Maintainers will get back to you, but it might take a while.

- **Dev Workflow:**
  - Use the `--release` flag to test.
  - Use `LINDERA_DICTIONARIES_PATH` (like `$HOME/.cache/meili/lindera`) to speed up builds.
  - Set `MEILI_NO_VERGEN` for faster dev, but keep it off for prod builds (it borks things).
  - For tests, we use insta (cargo-insta). Update snapshots if they change.
  - Macros for snapshot hashes to save space. For debugging, export `MEILI_TEST_FULL_SNAPS`.

- Testing docs locally:
  - Need Node.js and npm.
  - Generate OpenAPI file (more on this later... ran out of time lol).

Hope this helps! Hit me up on Discord if you need anything. Cheers!

OK, so listen up! Here's how we do releases. Got two types: minor (like 1.20) and patch (like 1.20.1). We use GitHub actions, so it's mostly automated. 

### For Minor Releases:
- Usually once a week, on Tuesdays.
- **Version bump PR**: Automated action bumps the version on `main`. Review & merge this.
- **Release branch + PR**: Once merged, will automagically make a `release/` branch and open a PR with a QA checklist.
  - Test locally (`just run-ui`).
  - If you gotta, cherry-pick last-minute fixes into the branch.
  - Download & test the zip from the PR.
  - When all green, tag & release as per the PR instructions.

### For Patch Releases:
- Happens right after a minor release is tagged.
- New branch is created (e.g., `release/1.25.1` from `release/1.25.0`), with version bumped & a PR open.
- Cherry-pick fixes into this branch.
- Tag & release when ready.

### TL;DR:
- Minor: Tuesdays, bump, test, tag.
- Patch: Post-minor, fix, tag.

Hope that’s clear! 🤞

Okay, so here’s the real lowdown on contributing to Helix, in like, the real talk way:

- You can totally look at those "good first issue" tags if you're new. 🐝
- Packaging help needed on lotsa distros! So, if you've got the know-how, go for it.
- For debugging with the Helix log file, remember:
  - Use `log::info!`, `warn!`, or `error!` to get stuff in there (`log::info!("helix!")`).
  - Add verbosity with `-v` (more `v`s for more verbosity).
  - If you want to see logs in a file: `cargo run -- --log foo.log` and then `tail -f foo.log` in another term.
- For dev, use `cargo run` for faster compile times instead of the release version.
- And if you want even faster compiles, try mold.
- Missing your favlang? Just throw in a tree-sitter grammar and some syntax highlight queries. It's pretty straightforward.
- If you're not using Nix and are getting rust-analyzer from rustup, you might need to do `rustup component add rust-analyzer` 'cause the `rust-toolchain.toml` doesn't fetch it.
- Check out `architecture.md` for the inner workings.
- To generate documentation from the code, run `xtask` stuff. For live preview of the book, install mdbook and do the usual `mdbook serve` thing.
- For testing:
  - Unit tests/docs tests: `cargo test --workspace`.
  - Integration tests: `cargo integration-test` is your friend. Set log level with `HELIX_LOG_LEVEL=debug`.
  - MacOS users: might hit "Too many open files" errors. Fix with `ulimit -n 10240`.

Got it? MSRV (Minimum Stable Rust Version) policy:
- Keep MSRV low for easy builds.
- When Firefox bumps MSRV, check Ubuntu packaging and update Helix in `Cargo.toml`, `.github/workflows/build.yml`, and `rust-toolchain.toml`.

Hope this helps! Good luck! 🚀

Hey new guy! So you're looking at contributing to Jan? Cool beans! 

*Jan's the offline AI assistant, like ChatGPT but totally private and local. Your contributions are super valuable. Let's make this thing accessible!*

Quick notes on components:
- **Web App**: React UI
- **Core SDK**: TypeScript, extension sys
- **Extensions**: Frontend support mods
- **Tauri Backend**: Rust native
- **Tauri Plugins**: Hardware & sys plugins

How it works:
- **JS Layer**: Web App imports SDK & extensions → all in browser/webview
- **To Backend**: Web App, SDK, Extensions → Tauri IPC (e.g., `await invoke('app_command', data)`)
- **Backend → Plugins**: No IPC, direct Rust lib calls
- **Response**: Plugin → Backend → IPC → Requester → UI updates

Example: Loading a Model
1. **Web App**: User clicks download
2. **Extension**: Handles download logic
3. **Tauri Backend**: Downloads file
4. **Extension**: Prepares model
5. **Tauri Plugin**: Starts llama.cpp
6. **Hardware Plugin**: Detects GPU, optimizes
7. **Model ready!**

Setup:
- Prereqs: Node.js ≥ 20.0.0, Yarn ≥ 4.5.3, Make ≥ 3.81, Rust (Tauri)
- On macOS: `xcodebuild -downloadComponent MetalToolchain`

Contributions:
- **Bug Reports**: Make sure it’s not reported yet → open an issue with system specs & error logs. Steps to reproduce are golden! Screenshots are key!
- **Enhancements**: New issue with title & description. Explain usefulness. Mockups are great!
- **Code Contribution**: Pick your path:
  - Frontend UI: `web-app/`
  - Shared API: `core/`
  - Backend: `src-tauri/`
  - Business logic: `extensions/`
  - Backend handler: `src-tauri/plugins/`
- Fork, new branch, make changes, commit, push, open PR against `main`

Code Standards:
- TS/JS: Required, ESLint + Prettier, functional React, no `any` (seriously!)
- Rust: `cargo fmt` + `clippy`, `Result` for errors, document public APIs

Got questions? Ping someone on Slack. Good luck! 🎉

Hey there, new buddy!

Quick rundown on how to jump into this project without drowning:

- Got a Q or want to suggest a feature? Go to the Discussions board instead of opening an issue, okay?

- Before you start, make sure you've got:
  - git
  - Node at LTS
  - Yarn v4 (enable corepack too)
  - Rust, stable version

- Start easy with "Good First Issue" and "Help Wanted" tags. Docs in `packages/core/core/src/Parcel.js` can help you get comfy.

- For big changes, propose and get feedback first. Then, pull request steps:
  1. Fork and new branch for your changes. (Important: keep 'em separate for cleaner PRs)
  2. Run `yarn` to get all the depen'
  3. If it's a fix or new feature, test it out. Ask for help if it's too complex.
  4. Commit `yarn.lock` if it's changed.
  5. Make sure CI steps work locally.

**Reminder:** Don't touch `package.json` versioning. 🚨🚨🚨

- Pull request details: include examples and test cases. Patience needed for reviews!

- Dev workflow cmds:
  - `yarn check-ts`: TS type checking
  - `yarn format`: for consistent code style
  - `yarn lint`: checks for stylistic errors
  - `yarn test`: run the tests

- Debugging: VSCode or CLion. VSCode uses JS Debug Terminal or Node.js config. Rust needs CodeLLDB extension. If breakpoints aren't working, try `PARCEL_WORKERS=0` or set `PARCEL_MAX_CONCURRENT_CALLS`.

- Plugins: disable caching with `--no-cache` flag or `shouldDisableCache: true` in Parcel options.

- Working from examples:
  - Don't commit examples!
  - Copy `simple` example in `packages/examples`, tweak it, and `yarn build`. Set `--no-cache` on `parcel build` for local changes.

- Testing outside of monorepo:
  - Use `/path/to/monorepo/packages/core/parcel/src/bin.js build src/index.html`. Make sure no `@parcel/*` plugins are installed.

- Releasing a new version:
  - Use the parcel3 workflow. From Actions tab, run with version (e.g., `3.0.0-alpha.1`) and check `publish`. Builds and publishes Parcel, and versions JS packages in `packages-v3` with Yarn.

Hope this helps, and good luck! 🍀

OK, so you're diving into OpenHuman, huh? Grab a coffee and let's get started. Here's the super messy, totally unofficial guide to getting up and running:

- **Code of Conduct**: First things first, we got a Code of Conduct we all gotta respect. So, you know, be nice.

- **Getting Started**:
  - Read the README – it's your ticket to knowing what we're actually doing here.
  - Check `docs/gitbooks/en/developing/architecture.md` for the current system architecture. Seriously, read this, it's super important.
  - Before you start coding, check the open issues and Discussions. Don't reinvent the wheel.
  - Stuck? `docs/SUPPORT.md` is your friend. It breaks down all your questions into neat little buckets.
  - Security issues? Don't file public issues. Go to `SECURITY.md` instead. It's all spelled out there.

- **Development Setup**:
  - **Prerequisites**:
    - Git: Latest stable version. You know, for cloning and stuff.
    - Node.js: Version 24.0.0 or newer. Make sure you got it.
    - pnpm: Version 10.10.0. This is a must for the repo.
    - Rust: Version 1.99.1. Install it with `rustup`. Also, install `rustfmt` and `clippy`.
    - CMake: Current stable. Optional, only needed for building `aws-lc-sys`.
    - Ninja: Current stable. Required on Windows. Without it, `git push` will fail because `rg: command not found` error.
    - ripgrep (`rg`): Current stable. Used for `lint:commands-tokens` step.
    - Vendored module sources: Run `git submodule update --init --recursive vendor/` before building.
    - macOS tools: Xcode Command Line Tools. Needed for desktop builds.
    - Linux desktop packages: You need GTK/WebKit/AppIndicator build deps.

  - **Windows-specific setup**:
    - Visual Studio C++ Build Tools: Install option 1 (Default installation). This gets you MSVC v143 and the Windows 11 SDK. It's a ~5.4 GB beast, so prepare for it.
    - Rust: Install as usual with `rustup`.
    - CMake and Ninja: You need Ninja as the CMake generator. `scripts/run-dev-win.sh` will exit if it can't find it.

So, that's the deal. Good luck, and if you get stuck, just ping me or someone else. We're all here to help.

Hey new buddy,

CODEWHALE - it's all about the community, so thanks for joining. We accept inputs, fixes, and even just saying "this looks off". It all matters.

**Quick Place Guide:**
- Bug/crash/surprise: Bug report
- Idea/feature: Feature request or just chat it up in Ideas
- Looks/reads/feels feedback: Feedback
- Questions: Use Q&A or Discord
- Security: Private advisory (never public issue)
- Fixes for open issues: Pull request (link the issue)
- Translations/providers/models/docs fixes: Pull request (no issue needed)
- New features: Open an issue first (why)

Not sure? Open an issue. Maintainers will move it if needed.

**Feature Requests:**
1. Open a feature request. Describe what you're trying to do and obstacles.
2. Tick "I want to open a PR" if you plan to build it.
3. Maintainer will reply with next steps or what's undecided. Pull requests are then quick to merge.

No issue first? We still read it, but it might take longer.

**Standing Projects (no issue needed):**
- **Translations:** Term lang packs, translated READMEs, website, and docs. Check `docs/i18n/`, `docs/zh_hans/`, `docs/id/`. Localization matrix and Chinese group help.
- **Providers/Models:** Add missing providers, new models, or update info. Use `check-provider-registry.py`.
- **Docs:** Fix typos, unclear steps, missing examples, outdated instructions.
- **Bug Fixes:** Describe the bug in the PR if no issue yet.
- **Planned Work:** Take anything in a milestone or "help wanted." Claim by commenting on issue to avoid duplicates.

**What Planned Work Issues Give You:**
- **Status:** What's on `main`, commit links, and next steps.
- **Ways to Help:** Files to read, `scripts/dev-test.sh` for local testing, and "done" criteria.

Got any questions, hit me up. I'm still figuring it out too. 🤓

Hey there! So Nushell is awesome and we're glad you're here! First things first, you gotta talk to the core team before making any BIG changes. Check out the "Proposing Design Changes" section for that.

When you're doing PRs, use this as your guide. There's a "Release Notes Summary" section in the PR template. This is super important for the user! Keep it short and sweet, focus on user impact only. Don't worry about filling it until your PR is almost done.

- **Release Notes Summary:** Brief, user-focused info. Can be a couple sentences. If it's a big change, use examples/screenshots. If you're stuck, talk to a core team member, they'll help you out.

- **Structuring Summary:** Small changes = 1-2 sentences. Big changes = multiple lines, add examples/screenshots. If your PR has multiple changes, you can add a more user-friendly title.

Other stuff:
- **Setup:** Gotcha covered in the docs.
- **Tests:** Run 'em all, no skips.
- **Useful commands:** Check the guide.
- **Debugging tips:** Super helpful, don't skip.
- **Experimental options:** Use with caution.

Git etiquette:
- Follow the guidelines in the repo.

Resources:
- FAQs in the developer docs.
- Platform support policy.
- Rust style guide.

TL;DR: Talk to the team, write clear release notes, follow the Git rules, and check out the FAQs. Good luck! 👍

Hey there! Just throwing down some quick notes to help you out. This is the gist of contributing to Firecracker, but it's a bit of a zoo. 🐶

- Lots to do here in Firecracker. Issues are up for grabs – especially the `good first issues` ones. Also, chime in with your use cases and ideas. Open an issue or hit us up on the Slack if you need quick feedback. 📢

- **Contribution Workflow**:
  1. Fork Firecracker, create a branch (give it a good name!).
  2. Make your changes, meeting the quality standards (check out the `tests/README.md` for how to run those).
  3. PR to the main branch. 🚀
  4. Add 2 reviewers (maintenance folk will help you here if you're new). Tweak your PR as per review comments, updating it with `git commit --amend` and force-pushing.
  5. Once it's blessed with 2 approvals, a maintainer will merge it.

- **Request for Comments (RFC)**:
  1. Same as above, but prefix your PR title with `[RFC]`.
  2. Discuss your proposal on the PR page or other channels, then update the PR with the discussion outcome.

- **Quality Standards**: Set up a pre-commit hook with those two commands they mention. `lint` checks and `checkstyle` runs for code quality. Note: if you run `checkstyle` solo, ditch the `--no-clippy`.

- Remember:
  - Separate logical changes into commits.
  - Each commit must pass unit and style tests.
  - Unit test coverage should go up.
  - New functionality needs integration tests.
  - Document public functions.
  - Commit messages gotta be descriptive (look at `tests/README.md` for examples).

- Oh, and `unsafe` is a big no-no. Use it only if necessary, and always comment why it's needed. 🛑

Hope this makes sense! Feel free to ask lots of questions, and good luck! 🍀

Hey new colleague! 🌟 Here's how we do things around here, super informal style:

- **Code Quality:** Everything follows the same rules, no matter who writes it. We use the repo’s formatter/lint settings, not your own. If you’re using AI or something, only use the skills inside `.agents/skills/`.

- **Code Formatting:** Use the repo’s `rust-toolchain.toml`. If your local setup doesn’t match CI, check your compiler, formatter, and Clippy versions against the shared style contract. For Rust changes:
  - Use `cargo fmt --all --check` and look at what it changes.
  - For behavior changes, run focused tests and Clippy. No point in testing if nothing is affected.
  - Only add compilation checks if needed (dunno why someone would default to `--all-features`, that’s crazy).

- **Quick Commands:** Check out the Makefile for shortcuts. For example:
  - `make test` needs `cargo-nextest` installed. Do `cargo install cargo-nextest --locked` or get the binary from https://nexte.st/docs/installation/. If all else fails, you can use `cargo test` but it ain’t reliable.
  - Some checks are Python-based (needs 3.11+). Make will sort this out but macOS typically has an older version, so install Python 3.12 with `brew install python@3.12` or use `uv run --python 3.12`. You can pin a specific interpreter with `RUSTFS_PYTHON=/path/to/python3.12`.
  - For a full breakdown of tests and what they do, check `docs/testing/README.md`.

- **Automated Pre-commit:** `make pre-commit` is quick, just formatting, repo guards, and compiling. `make pre-pr` is more thorough, covering everything, including checking CI gates before merging. Don’t skip CI just because you’re feeling lazy!

Hope this helps! Let me know if you have any questions. 🙃

Yo, welcome aboard! 😄

First up, you gotta clone the repo if you haven't already. If you did, make sure to init those submodules:

```
git submodule init
```

Rust is a must, duh. And you might need to install some other stuff depending on your system. Check that out later.

P.S. Got an email thing to set up? Mailpit is your guy. 📬

Before you start breaking things, get the tests to pass. Golden tests take forever, so skip those unless you're messing with models. 🏃‍♂️💨

Want to use a GPU? Make sure you have the right drivers:

- **CUDA for Nvidia** - Win, Lin
- **ROCm for AMD** - Win, Lin

Running Tabby with `cargo` is pretty much the same as Docker. For GPU accel:

- CUDA (NVIDIA):
  ```bash
  cargo run --bin tabby-server -- --gpu=cuda
  ```
- ROCm (AMD):
  ```bash
  cargo run --bin tabby-server -- --gpu=rocm
  ```
- Vulkan:
  ```bash
  cargo run --bin tabby-server -- --gpu=vulkan
  ```
- Metal (Apple M1/M2):
  ```bash
  cargo run --bin tabby-server -- --gpu=metal
  ```

You should see some output after compilation. Default is `localhost:8080`.

### Crates (Project Layout)

- `/crates/tabby` - Core app, main binary
- `/crates/tabby-common` - Shared interfaces and types
- `/crates/tabby-download` - Downloads models
- `/crates/tabby-scheduler` - Jobs for syncing and indexing
- `/crates/tabby-inference` - Interacting with models
- `/crates/llama-cpp-bindings` - Rust to C++ bindings
- `/ee/tabby-webserver` - Webserver with priv management and chatbot
- `/ee/tabby-db` - DB for the webserver
- `/ee/tabby-ui` - Webserver frontend

### Picking an Issue

Search for "open" and "good first issue" and go for it! If stuck, hit up Slack or mention someone in the issue.

### Code Review

Wow, new buddy, let’s dive into this. First off, you gotta set up your dev environment. Here’s the deal:

- Add Wasm target. 🖥️
- Install cargo-make. 🛠️

To see all the tasks, run `cargo make list`. Important ones are in the tests.

### Tests

Run all tests with `cargo make test`. 

- **Browser Tests:** Uses Geckodriver. If you use Firefox Developer Edition, you might hit an issue where `firefox-developer-edition` isn’t in the PATH. You can fix this by either installing the standard Firefox or creating a symlink. 🦊
- **Fetch Service Tests:** Needs httpbin server. If Docker is around, it'll set it up. Else, set `HTTPBIN_URL`. 💻
- **Macro Tests:** Update `stderr` files after changing tests, especially for `html!` macros. Use Rust 1.56 for the right errors. Run `cargo make test-overwrite` in `yew-macro`. 🚀

### Spell Checking

Use typos. CI runs it on PRs. Locally:

```bash
cargo make spell-check
```

False positives? Config in `_typos.toml`. 📝

### Linting

Check with `cargo make check`. Fix with `cargo +nightly fmt`. 🛠️

### Benchmarks

Use js-framework-benchmark. Clone bakape/js-framework-benchmark and read the README. 👍

### Writing APIs

Think about the user. Check out these guides:

- Rust API Guidelines
- Elegant Library APIs in Rust

### Website

Website source is in the `website/` directory. Mostly markdown edits. `website/README.md` has more details. 📝

Alright, so... Atuin! Cool! Here are the super important things to remember:

Alright, so yeah, we need contributors! But first things first:

- **CLA**: You gotta sign this Contributor License Agreement (CLA). It's a thing. Check if you've already signed it for Google (yep, that Google). If not, go sign it. Visit the link to check your agreements or sign a new one. 🖊️

- **Community Guidelines**: Oh, and yeah, we follow Google's Open Source Community Guidelines. Read 'em. 📜

Once that's out of the way:

- **Code Reviews**: Everything needs a code review, even if it’s from an insider. We use GitHub pull requests (PRs) for this. So, yeah, read up on GitHub Help for PRs. 🤓

- **CI Smoketest Credentials**: If the OAuth refresh token in the GitHub Actions smoketest needs updating, you gotta do this:

  1. Set creds file to output JSON
  2. Authenticate with the needed scopes
  3. Export and set the GitHub actions secret
  4. Clean up

  Got it? Remember, use the GitHub CLI (`gh`). 🛠️

- **Changesets**: Every PR needs a `.changeset/ .md` file. Use `patch` for fixes, `minor` for new features, `major` for breaking changes. Check out the AGENTS.md for more info. 📝

- **Input Validation & URL Safety**: This CLI is ready for AI/LLM agents. So, user inputs are suspect:

  | What you're doing | What to use |
  |---|---|
  | File path (`--output-dir`, `--dir`) | `validate_safe_output_dir()` or `validate_safe_dir_path()` |
  | URL path segment | `encode_path_segment()` |
  | Query parameters | `reqwest .query()` builder (no string interpolation here!) |
  | Resource name in URL (`--project`, `--space`) | `validate_resource_name()` |
  | Enum flag (`--msg-format`) | `value_parser` in `gmail/mod.rs`

  Got all that? 😬

- **Testing Expectations**: 

  - Happy-path and error-path tests for new validation logic.
  - Use `#[serial]` for tests that change the CWD.
  - Canonicalize tempdir paths.
  - Before submitting: run `cargo test && cargo clippy -- -D warnings`.

  Phew, that's a lot. 🤪

Gotcha! So here’s how you handle contributing to the Linera protocol in a way that’s less formal and more like quick notes:

- Use GitHub issues for tracking improvements, features, and bugs.
  - **Feature requests:** Always discuss with the team first to make sure it gets accepted. No surprises!
  - **Bug reports:** Make sure your report is super clear. Give detailed steps to reproduce the bug. No half explanations.
  
- **PRs (Pull Requests)**:
  1. Fork the repo and branch off `main`.
  2. Add tests if you’ve added new code. No code without tests!
  3. Update docs if you’re changing APIs. Keep it updated!
  4. Always run `cargo test && cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features`. Got to make sure everything compiles.
  5. Auto-format your changes with `cargo +nightly fmt`. CI won’t be happy if you skip this.
  6. Repeat steps 4 & 5 for Wasm if it applies. Don’t forget!

  Note: For a clean commit history, use `git rebase -i` and force push. It’s a pain but it helps the reviewers. Only push to `main` if a team member has accepted the PR.

- **Naming conventions**:
  - Rust: camelCase for types (like `GarageDoorOption`).
  - Local variables: snake_case and shorter when possible (`garage_door_option` -> `option` when clear).
  - Collections: go plural (`let values = vec![1, 2, 3];`).
  - Single letter vars (`i`, `x`, `n`) are okay for short-lived integers, like in loops.

- **API coding**: Follow Rust API guidelines.

- **Docs**:
  - Every public item needs a `///` doc comment.
  - `#[allow(missing_docs)]` is only for:
    1. Generated code (e.g., from `tonic::include_proto!`, etc.), add `#![allow(missing_docs)]` at the module level.
    2. `thiserror` enum variants with `#[error("…")]`.
    3. Big enums where docs would just restate what’s obvious.

  Remember: docs are your friend. They help others understand what you've done, and it’s a lot easier than digging through code. (Except for those big enums, of course. Clearly, those are the exception to the rule.)

Quick notes on contributing to wezterm. Seriously, every little bit helps, even fixing typos. 🙏

- **Docs**: There's never enough! You can pretty much do anything to improve them. 🚀
  
  - Build 'em yourself with `build-docs.sh`. It's cool 'cause it auto-reloads in your browser. Pass args to `mkdocs serve` for more info.

- **Sys-specific stuff**: Instructions are Ubuntu biased. Write `get-deps` script steps instead of stuffing the README. 💻

- **Coding**: Yay! If new to Rust, check out the Rust guide. 🦀

  - Build from src: Need local Rust toolchain & specific deps. Windows has extra steps, check the guide. 📘

- **Folders**: 
  - `term`: Core terminal model code, agnostic of windowing systems. Very `xterm` compatible! Check this out: [https://invisible-island.net/xterm/ctlseqs/ctlseqs.html](https://invisible-island.net/xterm/ctlseqs/ctlseqs.html)
  - `src`: GUI renderer code. GUI changes go here. 🖥️

- **Iterating**: Use `cargo check` to sanity check, type-check only, super fast. Use `cargo run` for quick tests in debug mode. 😎

  - Use gdb for examining local vars. Start WezTerm with `wezterm-gui start --always-new-process` to see Mux logs. Test custom config files with `wezterm-gui --config-file ./test-conf.lua …`.

- **Tests**: IMPORTANT! Include tests with your changes. Add comments for clarity! 📝
  
  - Run tests with `cargo test`.

- **NixOS VM Testing**: For clean env testing, use `testing-on-gnome` or `testing-on-plasma` VMs. Make sure Nix is installed and flakes are enabled. 🧪

- **Resolve an issue:** Either prove it's not a bug or submit a PR that fixes it. Make sure it's reviewable and clear what changes you're making.

### General help

Got stuck after reading docs? Open an issue asking for help. In return, please contribute a doc PR to help others.

**Reminder:** Check out the Rust Code of Conduct [coc]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md for what’s expected 'round here.

That's more or less it! Go on and get started. 😊

Hey there! So, Rocket is a pretty cool project, but it's a bit of a beast. You gotta know what you're getting into. First off, **read this doc before you start** – don't ask why, just do it.

**Pull Requests 101:**
- Got a PR in mind? Better read up on [Code Style Conventions], [Commit Message Guidelines], and [Testing] first. Seriously, it's not optional.
- If you're tackling an open issue, got to check out [Resolving an Open Issue]. If you're adding something new, make sure no one else has proposed it. Look at [issues] and [pull requests]. Follow [Implementing an Unproposed Feature] if it's truly new.
- For everything else, check out [Other Common Contributions].

**Quality Bar:**
- **Comments:** Complex stuff needs comments.
- **Docs:** Public functions = gotta have doc comments with examples.
- **Style:** Follow the [Code Style Conventions].
- **Simple:** Keep it simple and idiomatic.
- **Tests:** Write tests for everything new or changed. Must pass them.
- **Focused:** Do what you're supposed to do and nothing more.

**Squashing Open Issues:**
1. First, check if someone’s already proposed a solution. If not, comment on the issue with your proposed solution. Include test cases and examples. _This is super important!_
2. Write a failing test case. If you can't write real tests (e.g., new API), write a mock one. _This'll guide you._
3. Start coding the basic functionality. Pass the tests, and submit the PR. _Don't mess with docs yet._
4. Wait for a review. If no review after a few days, ping a maintainer. Once reviewed, integrate the feedback. Once it passes tests and fits the project, it's conditionally approved. Then you polish: docs, style, and more testing. _Merge when it's shiny._

**New Feature?**
- **Do not** submit a PR without first proposing the design and getting feedback. We take features _super seriously_ because they affect usability.
- To propose a new feature, create a [new feature request] issue.

Hope this helps! Good luck! 🚀

Cap = Loom alternative, video messaging thing. Still pretty new so stuff changes a lot.

- Want to help? 🙏
  - Bugs? Report them.
  - Got ideas? Hit us up on Discord.
  - Code contributions? Submit a PR.

Setup madness:
- Node 24+
- Rust (1.88.0 via rustup), but the desktop app needs its own toolchain which rustup handles
- Bun 1.4.4
- Docker (use OrbStack, it's cool)

Got all that? Sweet, now:
- `bun install`, then `bun run env-setup` (asked about what you're doing, Docker, MySQL, etc.)
- `bun run cap-setup` (installs FFmpeg and friends)

Windows & Mac gotchas:
- Windows: make sure llvm, clang, and VCPKG are installed. Mac: cmake.
- `bun run cap-setup` doesn't cover these yet tho.

Running stuff:
- `bun run dev` for both desktop & web
- `bun run dev:desktop` or `bun run dev:web` for just one

Desktop app (`@cap/desktop`):
- Rust + GPUI, check out `apps/desktop-gpui` (README has all the build details)
- `bun run dev:desktop` to get started
  - macOS: saves state, rebuilds on save
  - Windows/Linux: build/run once, first build takes a while

Oh, and permissions on macOS? Give 'em to Terminal.app, not Cap, or it'll be a headache.

Where are my recordings? Look here:
- macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/so.cap.desktop/recordings`
- Windows: `%APPDATA%\so.cap.desktop\recordings`
- Linux: `~/.local/share/so.cap.desktop/recordings`

Web app (`@cap/web`):
- `bun run dev` or `bun run dev:web` with Docker for DB/S3
- Just web? Go to `./apps/web` and `bun run dev`

P.S. This guide is a WIP; stuff might change. Good luck! 🍀

Alright, here's the deal with the Docker build workflows in the fhevm repo:

- **We only build Docker images if relevant files have changed.** This way, we skip unnecessary builds and save time. #win

- **If no changes happened, we re-tag the existing images.** So every commit on `main` or `release/vx.y.z` always gets a corresponding Docker tag, even if we don't rebuild.

- **Deterministic build cancellation:** If multiple PRs get merged at the same time on `main` or `release/vx.y.z`, only the latest commit's workflow will run. This is handled by the `is-latest-commit.yml` workflow. 🙌

---

The `is-latest-commit.yml` workflow:
- Uses `git ls-remote` to get the latest commit SHA from the branch.
- Compares it to `github.sha` (current commit).
- Outputs `is_latest: true` if the current commit is still the latest. Otherwise, `false`. #skip rest of the workflow

---

`check-changes-for-docker-build.yml` workflow:
- On `push` to `main`/`release/vx.y.z`, it finds the most recent commit with a published Docker image.
- Uses `dorny/paths-filter` to check if relevant files have changed since that commit.
- Tells us if we need to rebuild and gives the base commit for re-tagging.

---

`re-tag-docker-image.yml` workflow:
- Just creates a new tag for an existing Docker image without rebuilding. Quick and easy.

---

**Patterns for Docker build workflows:**
- **Simple Pattern (Single Image):** Used for single image builds. Decision logic is right in the job `if` conditions.
- **Complex Pattern (Multiple Images):** Used for workflows that build multiple images. A `build-decisions` job handles the logic for each service. Less duplicate code here.

---

**Deterministic Build Cancellation:** To avoid the race conditions when PRs get merged fast:
1. `is-latest-commit.yml` checks if the current commit is still the latest on `main`.
2. If it is, proceed with the build or re-tag. If not, skip.
- This only applies on `main` pushes. 🚫 other branches

- **Concurrency groups** still prevent duplicate builds of the same service, but `is-latest-commit` checks handle the coordination across workflows.

Alright, so ya wanna hack on eza, huh? Got a few things u gotta know first:

- Read the Code of Conduct (Contributor Covenant). It's important.
- Make sure ur commits follow Conventional Commits & Semantic Versioning.
- Check out the Security Policy.
- Know that it's FOSS (Free and Open Source).

Now, for the fun part - hacking:

1. Install Nix with the "experimental" flakes. Super important.
2. Install `direnv` too. It saves a lot of hassle.
3. When in the eza repo, `direnv allow` if ya got `direnv`. Otherwise, `nix develop` works in a pinch.
4. Dev environment includes checks, lints, and a pre-commit hook to keep ur commits clean.

Commands u’ll use a lot:
- `nix flake check`: sanity checks.
- `nix build`: build time.
- `nix build .#test`: run those tests.
- `nix build .#clippy`: clippy time.
- `nix fmt`: automagically formats ur code.
- `just itest`: integration tests.

For non-nix users:
- Use traditional `pre-commit` hooks. Install with `brew|pip install pre-commit` & run `pre-commit install -c .pre-commit-config-non-nix.yaml`.

For compiling the manual pages:
- Need pandoc. Nix flake should have it covered.
- Try `just man` to compile Markdown into manual pages. Ends up in `target/man`.

Libgit2 is a dep for certain features. If it's giving u issues, use `cargo build --no-default-features`.

For musl compile:
- Need `vendored-openssl`. Full command: `cargo build --release --target=x86_64-unknown-linux-musl --features vendored-openssl,git`.

Read more about tests in the "testing on eza" doc.

Creating a PR:
- Use the pull request template.
- Make sure ur changes work. Document how u tested in the PR.
- Check for regressions.
- If ur PR adds a flag:
  - Add completions for bash, zsh, fish, nushell.
  - Update the man page.
  - Add ur option to the help flag.
  - Add ur option to the README.md.

Before submitting:
- Run `nix flake check` & fix all issues.
- Use `nix fmt` for formatting.
- Most clippy issues can be fixed with `cargo clippy --fix` (but maybe fix 'em yerself for practice).

Hey new guy! 😄 Here's how we roll around here, kinda messy but get stuff done:

- **GitHub**: For all discussions, bugs, q's, etc. Might change as we grow.
- **Discord**: Casual hangouts, but keep it clean, Code of Conduct applies.

- **Rust setup**: Use `rustup` to get the stable toolchain.
- **Clone the repo**, then `cd tools`.
- **Build all packages**: You'll use the `rome` bin in `rome_cli`.

- **Just (the tool)**: Makes life easier. Install it with your OS pkg mgr, way better than `cargo install`.
  - Run `just install-tools`, and you're set to hack with Rome & Rust! 🚀

- **Testing**:
  - Run all tests: `just test`.
  - For a single crate: `just test <crate-name>`.
  - For doctests: add `--test-args=--doc` to the command.
  - **Snapshots** with `insta`: If it fails, use `cargo insta accept/reject/review`.

- **Checks**: Before committing & opening a PR, run `just check`.
  - This runs CI: format, lint, tests, gen code. Everything should be green 🟢, then commit all.

- **Language Server**: Build with `just build`, use `--release` for benchmarks.
  - **VS Code Extension**: Install from Marketplace, set `"rome.lspBin"` in VS Code to the bin path.
  - Windows lock: Can't mod an exe while running, so recompile Rome when the extension is off.
  - Stop daemon: Use `rome stop` with editor closed.
  - Build from source: `cd editors/vscode` & run `just build`, make `rome_lsp.vsix` & install with `code --install-extension rome_lsp.vsix`.
  - **Logs**: Check `rome-logs` in the temp folder for any daemon activity.

- **User files**: Add local dev stuff to a global gitignore, not within Rome.

- **Node.js**: For backend dev, build `wasm-nodejs` & `backend-jsonrpc`.

That's it! Hit me up if you're stuck or have q's. Good luck!

So, uh, creating a release... here's how it goes down:

- Major versions get detailed summaries. Minor versions, like weekly or as needed, but no big fuss. Version format is `0.x.y` where `x` is major and `y` is minor. Got it?

- `crates.io` releases: all auto. Configured in `release-plz.toml`. Run by the `Release-plz` workflow.

1. Need a new demo gif? Use vhs (check README for install).
2. Switch to `images` branch, move `demo2.gif` to `examples/`, commit, push. (Side note: vhs is kinda cool once you get the hang of it...)
3. Get permalink and add `?raw=true` for the image URL. Update the main README. Don’t add the gif to git directly 'cause binary files are a pain in the butt.
4. If there are breaking changes, note them in `BREAKING-CHANGES.md`.
5. Commit and push changes to `main`.
6. Every `main` push: `release-plz` opens (or updates) a release PR that bumps `Cargo.toml` and updates `CHANGELOG.md` (generated via `git-cliff`, config in `cliff.toml`).
7. Merge that PR into `main` and it'll trigger the release job: tags the release (like `ratatui-v0.30.2`), pushes to `crates.io`, and creates a GitHub Release. Keep an eye on the `Release-plz` workflow to make sure it finishes up.

Phew, that’s the gist. Good luck!

Hey there! 😄 So, you're diving into Vector, cool! Here's what you need to know, kinda messy but it'll get you through:

- **GitHub & Pull Requests 101**: You gotta be comfy with GitHub and the PR workflow. 🚀
- **Read the Docs**: Make sure you've read Vector's docs. 📚
- **Vector Community**: Don't hesitate to reach out for help; the community is your friend. 👥
- **AI Policy**: If you're gonna use AI in your work, read the AI Policy first. 🤖

---

### Your First Contribution

- For big PRs or breaking changes, **get an issue first**! Check if one exists or open a new one. 🤔
  - This'll give you a vibe on if your change will fly.
- **Fork the repo** if you're not a part of the team already. 🍴
- **Create a new branch** and then make your changes. 🍂
- **Submit a PR** to the main repo. Wait for a Vector team member to review; it could take a bit. 🕒

#### New Sources, Sinks, & Transforms

- If you're adding a new source, sink, or transform, awesome! 🎉
  - Check if a GitHub issue exists, if not, open one to discuss.
  - Maintainers will look at your proposal with this checklist:
    - Can this be done with an existing component? (e.g., Azure Event Hub = Kafka sink) 🤔
    - Can we wrap around an existing component? (e.g., Axiom = Elasticsearch) ✨
    - Is there enough demand for this? How painful is the workaround for users? 🤦‍♂️
    - Are you or the org behind the service doing this? Are you committed to maintaining it? 🌿
    - What's the complexity and maintenance burden of this? 🤔
    - How will you test and QA this? 🧪

---

### Workflow

- **Git Branches**: Create new branches for changes. 🍃
- **Git Commits**: Keep your commits neat and tidy. ✨
- **Style**: Follow style guides. 📖
- **GitHub PRs**: Make your PRs clear. 🚀
- **Reviews & Approvals**: Get your PR reviewed and approved. 🧑‍💼
- **Merge Style**: Know how to merge stuff. 📝
- **CI**: Continuous Integration, gotta love it. 🤖
- **Releasing**: How to release your changes. 🎉
- **Testing**: Run your tests, both daily and for flakey ones. 🕵️‍♀️
  - **Running Tests Locally**: Make sure you can run tests locally. 🏡
- **Dependencies**: Keep an eye on your dependencies. 🔗

---

### Legal

- **CLA**: Sign the Contributor License Agreement if you're outside the team. 📝

Hope this helps! Hit me up if you have any questions. 📧

Hey there,

So, Prime Agent is chill - everything's on GitHub. First things first, don't even think about sending a PR or using Issues for new stuff. Go to Discussions and pick a category: general Q&A, bug, or feature request. Always check if someone else has already posted something similar. Be detailed but no API keys or tokens, okay? 🙏

For security stuff, PM the maintainers directly. Don't freak if your Issue gets closed - they'll point you to Discussions.

Maintainers decide when to create an Issue from a Discussion. If they do, it's 'cause they're thinking about it. But don't jump into coding yet - wait for a direct invite. No invites, no PR. Period. 🛑

Now, for making actual code contributions, you gotta be a trusted contributor. That means the maintainers have to vouch for you. How do you get there? Get involved in Discussions, help out with issues, do some testing, add to docs, y'know, be helpful. No formal app, just be a reliable member of the community.

Once you’re in, and a maintainer invites a PR, here's what to do:
1. Keep it simple. Only the changes related to the Issue/Discussion.
2. Follow the dev rules in AGENTS.md and use those Makefile commands (`make check`, `make deny`, `make windows-cross`).
3. Update tests if the behavior changes.
4. Run checks locally and explain 'em in your PR.
5. Don't go off-script with refactors or adding new stuff.

If your PR gets closed, it might be 'cause it strayed from the task or didn't fit the big picture. Just remember, stay focused and be patient. It’s a team effort!

Alright, so here's the deal for contributing to RustPython. Super welcoming place, and they've got a **Discord** where you can get guidance if you need it. 

First off, to find stuff to work on:
- Check out issues tagged as `good first issue`, super helpful for beginners.
- Browse through the issue tracker for any other open issues.
- You can bump CPython compatibility by increasing unittest coverage. Look at this pinned issue for what needs to be updated.
- Go through the source code, especially the built-in functions and object methods. These are usually the simplest to contribute to.
- Run `python -I scripts/whats_left.py` to find any unimplemented methods.

**AI Policy**: All AI contributions gotta follow the AI Policy here or it’ll get closed. No exceptions.

For setting up your dev environment:
- Make sure you’ve got the latest stable Rust version (e.g. 1.92.0). Use `rustc --version` to check.
- If you’ve got `rustup`, update to the latest stable: `rustup update stable`.
- If you don’t have Rust, do `rustup toolchain install stable` to get it.
- Need CPython version 3.15 or higher. Install via package manager, Python website, or using Anaconda.
- On **macOS**, if `libffi-sys` compilation fails, ensure `autoconf`, `automake`, and `libtool` are installed. Use `brew install autoconf automake libtool` to get them.
- Optional: Install `pytest` using `python3 -m pip install pytest` if you want to test Python snippets.

**Code Style**: 
- Rust code uses the default `rustfmt` style. Just run `cargo fmt` to autoformat.
- Use `cargo clippy` to lint the Rust code.
- Custom Python code should follow PEP 8. We use `ruff` for that.
- And `cspell` for spell checking, ensuring everything is spelled right.

**Testing**:
- Python snippets in `extra_tests/snippets` can be tested with `pytest`.
- Rust unit tests: `cargo test`.
- `rustpython-capi` tests: run from its own directory.
- Python unit tests: compile RustPython and run the test module.

Test options:
- `-j N` for parallel testing (where N is usually the number of cores, like `-j 4`).
- `-v` for verbose mode.
- `testname` to run a specific test (e.g. `test_cmath` in `Lib/test/test_cmath`).

Example:
- All tests in parallel: `cargo test -j 4`.
- Only `test_cmath` verbosely: `python3 -m pytest Lib/test/test_cmath.py -v`.

**Linux Testing from macOS**: Use Apple’s `container` CLI. Check out the one-time setup and running tests sections.

**Profiling**: Build in `release` mode... (didn’t get to finish this part in the official guide) but that’s basically how you set it up and what you do.

Hey new person,

So, you wanna contribute to Gleam? Cool! First things first, read the [code of conduct][coc] (it's a must), just to stay on the right side of things. [coc]: https://github.com/gleam-lang/gleam/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md

If you find a bug, check [GitHub issues][issues] to see if it's already there. If not, open a new one. Could be a compiler crash, wrong return value, or just unclear docs. Don't overthink it; open a ticket and we'll figure it out. [issues]: https://github.com/gleam-lang/gleam/issues

For code contributions, read the `docs/compiler/README.md` file first. It's like the blueprint for this whole shebang.

Steps for code changes:
1. Grab an issue or open one if you're adding something new. Comment that you're working on it. Might need to discuss the details if it's a big change.
2. Update `CHANGELOG.md`.
3. Open a pull request and make sure tests and build pass, else CI will fail.
4. The Gleam team will review and might give feedback. Could be a few rounds of this.
5. Once approved, it gets rebased into `main`.

Quick note: No AI contributions allowed, just us humans here (😎).

For communication, keep it human-written. No AI summaries or generated text. Use tools for spelling and grammar if needed but disclose if the message was translated from another language.

For local dev, you'll need Rust, Erlang, Elixir, NodeJS, Deno, and Bun installed for compiler tests. For language integration, just Rust, Erlang, and NodeJS. If you don't have Rust or Cargo, use a Docker sandbox (command in the dir).

Rust dev tips:
- Use `GLEAM_LOG=trace` for debugging.
- Clippy errors? Run it locally and upgrade Rust to the latest stable version if you still hit issues.

Hey there! So, you wanna contribute to Wasmer? Cool! Here’s a quick rundown:

- **Issues & Feature Requests**: Use the issue template. If it’s a bug, give us a failing example so we can replicate it. 🚨 **If it’s a security vuln, don’t do it in a public PR!** Follow the private process in SECURITY.md. Public fixes before disclosure can be dangerous.

- **Code Style**: Write comments that explain the "why", not just the "what". And keep your functions short and focused on one thing.

- **Lint and Format**: CI won’t like you if you have lint or format errors. So before you push:
  - Run `make lint` to check everything.
  - `cargo fmt` will format most stuff, but it skips `lib/wasix/tests/wasm_tests`. Use `rustfmt --edition 2024` for those.

- **Pull Requests**: 
  - For big changes, open a GitHub issue first. Check if it’s a go.
  - Title format: `fix(Singlepass):`, `feat(wasix):`, `feat!:` for breaking changes, `chore:`, `deps:`.
  - Before submitting: `make lint`, then `cargo test` in the crates you changed, then a CLI build.
  - **Don’t touch** `CHANGELOG.md` or crate versions manually. 🚫
  - If you’re touching macOS or musl stuff, add the `macos` or `musl` label. CI needs it.
  - Oh, and don’t commit submodule pointer bumps in unrelated PRs. 🤦‍♂️

- **Common Build Issues**: 
  - If you get `Didn't find usable system-wide LLVM`, you need LLVM 23. Install it or build with `ENABLE_LLVM=0`. Check the Building Wasmer from Source doc for more.

Hope this helps! 😄

Okay, so you wanna get into xi-editor? Cool, start by reading the docs and check out some issues and PRs to see what's up. Join Zulip or IRC to chat with others; you can sign up with your GitHub. Clone the repos you like and make sure you can build and run tests. If something’s broken, report it by opening an issue. 

When you open an issue, make sure you include all the details you can think of. Like, if it’s a bug, what are the steps to reproduce it? And if it’s a feature request, explain what you want and how it would work. Use the GitHub search to check if someone else has already raised the same thing.

Got questions or wanna talk about features? Dive into the discussion issues on GitHub. Be nice though, remember everyone’s at different levels. Don’t be afraid to ask for clarifications; if you’re confused, others probably are too.

If the docs are confusing, open an issue or PR to fix them. New contributors are great for this since you can spot where things are unclear.

To really get a grip on things, review other people’s PRs. If you don’t understand something, ask! And testing changes, especially fixes and new features, is super helpful. Just check it out and see if it works, try to break it, and report back.

When you’re ready to make a change, find something to work on. Look for issues tagged 'help wanted' or 'easy' to start. If you can't find anything, hit up Zulip or IRC for suggestions, or just play around until you see something that's missing. 

Before diving in, think about whether it’s a small fix or something bigger. If it’s small, you can probably just go ahead, but for bigger changes, you might want to discuss it first.

Yo! So you're diving into the release process, huh? Here's the deal in no particular order:

Starts with version x.y.0-snapshot, gotta find it in all Cargo.toml files. 📂

For the CHANGELOG:
- Tag issues with Enhancement or Bug
- Add a target milestone
- PR description starts with a verb, e.g., "Fixes, Enhances, etc."
- Link to the issue(s)

Release process:
- Kick off the `release.yml` workflow on `master`. Fill in `Desired delivery version` with `x.y.z`. It'll do a bunch:
  - Clean old release 🧹
  - Make `release/x.y.0` branch
  - Update all toml, crates, and docs to `x.y.0`
  - Generate CHANGELOG
  - Commit updates 📝
  - Tag `x.y.0`
  - Draft GitHub release
  - Make PR from `release/x.y.0` to `master`
- Test it out on some external project
- Change the draft release to public on GitHub 🚀
- Accept the PR with `/accept` 🆗
- Go for `update-branch-version.yml` workflow on `master`, put in the `desired SNAPSHOT version`. It'll make a `bot/update-branch-version-master` branch, update all toml, crates, and man with it, and commit all changes.
- Accept that PR with `/accept` 🆗
- Manually build and push other packages like chocolatey, winget, brew, node, docker, etc... 🚛

Hotfix steps:
- Create branch `release/x.y.z` from tag `x.y.z` and bump the patch version. Like `release/6.1.1` from `6.1.0`
- Work on a fix branch then merge to `release/x.y.z`
- Run `release.yml` workflow on `release/x.y.z`, fill in `Desired delivery version` with `x.y.z`
- Same steps as above for tagging, drafting, and publishing
- Close PR from `release/x.y.z` to `master` and manage commits manually for a neat history. 🧹

Post-release:
- Push to Chocolatey, Winget, Docker, Brew, and crates.io 😅

Hope this makes sense! 🤞

- Easy issues? Look for `help wanted` or `good first issue` tags.

- LLMs? Fine for reviewing/issues/code understanding. But no coding with LLMs unless a real human reviews, edits, tests & signs off. Slop or sounding like a LLM? You're banned. 🚫

Hey there! So you wanna contribute to Burn, huh? Cool! Here's the scoop:

- First off, check out the open issues. Look for those tagged as `good first issue`. Those are usually the best for newbies. You can also open a new issue if your idea isn't already there. But make it short and clear. No one likes a rambling issue. 🤦‍♂️

- Got questions or just wanna chat? Join us on Discord. It's like our virtual watercooler. The Contributor Book is your go-to for setup and common tasks. Also, if you're into coding, read AGENTS.md for PR stuff and other repo tips.

- When you're ready to submit a PR, keep it tight. Title and a short description of what you did and why. Link to the issue (if there is one). Some test results can be good too. Small and focused PRs are preferable. Big, messy PRs are not your friend. 🤢

- Draft PRs mean they're not ready. CI checks should pass before asking for a review, but don't sweat it too much if it fails once in a while. Just ping us on Discord or the PR if you're stuck. 

- Titles and commit messages: Use Conventional Commits (type(scope): description). Add a `!` if it's a breaking change and explain how to migrate. 

- Change Ownership: This is big. You gotta know and justify every change you make, whether you wrote it yourself or AI helped. Read, understand, and test everything before you submit. 🧐

- AI Assistance: Sure, AI can help. But at the end of the day, you're the author. Review what it generates, edit it to fit the style, and make sure it works. No "AI did it" excuses for low-quality code.

- Before submitting a PR, double-check if there's an existing issue and read up on the codebase. The Contributor Book is your best friend here.

That's pretty much it! Good luck and remember: it's better to ask for help than to go ahead blindly.😄

Hey there! Welcome aboard! Here's what you need to know, pretty much in no particular order and with a bunch of side remarks... 😄

**Issue**:
- Use the issue tracker to give feedback, share tips, and talk about how you use Arthas for effective troubleshooting. :bowtie:
- Got to https://github.com/alibaba/arthas/issues for all the feedback action.

**Docs**:
- Docs are under `site/docs/`. If you want to update them, submit a PR.

**Online Tutorials**:
- Check the README.MD in the killercoda branch.

**Dev Stuff**:
- Arthas runs on JDK6+ but use JDK8 for compiling. Stay away from higher versions, they'll give you headaches. Check here: https://github.com/alibaba/arthas/tree/master/.github/workflows
- For jfr issues, use `8u262` or later versions of openjdk8 or zulu jdk8. Read more here: https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/jdk8u-dev/2020-July/012143.html

**Local Installation**:
- Note: After modding `arthas-vmtool` related codes, you gotta manually copy the results to the `lib/` path in this repo. Auto-copying doesn't happen.
- Use `as-package.sh` to package; it auto-installs the latest Arthas to `~/.arthas` and auto-loads the latest version when debugging.
- For faster local iteration, run `./as-package.sh --fast` (skips `clean` and `site` module's doc build). Rebuild docs by running without `--fast` or use `./mvnw clean package -DskipTests -P full`.
- To build jni, you need a cpp compiling env. On a Mac, install xcode; on Windows, install gcc.
- When using `as.sh`, it fetches the latest version under `~/.arthas/lib`. `as-package.sh` gets the version from `pom.xml` and appends the current timestamp, e.g., `3.0.5.20180917161808`.
- You can also use `./mvnw clean package -DskipTests`, which generates a `zip` under `packaging/target/`. But remember, `as.sh` starts by loading the version from `~/.arthas/lib`.

**Start Arthas in Specified Version**:
- When you have multiple versions, use `--use-version` to specify which Arthas version to start debugging with.
- Use `--versions` to list all available versions.

**Debug**:
- You can debug Arthas in IDEA.

**Full Packaging**:
- For packaging the whole project, you need to execute some commands. ... (details a bit fuzzy here 😅)

**Release Steps** (side remark: not super organized here, but hey, it works):
- If arthas-vmtool has updates, manually trigger the action to build and commit the new dynamic library file to the lib directory: https://github.com/alibaba/arthas/actions/workflows/build-vmtool.yaml
- Modify versions in `as.sh`, `Bootstrap.java`, and Dockerfile. Update local `settings.xml` too.
- Run `gpg --sign /tmp/2.txt` to start the gpg background process (important for successful builds).
- Run `mvn clean deploy -DskipTests -P full -P release`.
- Go to https://central.sonatype.com/publishing/deployments and Publish your Deployment.
- After publishing, check if it's synced to the repo here: https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/com/taobao/artha

Hope this helps and isn't too confusing! 😂

*Hey there, new guy! Got a ton of stuff to dive into with Selenium. Here's the skinny:*

- **Bug Reports**: *Yo, if you see a bug, head to the Issue tracker, not for support tho. Make sure you give clear steps to repro the issue, what you get vs what you expected. Slack for bigger ideas or non-tech stuff.* 🐛

- *Use AI tools to help write code, tests, and docs, but **you** gotta be the author. Read, review, and understand everything. Must be able to explain without referring back to the tool.*

- *Don’t use `Co-Authored-By` tags for AI tools. Just mention it in the PR description.*

- *AI assistance shouldn’t lower the quality bar. Must include tests where possible. No low-effort PRs.*

- *You’re still responsible for copyright and licensing. Use AI tools responsibly.*

### Step 1: Fork & Clone
- *Just fork it on GitHub and clone it locally. Use `--depth 1` for a quick clone since the repo is over 2GB. Dependencies are in the `_third-party/_` dir.*

*Good luck, and don't forget to check out the `good first issue` tags for some easy wins! 😄*

So, y'know how Apollo works? It's like a big club where anyone can join if they're into the project. Here's how it goes down:

- **Users**: Just use the project. No special stuff needed. They're super important 'cause without them, the project's pointless.

- **Contributors**: These are people who actually do stuff. Like merge PRs (Pull Requests), answer tech questions, test stuff, review PRs, improve docs, find/fix bugs, write articles about the code, talk about Apollo at conferences, and join in on feature discussions.

  - To be a Contributor, you need to merge at least one PR or do any of the above.

- **Members**: These are Contributors who've really stepped up and done a bunch o' stuff. They get added to the Apollo org on GitHub.

  - To become a Member, you gotta have:
    - 2FA (Two-Factor Auth) on GitHub
    - Made multiple contributions (PRs, comments, etc.)
    - Submit a request in the apollo-community repo
    - Get sponsored by 2 PMC members with a `+1`

  - As a Member, you get to triage (sort out) issues and PRs, and you're responsible for your own code after it's accepted.

- **Committers**: These are big players who've shown they’re really dedicated to the project. They’re selected by the PMCs for their top-notch work.

  - To be a Committer, you gotta:
    - Show good sense in PR reviews
    - Show deep understanding of Apollo by finishing tasks:
      - 2+ Medium-difficulty tasks
      - 1+ Hard-difficulty task
    - Get nominated by a PMC member with more `+1s` than `-1s`

  - As a Committer, you get write access, control code quality, guiding contributors, and join design discussions.

- **Project Management Committee (PMC)**: This is the core management team. They handle big decisions and keep everything running smoothly.

  - To join the PMC, you get invited and then there's a vote by existing PMCs.

  - As a PMC member, you handle security issues, nominate new committers and PMCs, vote on new members, and make big decisions for Apollo.

So, that's the gist of it. Crazy, right? But hey, it's all about contributing and moving up through the ranks!

Hey there,

So you want to contribute? Cool! Here's how you do it:

- First, **bug reports** and **feature requests**? Use GitHub Issues. Make sure to check existing issues so you don’t post a dup. 😅
- **Security vulns**? Don't post publically. See `security.md`. 🚨

You'll need these tools:
- **JDK 25** (don't forget)
- **Maven 3.9.x** (recent release, pls)
- **Docker** (for Testcontainers tests)

Node.js and Yarn are handled by Maven build, so you're good unless you're working directly on the UI. 🤓

**Repo Layout**:
- Modules: `common` (shared code), `dao` (persistence), `rule-engine` (rule engine), `transport` (MQTT, HTTP, etc.), `integration` (3rd party integrations), `edqs` (Entity Data Query Service), `application` (main app), `ui-ngx` (Angular UI), `msa` (microservices), `rest-client` (Java REST), `netty-mqtt` (MQTT client), `tools` (dev tools), `packaging` (deb/rpm/zip), `monitoring` (monitoring service), `migrator` (data migration), `report` (report gen).

**Building**: 
- Use `-Dpkg.skip=true` to skip deb/rpm/zip stuff. Handy for dev.
- `-Dpkg.skip.bootjar=true` skips the boot jar, `-Dpkg.skip.deb=true` avoids the deb, `-Dpkg.skip.rpm=true` skips the rpm, `-Dpkg.skip.zip=true` skips the zip. 
- If you're building `msa/*` Docker images or running the black-box suite, you need the `.deb`.

Building UI alone:
- Go to `ui-ngx`

**Running tests**:
- Use `-pl/-am` to scope build for a single module.
- Full backend test suite in parallel? Use `mvn verify -Dsurefire.forkCount=10 -Dsurefire.threadCount=2 -Dmaven.test.failure.ignore=true`
- For a small change, just run `mvn test` on the module you touched.

### Docker API version issue:
- If `dao` or `application` tests fail with "unsupported Docker API version," adjust Docker's API version in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` or via Docker Desktop's UI. Restart Docker after.

Hope this helps! 😄

Hey there! 📝 So, this is kinda how you contribute to the RocketMQ project, super messy notes version:

- Contributions welcome! 🎉 Small fixes or huge features, we love it all.
- Aim for high-quality code with good docs. Also, appreciate contributions to the ecosystem and integration tools.
- Not just code! Docs, integrations, etc., are also super valuable.

### Reading:
- Contributors Tech Guide (definitely read this)
- Get involved! (yeah, you should)

### Contributing Code:
- For non-trivial changes, add some unit tests.
- New features/APIs? Start a RIP (RFC 🤭) and get consensus first.
- If we're slow to respond, just give us a nudge, we sometimes drop the ball.

#### Squashing Commits:
1. Check your commit history: `git log`
2. Squash 'em: `git rebase -i HEAD~N`
3. Pick first commit
4. Change others to "fixup"
5. Force push to overwrite: `git push -u origin ROCKETMQ-9999 --force`
6. Now you got one commit, super tidy for review.

More details on squashing? Stackoverflow has ya covered. 🦾

### Becoming a Committer:
- Show us your skills with a series of contributions.
- Good taste and interest in the project go a long way.
- Existing committers can guide you through becoming one.

### Contribution Points:
- Wiki & JavaDoc
- SDKs: C++, .Net, Php, Python, Go, Node.js
- Connectors

#### Prerequisites (read this part carefully):
- **Readability**: Must have Javadoc, extra doc for important methods.
- **Testability**: At least 80% unit test coverage.
- **Maintainability**: Follow checkstyle, update at least every 3 months.
- **Deployability**: Deploy into maven repo, please! 🙏

Okay, so here's how we do a release for OpenZipkin, super chaotic style:

- First up, make sure all dependencies are current or write down why they're not. Security workflow is a big deal here. Needs to be clean.

- Before you start, announce on gitter that you're doing a release. This is a 10-minute window, so no one should push to master. If they do, and something breaks, you gotta redo the release tag. Oops.

- Git tag: Use `release-MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. Example: `git tag release-1.18.1 && git push origin release-1.18.1`. Simple enough.

- CI time: Wait for the magic to happen. `release-MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` triggers `build-bin/maven/maven_release`. It makes commits, tags, and bumps the version. The `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` tag then triggers `build-bin/deploy`:
  * Jars go to Sonatype first, then to Maven Central.
  * Javadoc goes to https://zipkin.io/brave/[version].
  * Docker images are pushed to registries.

- Quick note: Maven search takes longer than direct links. So, use direct links if you can.

- **Credentials:** The release uses creds for stuff. If you see '401 unauthorized', check [.github/workflows/deploy.yml] and the org secrets. (Side note: totally annoying when these break.)

- Snapshots: If you need to test creds, try a manual snapshot deploy from your laptop. This checks if your creds are valid without messing everything up.

- If CI is down or just not working, remember, this is just a normal Maven project. You can do it manually. But, if Sonatype is down, good luck with that.

So, here's how you do stuff around here:

- We got a code of conduct, so don't be a jerk. Got questions? Hit up Discord or make an issue.

- When you fix something, focus on one thing. Don't go messing with whitespace and fixing bugs at the same time. Keep it tight, minimal changes is the goal.
